text: She went so far that the boys actually began to mock at him on her account and taunt him with being a “mother’s darling.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But the boy could take his own part.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He was a resolute boy, “tremendously strong,” as was rumored in his class, and soon proved to be the fact; he was agile, strong-willed, and of an audacious and enterprising temper.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He was good at lessons, and there was a rumor in the school that he could beat the teacher, Dardanelov, at arithmetic and universal history.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Though he looked down upon every one, he was a good comrade and not supercilious.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He accepted his schoolfellows’ respect as his due, but was friendly with them.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Above all, he knew where to draw the line.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He could restrain himself on occasion, and in his relations with the teachers he never overstepped that last mystic limit beyond which a prank becomes an unpardonable breach of discipline.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But he was as fond of mischief on every possible occasion as the smallest boy in the school, and not so much for the sake of mischief as for creating a sensation, inventing something, something effective and conspicuous.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He was extremely vain.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He knew how to make even his mother give way to him; he was almost despotic in his control of her.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: She gave way to him, oh, she had given way to him for years.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The one thought unendurable to her was that her boy had no great love for her.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: She was always fancying that Kolya was “unfeeling” to her, and at times, dissolving into hysterical tears, she used to reproach him with his coldness.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The boy disliked this, and the more demonstrations of feeling were demanded of him the more he seemed intentionally to avoid them.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Yet it was not intentional on his part but instinctive—it was his character.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: His mother was mistaken; he was very fond of her.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He only disliked “sheepish sentimentality,” as he expressed it in his schoolboy language.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: There was a bookcase in the house containing a few books that had been his father’s.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya was fond of reading, and had read several of them by himself.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: His mother did not mind that and only wondered sometimes at seeing the boy stand for hours by the bookcase poring over a book instead of going to play.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: And in that way Kolya read some things unsuitable for his age.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Though the boy, as a rule, knew where to draw the line in his mischief, he had of late begun to play pranks that caused his mother serious alarm.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: It is true there was nothing vicious in what he did, but a wild mad recklessness.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: It happened that July, during the summer holidays, that the mother and son went to another district, forty-five miles away, to spend a week with a distant relation, whose husband was an official at the railway station (the very station, the nearest one to our town, from which a month later Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov set off for Moscow).

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: There Kolya began by carefully investigating every detail connected with the railways, knowing that he could impress his schoolfellows when he got home with his newly acquired knowledge.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But there happened to be some other boys in the place with whom he soon made friends.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Some of them were living at the station, others in the neighborhood; there were six or seven of them, all between twelve and fifteen, and two of them came from our town.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The boys played together, and on the fourth or fifth day of Kolya’s stay at the station, a mad bet was made by the foolish boys.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya, who was almost the youngest of the party and rather looked down upon by the others in consequence, was moved by vanity or by reckless bravado to bet them two roubles that he would lie down between the rails at night when the eleven o’clock train was due, and would lie there without moving while the train rolled over him at full speed.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: It is true they made a preliminary investigation, from which it appeared that it was possible to lie so flat between the rails that the train could pass over without touching, but to lie there was no joke!

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya maintained stoutly that he would.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: At first they laughed at him, called him a little liar, a braggart, but that only egged him on.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: What piqued him most was that these boys of fifteen turned up their noses at him too superciliously, and were at first disposed to treat him as “a small boy,” not fit to associate with them, and that was an unendurable insult.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: And so it was resolved to go in the evening, half a mile from the station, so that the train might have time to get up full speed after leaving the station.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The boys assembled.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: It was a pitch-dark night without a moon.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: At the time fixed, Kolya lay down between the rails.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The five others who had taken the bet waited among the bushes below the embankment, their hearts beating with suspense, which was followed by alarm and remorse.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: At last they heard in the distance the rumble of the train leaving the station.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Two red lights gleamed out of the darkness; the monster roared as it approached.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Run, run away from the rails,” the boys cried to Kolya from the bushes, breathless with terror.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But it was too late: the train darted up and flew past.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The boys rushed to Kolya.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He lay without moving.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: They began pulling at him, lifting him up.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He suddenly got up and walked away without a word.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Then he explained that he had lain there as though he were insensible to frighten them, but the fact was that he really had lost consciousness, as he confessed long after to his mother.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: In this way his reputation as “a desperate character,” was established for ever.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He returned home to the station as white as a sheet.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Next day he had a slight attack of nervous fever, but he was in high spirits and well pleased with himself.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The incident did not become known at once, but when they came back to the town it penetrated to the school and even reached the ears of the masters.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But then Kolya’s mother hastened to entreat the masters on her boy’s behalf, and in the end Dardanelov, a respected and influential teacher, exerted himself in his favor, and the affair was ignored.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Dardanelov was a middle-aged bachelor, who had been passionately in love with Madame Krassotkin for many years past, and had once already, about a year previously, ventured, trembling with fear and the delicacy of his sentiments, to offer her most respectfully his hand in marriage.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But she refused him resolutely, feeling that to accept him would be an act of treachery to her son, though Dardanelov had, to judge from certain mysterious symptoms, reason for believing that he was not an object of aversion to the charming but too chaste and tender-hearted widow.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya’s mad prank seemed to have broken the ice, and Dardanelov was rewarded for his intercession by a suggestion of hope.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The suggestion, it is true, was a faint one, but then Dardanelov was such a paragon of purity and delicacy that it was enough for the time being to make him perfectly happy.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He was fond of the boy, though he would have felt it beneath him to try and win him over, and was severe and strict with him in class.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya, too, kept him at a respectful distance.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He learned his lessons perfectly; he was second in his class, was reserved with Dardanelov, and the whole class firmly believed that Kolya was so good at universal history that he could “beat” even Dardanelov.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya did indeed ask him the question, “Who founded Troy?” to which Dardanelov had made a very vague reply, referring to the movements and migrations of races, to the remoteness of the period, to the mythical legends.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But the question, “Who had founded Troy?” that is, what individuals, he could not answer, and even for some reason regarded the question as idle and frivolous.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But the boys remained convinced that Dardanelov did not know who founded Troy.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya had read of the founders of Troy in Smaragdov, whose history was among the books in his father’s bookcase.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: In the end all the boys became interested in the question, who it was that had founded Troy, but Krassotkin would not tell his secret, and his reputation for knowledge remained unshaken.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: After the incident on the railway a certain change came over Kolya’s attitude to his mother.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: When Anna Fyodorovna (Madame Krassotkin) heard of her son’s exploit, she almost went out of her mind with horror.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: She had such terrible attacks of hysterics, lasting with intervals for several days, that Kolya, seriously alarmed at last, promised on his honor that such pranks should never be repeated.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He swore on his knees before the holy image, and swore by the memory of his father, at Madame Krassotkin’s instance, and the “manly” Kolya burst into tears like a boy of six.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: And all that day the mother and son were constantly rushing into each other’s arms sobbing.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Next day Kolya woke up as “unfeeling” as before, but he had become more silent, more modest, sterner, and more thoughtful.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Six weeks later, it is true, he got into another scrape, which even brought his name to the ears of our Justice of the Peace, but it was a scrape of quite another kind, amusing, foolish, and he did not, as it turned out, take the leading part in it, but was only implicated in it.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But of this later.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: His mother still fretted and trembled, but the more uneasy she became, the greater were the hopes of Dardanelov.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: It must be noted that Kolya understood and divined what was in Dardanelov’s heart and, of course, despised him profoundly for his “feelings”; he had in the past been so tactless as to show this contempt before his mother, hinting vaguely that he knew what Dardanelov was after.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But from the time of the railway incident his behavior in this respect also was changed; he did not allow himself the remotest allusion to the subject and began to speak more respectfully of Dardanelov before his mother, which the sensitive woman at once appreciated with boundless gratitude.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But at the slightest mention of Dardanelov by a visitor in Kolya’s presence, she would flush as pink as a rose.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: At such moments Kolya would either stare out of the window scowling, or would investigate the state of his boots, or would shout angrily for “Perezvon,” the big, shaggy, mangy dog, which he had picked up a month before, brought home, and kept for some reason secretly indoors, not showing him to any of his schoolfellows.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He bullied him frightfully, teaching him all sorts of tricks, so that the poor dog howled for him whenever he was absent at school, and when he came in, whined with delight, rushed about as if he were crazy, begged, lay down on the ground pretending to be dead, and so on; in fact, showed all the tricks he had taught him, not at the word of command, but simply from the zeal of his excited and grateful heart.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: I have forgotten, by the way, to mention that Kolya Krassotkin was the boy stabbed with a penknife by the boy already known to the reader as the son of Captain Snegiryov.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Ilusha had been defending his father when the schoolboys jeered at him, shouting the nickname “wisp of tow.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: And so on that frosty, snowy, and windy day in November, Kolya Krassotkin was sitting at home.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: It was Sunday and there was no school.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: It had just struck eleven, and he particularly wanted to go out “on very urgent business,” but he was left alone in charge of the house, for it so happened that all its elder inmates were absent owing to a sudden and singular event.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Madame Krassotkin had let two little rooms, separated from the rest of the house by a passage, to a doctor’s wife with her two small children.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: This lady was the same age as Anna Fyodorovna, and a great friend of hers.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Her husband, the doctor, had taken his departure twelve months before, going first to Orenburg and then to Tashkend, and for the last six months she had not heard a word from him.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Had it not been for her friendship with Madame Krassotkin, which was some consolation to the forsaken lady, she would certainly have completely dissolved away in tears.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: And now, to add to her misfortunes, Katerina, her only servant, was suddenly moved the evening before to announce, to her mistress’s amazement, that she proposed to bring a child into the world before morning.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: It seemed almost miraculous to every one that no one had noticed the probability of it before.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The astounded doctor’s wife decided to move Katerina while there was still time to an establishment in the town kept by a midwife for such emergencies.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: As she set great store by her servant, she promptly carried out this plan and remained there looking after her.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: By the morning all Madame Krassotkin’s friendly sympathy and energy were called upon to render assistance and appeal to some one for help in the case.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: So both the ladies were absent from home, the Krassotkins’ servant, Agafya, had gone out to the market, and Kolya was thus left for a time to protect and look after “the kids,” that is, the son and daughter of the doctor’s wife, who were left alone.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya was not afraid of taking care of the house, besides he had Perezvon, who had been told to lie flat, without moving, under the bench in the hall.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Every time Kolya, walking to and fro through the rooms, came into the hall, the dog shook his head and gave two loud and insinuating taps on the floor with his tail, but alas! the whistle did not sound to release him.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya looked sternly at the luckless dog, who relapsed again into obedient rigidity.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The one thing that troubled Kolya was “the kids. He looked, of course, with the utmost scorn on Katerina’s unexpected adventure, but he was very fond of the bereaved “kiddies,” and had already taken them a picture-book.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Nastya, the elder, a girl of eight, could read, and Kostya, the boy, aged seven, was very fond of being read to by her.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Krassotkin could, of course, have provided more diverting entertainment for them.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He could have made them stand side by side and played soldiers with them, or sent them hiding all over the house.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He had done so more than once before and was not above doing it, so much so that a report once spread at school that Krassotkin played horses with the little lodgers at home, prancing with his head on one side like a trace-horse.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But Krassotkin haughtily parried this thrust, pointing out that to play horses with boys of one’s own age, boys of thirteen, would certainly be disgraceful “at this date,” but that he did it for the sake of “the kids” because he liked them, and no one had a right to call him to account for his feelings.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The two “kids” adored him.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But on this occasion he was in no mood for games.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He had very important business of his own before him, something almost mysterious.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Meanwhile time was passing and Agafya, with whom he could have left the children, would not come back from market.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He had several times already crossed the passage, opened the door of the lodgers’ room and looked anxiously at “the kids” who were sitting over the book, as he had bidden them.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Every time he opened the door they grinned at him, hoping he would come in and would do something delightful and amusing.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But Kolya was bothered and did not go in.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: At last it struck eleven and he made up his mind, once for all, that if that “damned” Agafya did not come back within ten minutes he should go out without waiting for her, making “the kids” promise, of course, to be brave when he was away, not to be naughty, not to cry from fright.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: With this idea he put on his wadded winter overcoat with its catskin fur collar, slung his satchel round his shoulder, and, regardless of his mother’s constantly reiterated entreaties that he would always put on goloshes in such cold weather, he looked at them contemptuously as he crossed the hall and went out with only his boots on.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Perezvon, seeing him in his outdoor clothes, began tapping nervously, yet vigorously, on the floor with his tail.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Twitching all over, he even uttered a plaintive whine.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But Kolya, seeing his dog’s passionate excitement, decided that it was a breach of discipline, kept him for another minute under the bench, and only when he had opened the door into the passage, whistled for him.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The dog leapt up like a mad creature and rushed bounding before him rapturously.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya opened the door to peep at “the kids. They were both sitting as before at the table, not reading but warmly disputing about something. The children often argued together about various exciting problems of life, and Nastya, being the elder, always got the best of it. If Kostya did not agree with her, he almost always appealed to Kolya Krassotkin, and his verdict was regarded as infallible by both of them. This time the “kids’” discussion rather interested Krassotkin, and he stood still in the passage to listen.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The children saw he was listening and that made them dispute with even greater energy.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I shall never, never believe,” Nastya prattled, “that the old women find babies among the cabbages in the kitchen-garden. It’s winter now and there are no cabbages, and so the old woman couldn’t have taken Katerina a daughter.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya whistled to himself.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Or perhaps they do bring babies from somewhere, but only to those who are married.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kostya stared at Nastya and listened, pondering profoundly.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Nastya, how silly you are!” he said at last, firmly and calmly.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “How can Katerina have a baby when she isn’t married?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Nastya was exasperated.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You know nothing about it,” she snapped irritably.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Perhaps she has a husband, only he is in prison, so now she’s got a baby.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “But is her husband in prison?” the matter-of-fact Kostya inquired gravely.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Or, I tell you what,” Nastya interrupted impulsively, completely rejecting and forgetting her first hypothesis.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “She hasn’t a husband, you are right there, but she wants to be married, and so she’s been thinking of getting married, and thinking and thinking of it till now she’s got it, that is, not a husband but a baby.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Well, perhaps so,” Kostya agreed, entirely vanquished.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “But you didn’t say so before. So how could I tell?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Come, kiddies,” said Kolya, stepping into the room.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You’re terrible people, I see.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “And Perezvon with you!” grinned Kostya, and began snapping his fingers and calling Perezvon.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I am in a difficulty, kids,” Krassotkin began solemnly, “and you must help me. Agafya must have broken her leg, since she has not turned up till now, that’s certain. I must go out. Will you let me go?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The children looked anxiously at one another.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Their smiling faces showed signs of uneasiness, but they did not yet fully grasp what was expected of them.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You won’t be naughty while I am gone? You won’t climb on the cupboard and break your legs? You won’t be frightened alone and cry?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: A look of profound despondency came into the children’s faces.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “And I could show you something as a reward, a little copper cannon which can be fired with real gunpowder.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The children’s faces instantly brightened.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Show us the cannon,” said Kostya, beaming all over.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Krassotkin put his hand in his satchel, and pulling out a little bronze cannon stood it on the table.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Ah, you are bound to ask that! Look, it’s on wheels. He rolled the toy on along the table. “And it can be fired off, too. It can be loaded with shot and fired off.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “And it could kill any one?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “It can kill any one; you’ve only got to aim at anybody,” and Krassotkin explained where the powder had to be put, where the shot should be rolled in, showing a tiny hole like a touch-hole, and told them that it kicked when it was fired.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The children listened with intense interest.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: What particularly struck their imagination was that the cannon kicked.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “And have you got any powder?

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Nastya inquired.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Yes.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Show us the powder, too,” she drawled with a smile of entreaty.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Krassotkin dived again into his satchel and pulled out a small flask containing a little real gunpowder.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He had some shot, too, in a screw of paper.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He even uncorked the flask and shook a little powder into the palm of his hand.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “One has to be careful there’s no fire about, or it would blow up and kill us all,” Krassotkin warned them sensationally.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The children gazed at the powder with an awe-stricken alarm that only intensified their enjoyment.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But Kostya liked the shot better.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “And does the shot burn?” he inquired.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “No, it doesn’t.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Give me a little shot,” he asked in an imploring voice.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I’ll give you a little shot; here, take it, but don’t show it to your mother till I come back, or she’ll be sure to think it’s gunpowder, and will die of fright and give you a thrashing.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Mother never does whip us,” Nastya observed at once.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I know, I only said it to finish the sentence. And don’t you ever deceive your mother except just this once, until I come back. And so, kiddies, can I go out? You won’t be frightened and cry when I’m gone?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “We sha—all cry,” drawled Kostya, on the verge of tears already.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “We shall cry, we shall be sure to cry,” Nastya chimed in with timid haste.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Oh, children, children, how fraught with peril are your years! There’s no help for it, chickens, I shall have to stay with you I don’t know how long. And time is passing, time is passing, oogh!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Tell Perezvon to pretend to be dead!

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kostya begged.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “There’s no help for it, we must have recourse to Perezvon.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Ici, Perezvon.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: And Kolya began giving orders to the dog, who performed all his tricks.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He was a rough-haired dog, of medium size, with a coat of a sort of lilac-gray color.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He was blind in his right eye, and his left ear was torn.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He whined and jumped, stood and walked on his hind legs, lay on his back with his paws in the air, rigid as though he were dead.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: While this last performance was going on, the door opened and Agafya, Madame Krassotkin’s servant, a stout woman of forty, marked with small-pox, appeared in the doorway.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: She had come back from market and had a bag full of provisions in her hand.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Holding up the bag of provisions in her left hand she stood still to watch the dog.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Though Kolya had been so anxious for her return, he did not cut short the performance, and after keeping Perezvon dead for the usual time, at last he whistled to him.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The dog jumped up and began bounding about in his joy at having done his duty.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Only think, a dog!

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Agafya observed sententiously.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Why are you late, female?” asked Krassotkin sternly.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Female, indeed! Go on with you, you brat.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Brat?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Yes, a brat. What is it to you if I’m late; if I’m late, you may be sure I have good reason,” muttered Agafya, busying herself about the stove, without a trace of anger or displeasure in her voice.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: She seemed quite pleased, in fact, to enjoy a skirmish with her merry young master.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Listen, you frivolous young woman,” Krassotkin began, getting up from the sofa, “can you swear by all you hold sacred in the world and something else besides, that you will watch vigilantly over the kids in my absence? I am going out.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “And what am I going to swear for?” laughed Agafya.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I shall look after them without that.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “No, you must swear on your eternal salvation. Else I shan’t go.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Well, don’t then. What does it matter to me? It’s cold out; stay at home.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Kids,” Kolya turned to the children, “this woman will stay with you till I come back or till your mother comes, for she ought to have been back long ago. She will give you some lunch, too. You’ll give them something, Agafya, won’t you?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “That I can do.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Good-by, chickens, I go with my heart at rest. And you, granny,” he added gravely, in an undertone, as he passed Agafya, “I hope you’ll spare their tender years and not tell them any of your old woman’s nonsense about Katerina. Ici, Perezvon!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Get along with you!” retorted Agafya, really angry this time.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Ridiculous boy! You want a whipping for saying such things, that’s what you want!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But Kolya did not hear her.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: At last he could go out.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: As he went out at the gate he looked round him, shrugged up his shoulders, and saying “It is freezing,” went straight along the street and turned off to the right towards the market-place.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: When he reached the last house but one before the market-place he stopped at the gate, pulled a whistle out of his pocket, and whistled with all his might as though giving a signal.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He had not to wait more than a minute before a rosy-cheeked boy of about eleven, wearing a warm, neat and even stylish coat, darted out to meet him.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: This was Smurov, a boy in the preparatory class (two classes below Kolya Krassotkin), son of a well-to-do official.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Apparently he was forbidden by his parents to associate with Krassotkin, who was well known to be a desperately naughty boy, so Smurov was obviously slipping out on the sly.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He was—if the reader has not forgotten—one of the group of boys who two months before had thrown stones at Ilusha.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He was the one who told Alyosha Karamazov about Ilusha.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I’ve been waiting for you for the last hour, Krassotkin,” said Smurov stolidly, and the boys strode towards the market-place.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I am late,” answered Krassotkin.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I was detained by circumstances. You won’t be thrashed for coming with me?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Come, I say, I’m never thrashed! And you’ve got Perezvon with you?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Yes.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You’re taking him, too?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Yes.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Ah! if it were only Zhutchka!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “That’s impossible. Zhutchka’s non-existent. Zhutchka is lost in the mists of obscurity.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Ah! couldn’t we do this? Smurov suddenly stood still. “You see Ilusha says that Zhutchka was a shaggy, grayish, smoky-looking dog like Perezvon. Couldn’t you tell him this is Zhutchka, and he might believe you?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Boy, shun a lie, that’s one thing; even with a good object—that’s another. Above all, I hope you’ve not told them anything about my coming.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Heaven forbid! I know what I am about. But you won’t comfort him with Perezvon,” said Smurov, with a sigh.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You know his father, the captain, ‘the wisp of tow,’ told us that he was going to bring him a real mastiff pup, with a black nose, to-day. He thinks that would comfort Ilusha; but I doubt it.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “And how is Ilusha?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Ah, he is bad, very bad! I believe he’s in consumption: he is quite conscious, but his breathing! His breathing’s gone wrong. The other day he asked to have his boots on to be led round the room. He tried to walk, but he couldn’t stand. ‘Ah, I told you before, father,’ he said, ‘that those boots were no good. I could never walk properly in them. He fancied it was his boots that made him stagger, but it was simply weakness, really. He won’t live another week. Herzenstube is looking after him. Now they are rich again—they’ve got heaps of money.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “They are rogues.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Who are rogues?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Doctors and the whole crew of quacks collectively, and also, of course, individually. I don’t believe in medicine. It’s a useless institution. I mean to go into all that. But what’s that sentimentality you’ve got up there? The whole class seems to be there every day.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Not the whole class: it’s only ten of our fellows who go to see him every day. There’s nothing in that.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “What I don’t understand in all this is the part that Alexey Karamazov is taking in it. His brother’s going to be tried to-morrow or next day for such a crime, and yet he has so much time to spend on sentimentality with boys.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “There’s no sentimentality about it. You are going yourself now to make it up with Ilusha.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Make it up with him? What an absurd expression! But I allow no one to analyze my actions.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “And how pleased Ilusha will be to see you!

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He has no idea that you are coming.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Why was it, why was it you wouldn’t come all this time?

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Smurov cried with sudden warmth.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “My dear boy, that’s my business, not yours. I am going of myself because I choose to, but you’ve all been hauled there by Alexey Karamazov—there’s a difference, you know. And how do you know? I may not be going to make it up at all. It’s a stupid expression.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “It’s not Karamazov at all; it’s not his doing. Our fellows began going there of themselves. Of course, they went with Karamazov at first. And there’s been nothing of that sort—no silliness. First one went, and then another. His father was awfully pleased to see us. You know he will simply go out of his mind if Ilusha dies. He sees that Ilusha’s dying. And he seems so glad we’ve made it up with Ilusha. Ilusha asked after you, that was all. He just asks and says no more. His father will go out of his mind or hang himself. He behaved like a madman before. You know he is a very decent man. We made a mistake then. It’s all the fault of that murderer who beat him then.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Karamazov’s a riddle to me all the same. I might have made his acquaintance long ago, but I like to have a proper pride in some cases. Besides, I have a theory about him which I must work out and verify.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya subsided into dignified silence.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Smurov, too, was silent.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Smurov, of course, worshiped Krassotkin and never dreamed of putting himself on a level with him.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Now he was tremendously interested at Kolya’s saying that he was “going of himself” to see Ilusha.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He felt that there must be some mystery in Kolya’s suddenly taking it into his head to go to him that day.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: They crossed the market-place, in which at that hour were many loaded wagons from the country and a great number of live fowls.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The market women were selling rolls, cottons and threads, etc., in their booths.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: These Sunday markets were naïvely called “fairs” in the town, and there were many such fairs in the year.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Perezvon ran about in the wildest spirits, sniffing about first one side, then the other.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: When he met other dogs they zealously smelt each other over according to the rules of canine etiquette.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I like to watch such realistic scenes, Smurov,” said Kolya suddenly.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Have you noticed how dogs sniff at one another when they meet? It seems to be a law of their nature.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Yes; it’s a funny habit.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “No, it’s not funny; you are wrong there. There’s nothing funny in nature, however funny it may seem to man with his prejudices. If dogs could reason and criticize us they’d be sure to find just as much that would be funny to them, if not far more, in the social relations of men, their masters—far more, indeed. I repeat that, because I am convinced that there is far more foolishness among us. That’s Rakitin’s idea—a remarkable idea. I am a Socialist, Smurov.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “And what is a Socialist?” asked Smurov.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “That’s when all are equal and all have property in common, there are no marriages, and every one has any religion and laws he likes best, and all the rest of it. You are not old enough to understand that yet. It’s cold, though.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Yes, twelve degrees of frost. Father looked at the thermometer just now.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Have you noticed, Smurov, that in the middle of winter we don’t feel so cold even when there are fifteen or eighteen degrees of frost as we do now, in the beginning of winter, when there is a sudden frost of twelve degrees, especially when there is not much snow. It’s because people are not used to it. Everything is habit with men, everything even in their social and political relations. Habit is the great motive-power. What a funny-looking peasant!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya pointed to a tall peasant, with a good-natured countenance in a long sheepskin coat, who was standing by his wagon, clapping together his hands, in their shapeless leather gloves, to warm them.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: His long fair beard was all white with frost.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “That peasant’s beard’s frozen,” Kolya cried in a loud provocative voice as he passed him.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Lots of people’s beards are frozen,” the peasant replied, calmly and sententiously.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Don’t provoke him,” observed Smurov.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “It’s all right; he won’t be cross; he’s a nice fellow. Good-by, Matvey.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Good-by.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Is your name Matvey?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Yes. Didn’t you know?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “No, I didn’t. It was a guess.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You don’t say so! You are a schoolboy, I suppose?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Yes.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You get whipped, I expect?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Nothing to speak of—sometimes.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Does it hurt?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Well, yes, it does.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Ech, what a life!

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The peasant heaved a sigh from the bottom of his heart.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Good-by, Matvey.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Good-by. You are a nice chap, that you are.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The boys went on.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “That was a nice peasant,” Kolya observed to Smurov.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I like talking to the peasants, and am always glad to do them justice.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Why did you tell a lie, pretending we are thrashed?” asked Smurov.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I had to say that to please him.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “How do you mean?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You know, Smurov, I don’t like being asked the same thing twice. I like people to understand at the first word. Some things can’t be explained. According to a peasant’s notions, schoolboys are whipped, and must be whipped. What would a schoolboy be if he were not whipped? And if I were to tell him we are not, he’d be disappointed. But you don’t understand that. One has to know how to talk to the peasants.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Only don’t tease them, please, or you’ll get into another scrape as you did about that goose.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “So you’re afraid?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Don’t laugh, Kolya. Of course I’m afraid. My father would be awfully cross. I am strictly forbidden to go out with you.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Don’t be uneasy, nothing will happen this time. Hallo, Natasha!” he shouted to a market woman in one of the booths.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Call me Natasha! What next! My name is Marya,” the middle-aged market woman shouted at him.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I am so glad it’s Marya. Good-by!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Ah, you young rascal! A brat like you to carry on so!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I’m in a hurry.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: I can’t stay now.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: You shall tell me next Sunday.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya waved his hand at her, as though she had attacked him and not he her.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I’ve nothing to tell you next Sunday. You set upon me, you impudent young monkey. I didn’t say anything,” bawled Marya.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You want a whipping, that’s what you want, you saucy jackanapes!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: There was a roar of laughter among the other market women round her.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Suddenly a man in a violent rage darted out from the arcade of shops close by.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He was a young man, not a native of the town, with dark, curly hair and a long, pale face, marked with smallpox.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He wore a long blue coat and a peaked cap, and looked like a merchant’s clerk.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He was in a state of stupid excitement and brandished his fist at Kolya.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I know you!” he cried angrily, “I know you!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya stared at him.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He could not recall when he could have had a row with the man.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But he had been in so many rows in the street that he could hardly remember them all.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Do you?” he asked sarcastically.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “I know you! I know you!” the man repeated idiotically.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “So much the better for you. Well, it’s time I was going. Good-by!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You are at your saucy pranks again?” cried the man.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You are at your saucy pranks again? I know, you are at it again!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “It’s not your business, brother, if I am at my saucy pranks again,” said Kolya, standing still and scanning him.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Not my business?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “No; it’s not your business.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Whose then? Whose then? Whose then?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “It’s Trifon Nikititch’s business, not yours.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “What Trifon Nikititch?” asked the youth, staring with loutish amazement at Kolya, but still as angry as ever.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya scanned him gravely.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Have you been to the Church of the Ascension?” he suddenly asked him, with stern emphasis.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “What Church of Ascension? What for? No, I haven’t,” said the young man, somewhat taken aback.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Do you know Sabaneyev?

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Kolya went on even more emphatically and even more severely.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “What Sabaneyev? No, I don’t know him.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Well then you can go to the devil,” said Kolya, cutting short the conversation; and turning sharply to the right he strode quickly on his way as though he disdained further conversation with a dolt who did not even know Sabaneyev.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Stop, heigh! What Sabaneyev?” the young man recovered from his momentary stupefaction and was as excited as before.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “What did he say?

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He turned to the market women with a silly stare.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The women laughed.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You can never tell what he’s after,” said one of them.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “What Sabaneyev is it he’s talking about?” the young man repeated, still furious and brandishing his right arm.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “It must be a Sabaneyev who worked for the Kuzmitchovs, that’s who it must be,” one of the women suggested.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The young man stared at her wildly.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “For the Kuzmitchovs?” repeated another woman.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “But his name wasn’t Trifon. His name’s Kuzma, not Trifon; but the boy said Trifon Nikititch, so it can’t be the same.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “His name is not Trifon and not Sabaneyev, it’s Tchizhov,” put in suddenly a third woman, who had hitherto been silent, listening gravely.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Alexey Ivanitch is his name. Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Not a doubt about it, it’s Tchizhov,” a fourth woman emphatically confirmed the statement.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The bewildered youth gazed from one to another.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “But what did he ask for, what did he ask for, good people?” he cried almost in desperation.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “‘Do you know Sabaneyev?’ says he. And who the devil’s to know who is Sabaneyev?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You’re a senseless fellow. I tell you it’s not Sabaneyev, but Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch Tchizhov, that’s who it is!” one of the women shouted at him impressively.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “What Tchizhov? Who is he? Tell me, if you know.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “That tall, sniveling fellow who used to sit in the market in the summer.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “And what’s your Tchizhov to do with me, good people, eh?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “How can I tell what he’s to do with you?” put in another.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You ought to know yourself what you want with him, if you make such a clamor about him. He spoke to you, he did not speak to us, you stupid. Don’t you really know him?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Know whom?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Tchizhov.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “The devil take Tchizhov and you with him. I’ll give him a hiding, that I will. He was laughing at me!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Will give Tchizhov a hiding! More likely he will give you one. You are a fool, that’s what you are!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Not Tchizhov, not Tchizhov, you spiteful, mischievous woman. I’ll give the boy a hiding. Catch him, catch him, he was laughing at me!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: The woman guffawed.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: But Kolya was by now a long way off, marching along with a triumphant air.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: Smurov walked beside him, looking round at the shouting group far behind.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He too was in high spirits, though he was still afraid of getting into some scrape in Kolya’s company.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “What Sabaneyev did you mean?” he asked Kolya, foreseeing what his answer would be.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “How do I know? Now there’ll be a hubbub among them all day. I like to stir up fools in every class of society. There’s another blockhead, that peasant there. You know, they say ‘there’s no one stupider than a stupid Frenchman,’ but a stupid Russian shows it in his face just as much. Can’t you see it all over his face that he is a fool, that peasant, eh?”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Let him alone, Kolya. Let’s go on.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Nothing could stop me, now I am once off. Hey, good morning, peasant!”

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: A sturdy-looking peasant, with a round, simple face and grizzled beard, who was walking by, raised his head and looked at the boy.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: He seemed not quite sober.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Good morning, if you are not laughing at me,” he said deliberately in reply.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “And if I am?” laughed Kolya.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “Well, a joke’s a joke. Laugh away. I don’t mind. There’s no harm in a joke.”

title: The Brothers Karamazov

title: The Brothers Karamazov
text: “You see, Karamazov, Ilusha came into the preparatory class last spring. Well, you know what our preparatory class is—a lot of small boys. They began teasing Ilusha at once. I am two classes higher up, and, of course, I only look on at them from a distance. I saw the boy was weak and small, but he wouldn’t give in to them; he fought with them. I saw he was proud, and his eyes were full of fire. I like children like that. And they teased him all the more. The worst of it was he was horribly dressed at the time, his breeches were too small for him, and there were holes in his boots. They worried him about it; they jeered at him. That I can’t stand. I stood up for him at once, and gave it to them hot. I beat them, but they adore me, do you know, Karamazov? Kolya boasted impulsively; “but I am always fond of children. I’ve two chickens in my hands at home now—that’s what detained me to-day. So they left off beating Ilusha and I took him under my protection. I saw the boy was proud. I tell you that, the boy was proud; but in the end he became slavishly devoted to me: he did my slightest bidding, obeyed me as though I were God, tried to copy me. In the intervals between the classes he used to run to me at once, and I’d go about with him. On Sundays, too. They always laugh when an older boy makes friends with a younger one like that; but that’s a prejudice. If it’s my fancy, that’s enough. I am teaching him, developing him. Why shouldn’t I develop him if I like him? Here you, Karamazov, have taken up with all these nestlings. I see you want to influence the younger generation—to develop them, to be of use to them, and I assure you this trait in your character, which I knew by hearsay, attracted me more than anything. Let us get to the point, though. I noticed that there was a sort of softness and sentimentality coming over the boy, and you know I have a positive hatred of this sheepish sentimentality, and I have had it from a baby. There were contradictions in him, too: he was proud, but he was slavishly devoted to me, and yet all at once his eyes would flash and he’d refuse to agree with me; he’d argue, fly into a rage. I used sometimes to propound certain ideas; I could see that it was not so much that he disagreed with the ideas, but that he was simply rebelling against me, because I was cool in responding to his endearments. And so, in order to train him properly, the tenderer he was, the colder I became. I did it on purpose: that was my idea. My object was to form his character, to lick him into shape, to make a man of him ... and besides ... no doubt, you understand me at a word. Suddenly I noticed for three days in succession he was downcast and dejected, not because of my coldness, but for something else, something more important. I wondered what the tragedy was. I have pumped him and found out that he had somehow got to know Smerdyakov, who was footman to your late father—it was before his death, of course—and he taught the little fool a silly trick—that is, a brutal, nasty trick. He told him to take a piece of bread, to stick a pin in it, and throw it to one of those hungry dogs who snap up anything without biting it, and then to watch and see what would happen. So they prepared a piece of bread like that and threw it to Zhutchka, that shaggy dog there’s been such a fuss about. The people of the house it belonged to never fed it at all, though it barked all day. (Do you like that stupid barking, Karamazov? I can’t stand it.) So it rushed at the bread, swallowed it, and began to squeal; it turned round and round and ran away, squealing as it ran out of sight. That was Ilusha’s own account of it. He confessed it to me, and cried bitterly. He hugged me, shaking all over. He kept on repeating ‘He ran away squealing’: the sight of that haunted him. He was tormented by remorse, I could see that. I took it seriously. I determined to give him a lesson for other things as well. So I must confess I wasn’t quite straightforward, and pretended to be more indignant perhaps than I was. ‘You’ve done a nasty thing,’ I said, ‘you are a scoundrel. I won’t tell of it, of course, but I shall have nothing more to do with you for a time. I’ll think it over and let you know through Smurov’—that’s the boy who’s just come with me; he’s always ready to do anything for me—‘whether I will have anything to do with you in the future or whether I give you up for good as a scoundrel. He was tremendously upset. I must own I felt I’d gone too far as I spoke, but there was no help for it. I did what I thought best at the time. A day or two after, I sent Smurov to tell him that I would not speak to him again. That’s what we call it when two schoolfellows refuse to have anything more to do with one another. Secretly I only meant to send him to Coventry for a few days and then, if I saw signs of repentance, to hold out my hand to him again. That was my intention. But what do you think happened? He heard Smurov’s message, his eyes flashed. ‘Tell Krassotkin from me,’ he cried, ‘that I will throw bread with pins to all the dogs—all—all of them! ‘So he’s going in for a little temper. We must smoke it out of him. And I began to treat him with contempt; whenever I met him I turned away or smiled sarcastically. And just then that affair with his father happened. You remember? You must realize that he was fearfully worked up by what had happened already. The boys, seeing I’d given him up, set on him and taunted him, shouting, ‘Wisp of tow, wisp of tow! And he had soon regular skirmishes with them, which I am very sorry for. They seem to have given him one very bad beating. One day he flew at them all as they were coming out of school. I stood a few yards off, looking on. And, I swear, I don’t remember that I laughed; it was quite the other way, I felt awfully sorry for him, in another minute I would have run up to take his part. But he suddenly met my eyes. I don’t know what he fancied; but he pulled out a penknife, rushed at me, and struck at my thigh, here in my right leg. I didn’t move. I don’t mind owning I am plucky sometimes, Karamazov. I simply looked at him contemptuously, as though to say, ‘This is how you repay all my kindness! Do it again, if you like, I’m at your service. But he didn’t stab me again; he broke down, he was frightened at what he had done, he threw away the knife, burst out crying, and ran away. I did not sneak on him, of course, and I made them all keep quiet, so it shouldn’t come to the ears of the masters. I didn’t even tell my mother till it had healed up. And the wound was a mere scratch. And then I heard that the same day he’d been throwing stones and had bitten your finger—but you understand now what a state he was in! Well, it can’t be helped: it was stupid of me not to come and forgive him—that is, to make it up with him—when he was taken ill. I am sorry for it now. But I had a special reason. So now I’ve told you all about it ... but I’m afraid it was stupid of me.”
