How delightful! The first time I met an example of this handwriting, I was positively astonished, and where do you think I chanced to find it? In Switzerland, of all places! Now that is an ordinary English hand. It can hardly be improved, it is so refined and exquisite—almost perfection. This is an example of another kind, a mixture of styles. The copy was given me by a French commercial traveller. It is founded on the English, but the downstrokes are a little blacker, and more marked. Notice that the oval has some slight modification—it is more rounded. This writing allows for flourishes; now a flourish is a dangerous thing! Its use requires such taste, but, if successful, what a distinction it gives to the whole! It results in an incomparable type—one to fall in love with!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Dear me! How you have gone into all the refinements and details of the question! Why, my dear fellow, you are not a caligraphist, you are an artist! Eh, Gania?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Wonderful!” said Gania.

title: The Idiot
text: “And he knows it too,” he added, with a sarcastic smile.

title: The Idiot
text: “You may smile,—but there’s a career in this,” said the general.

title: The Idiot
text: “You don’t know what a great personage I shall show this to, prince. Why, you can command a situation at thirty-five roubles per month to start with. However, it’s half-past twelve,” he concluded, looking at his watch; “so to business, prince, for I must be setting to work and shall not see you again today. Sit down a minute. I have told you that I cannot receive you myself very often, but I should like to be of some assistance to you, some small assistance, of a kind that would give you satisfaction. I shall find you a place in one of the State departments, an easy place—but you will require to be accurate. Now, as to your plans—in the house, or rather in the family of Gania here—my young friend, whom I hope you will know better—his mother and sister have prepared two or three rooms for lodgers, and let them to highly recommended young fellows, with board and attendance. I am sure Nina Alexandrovna will take you in on my recommendation. There you will be comfortable and well taken care of; for I do not think, prince, that you are the sort of man to be left to the mercy of Fate in a town like Petersburg. Nina Alexandrovna, Gania’s mother, and Varvara Alexandrovna, are ladies for whom I have the highest possible esteem and respect. Nina Alexandrovna is the wife of General Ardalion Alexandrovitch, my old brother in arms, with whom, I regret to say, on account of certain circumstances, I am no longer acquainted. I give you all this information, prince, in order to make it clear to you that I am personally recommending you to this family, and that in so doing, I am more or less taking upon myself to answer for you. The terms are most reasonable, and I trust that your salary will very shortly prove amply sufficient for your expenditure. Of course pocket-money is a necessity, if only a little; do not be angry, prince, if I strongly recommend you to avoid carrying money in your pocket. But as your purse is quite empty at the present moment, you must allow me to press these twenty-five roubles upon your acceptance, as something to begin with. Of course we will settle this little matter another time, and if you are the upright, honest man you look, I anticipate very little trouble between us on that score. Taking so much interest in you as you may perceive I do, I am not without my object, and you shall know it in good time. You see, I am perfectly candid with you. I hope, Gania, you have nothing to say against the prince’s taking up his abode in your house?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, on the contrary! my mother will be very glad,” said Gania, courteously and kindly.

title: The Idiot
text: “I think only one of your rooms is engaged as yet, is it not? That fellow Ferd-Ferd—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Ferdishenko.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes—I don’t like that Ferdishenko. I can’t understand why Nastasia Philipovna encourages him so. Is he really her cousin, as he says?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh dear no, it’s all a joke. No more cousin than I am.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, what do you think of the arrangement, prince?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Thank you, general; you have behaved very kindly to me; all the more so since I did not ask you to help me. I don’t say that out of pride. I certainly did not know where to lay my head tonight. Rogojin asked me to come to his house, of course, but—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Rogojin? No, no, my good fellow. I should strongly recommend you, paternally,—or, if you prefer it, as a friend,—to forget all about Rogojin, and, in fact, to stick to the family into which you are about to enter.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Thank you,” began the prince; “and since you are so very kind there is just one matter which I—”

title: The Idiot
text: “You must really excuse me,” interrupted the general, “but I positively haven’t another moment now. I shall just tell Elizabetha Prokofievna about you, and if she wishes to receive you at once—as I shall advise her—I strongly recommend you to ingratiate yourself with her at the first opportunity, for my wife may be of the greatest service to you in many ways. If she cannot receive you now, you must be content to wait till another time. Meanwhile you, Gania, just look over these accounts, will you? We mustn’t forget to finish off that matter—”

title: The Idiot
text: The general left the room, and the prince never succeeded in broaching the business which he had on hand, though he had endeavoured to do so four times.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania lit a cigarette and offered one to the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: The latter accepted the offer, but did not talk, being unwilling to disturb Gania’s work.

title: The Idiot
text: He commenced to examine the study and its contents.

title: The Idiot
text: But Gania hardly so much as glanced at the papers lying before him; he was absent and thoughtful, and his smile and general appearance struck the prince still more disagreeably now that the two were left alone together.

title: The Idiot
text: Suddenly Gania approached our hero who was at the moment standing over Nastasia Philipovna’s portrait, gazing at it.

title: The Idiot
text: “Do you admire that sort of woman, prince?” he asked, looking intently at him.

title: The Idiot
text: He seemed to have some special object in the question.

title: The Idiot
text: “It’s a wonderful face,” said the prince, “and I feel sure that her destiny is not by any means an ordinary, uneventful one. Her face is smiling enough, but she must have suffered terribly—hasn’t she? Her eyes show it—those two bones there, the little points under her eyes, just where the cheek begins. It’s a proud face too, terribly proud! And I—I can’t say whether she is good and kind, or not. Oh, if she be but good! That would make all well!”

title: The Idiot
text: “And would you marry a woman like that, now?” continued Gania, never taking his excited eyes off the prince’s face.

title: The Idiot
text: “I cannot marry at all,” said the latter.

title: The Idiot
text: “I am an invalid.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Would Rogojin marry her, do you think?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why not? Certainly he would, I should think. He would marry her tomorrow!—marry her tomorrow and murder her in a week!”

title: The Idiot
text: Hardly had the prince uttered the last word when Gania gave such a fearful shudder that the prince almost cried out.

title: The Idiot
text: “What’s the matter?” said he, seizing Gania’s hand.

title: The Idiot
text: “Your highness! His excellency begs your presence in her excellency’s apartments!” announced the footman, appearing at the door.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince immediately followed the man out of the room.

title: The Idiot
text: All three of the Miss Epanchins were fine, healthy girls, well-grown, with good shoulders and busts, and strong—almost masculine—hands; and, of course, with all the above attributes, they enjoyed capital appetites, of which they were not in the least ashamed.

title: The Idiot
text: Elizabetha Prokofievna sometimes informed the girls that they were a little too candid in this matter, but in spite of their outward deference to their mother these three young women, in solemn conclave, had long agreed to modify the unquestioning obedience which they had been in the habit of according to her; and Mrs. General Epanchin had judged it better to say nothing about it, though, of course, she was well aware of the fact.

title: The Idiot
text: It is true that her nature sometimes rebelled against these dictates of reason, and that she grew yearly more capricious and impatient; but having a respectful and well-disciplined husband under her thumb at all times, she found it possible, as a rule, to empty any little accumulations of spleen upon his head, and therefore the harmony of the family was kept duly balanced, and things went as smoothly as family matters can.

title: The Idiot
text: Mrs. Epanchin had a fair appetite herself, and generally took her share of the capital mid-day lunch which was always served for the girls, and which was nearly as good as a dinner.

title: The Idiot
text: The young ladies used to have a cup of coffee each before this meal, at ten o’clock, while still in bed.

title: The Idiot
text: This was a favourite and unalterable arrangement with them.

title: The Idiot
text: At half-past twelve, the table was laid in the small dining-room, and occasionally the general himself appeared at the family gathering, if he had time.

title: The Idiot
text: Besides tea and coffee, cheese, honey, butter, pan-cakes of various kinds (the lady of the house loved these best), cutlets, and so on, there was generally strong beef soup, and other substantial delicacies.

title: The Idiot
text: On the particular morning on which our story has opened, the family had assembled in the dining-room, and were waiting the general’s appearance, the latter having promised to come this day.

title: The Idiot
text: If he had been one moment late, he would have been sent for at once; but he turned up punctually.

title: The Idiot
text: As he came forward to wish his wife good-morning and kiss her hands, as his custom was, he observed something in her look which boded ill.

title: The Idiot
text: He thought he knew the reason, and had expected it, but still, he was not altogether comfortable.

title: The Idiot
text: His daughters advanced to kiss him, too, and though they did not look exactly angry, there was something strange in their expression as well.

title: The Idiot
text: The general was, owing to certain circumstances, a little inclined to be too suspicious at home, and needlessly nervous; but, as an experienced father and husband, he judged it better to take measures at once to protect himself from any dangers there might be in the air.

title: The Idiot
text: However, I hope I shall not interfere with the proper sequence of my narrative too much, if I diverge for a moment at this point, in order to explain the mutual relations between General Epanchin’s family and others acting a part in this history, at the time when we take up the thread of their destiny.

title: The Idiot
text: I have already stated that the general, though he was a man of lowly origin, and of poor education, was, for all that, an experienced and talented husband and father.

title: The Idiot
text: Among other things, he considered it undesirable to hurry his daughters to the matrimonial altar and to worry them too much with assurances of his paternal wishes for their happiness, as is the custom among parents of many grown-up daughters.

title: The Idiot
text: He even succeeded in ranging his wife on his side on this question, though he found the feat very difficult to accomplish, because unnatural; but the general’s arguments were conclusive, and founded upon obvious facts.

title: The Idiot
text: The general considered that the girls’ taste and good sense should be allowed to develop and mature deliberately, and that the parents’ duty should merely be to keep watch, in order that no strange or undesirable choice be made; but that the selection once effected, both father and mother were bound from that moment to enter heart and soul into the cause, and to see that the matter progressed without hindrance until the altar should be happily reached.

title: The Idiot
text: Besides this, it was clear that the Epanchins’ position gained each year, with geometrical accuracy, both as to financial solidity and social weight; and, therefore, the longer the girls waited, the better was their chance of making a brilliant match.

title: The Idiot
text: But again, amidst the incontrovertible facts just recorded, one more, equally significant, rose up to confront the family; and this was, that the eldest daughter, Alexandra, had imperceptibly arrived at her twenty-fifth birthday.

title: The Idiot
text: Almost at the same moment, Afanasy Ivanovitch Totski, a man of immense wealth, high connections, and good standing, announced his intention of marrying.

title: The Idiot
text: Afanasy Ivanovitch was a gentleman of fifty-five years of age, artistically gifted, and of most refined tastes.

title: The Idiot
text: He wished to marry well, and, moreover, he was a keen admirer and judge of beauty.

title: The Idiot
text: Now, since Totski had, of late, been upon terms of great cordiality with Epanchin, which excellent relations were intensified by the fact that they were, so to speak, partners in several financial enterprises, it so happened that the former now put in a friendly request to the general for counsel with regard to the important step he meditated.

title: The Idiot
text: Might he suggest, for instance, such a thing as a marriage between himself and one of the general’s daughters?

title: The Idiot
text: Evidently the quiet, pleasant current of the family life of the Epanchins was about to undergo a change.

title: The Idiot
text: The undoubted beauty of the family, par excellence, was the youngest, Aglaya, as aforesaid.

title: The Idiot
text: But Totski himself, though an egotist of the extremest type, realized that he had no chance there; Aglaya was clearly not for such as he.

title: The Idiot
text: Perhaps the sisterly love and friendship of the three girls had more or less exaggerated Aglaya’s chances of happiness.

title: The Idiot
text: In their opinion, the latter’s destiny was not merely to be very happy; she was to live in a heaven on earth.

title: The Idiot
text: Aglaya’s husband was to be a compendium of all the virtues, and of all success, not to speak of fabulous wealth.

title: The Idiot
text: The two elder sisters had agreed that all was to be sacrificed by them, if need be, for Aglaya’s sake; her dowry was to be colossal and unprecedented.

title: The Idiot
text: The general and his wife were aware of this agreement, and, therefore, when Totski suggested himself for one of the sisters, the parents made no doubt that one of the two elder girls would probably accept the offer, since Totski would certainly make no difficulty as to dowry.

title: The Idiot
text: The general valued the proposal very highly.

title: The Idiot
text: He knew life, and realized what such an offer was worth.

title: The Idiot
text: The answer of the sisters to the communication was, if not conclusive, at least consoling and hopeful.

title: The Idiot
text: It made known that the eldest, Alexandra, would very likely be disposed to listen to a proposal.

title: The Idiot
text: Alexandra was a good-natured girl, though she had a will of her own.

title: The Idiot
text: She was intelligent and kind-hearted, and, if she were to marry Totski, she would make him a good wife.

title: The Idiot
text: She did not care for a brilliant marriage; she was eminently a woman calculated to soothe and sweeten the life of any man; decidedly pretty, if not absolutely handsome.

title: The Idiot
text: What better could Totski wish?

title: The Idiot
text: So the matter crept slowly forward.

title: The Idiot
text: The general and Totski had agreed to avoid any hasty and irrevocable step.

title: The Idiot
text: Alexandra’s parents had not even begun to talk to their daughters freely upon the subject, when suddenly, as it were, a dissonant chord was struck amid the harmony of the proceedings.

title: The Idiot
text: Mrs. Epanchin began to show signs of discontent, and that was a serious matter.

title: The Idiot
text: A certain circumstance had crept in, a disagreeable and troublesome factor, which threatened to overturn the whole business.

title: The Idiot
text: This circumstance had come into existence eighteen years before.

title: The Idiot
text: Close to an estate of Totski’s, in one of the central provinces of Russia, there lived, at that time, a poor gentleman whose estate was of the wretchedest description.

title: The Idiot
text: This gentleman was noted in the district for his persistent ill-fortune; his name was Barashkoff, and, as regards family and descent, he was vastly superior to Totski, but his estate was mortgaged to the last acre.

title: The Idiot
text: One day, when he had ridden over to the town to see a creditor, the chief peasant of his village followed him shortly after, with the news that his house had been burnt down, and that his wife had perished with it, but his children were safe.

title: The Idiot
text: Even Barashkoff, inured to the storms of evil fortune as he was, could not stand this last stroke.

title: The Idiot
text: He went mad and died shortly after in the town hospital.

title: The Idiot
text: His estate was sold for the creditors; and the little girls—two of them, of seven and eight years of age respectively,—were adopted by Totski, who undertook their maintenance and education in the kindness of his heart.

title: The Idiot
text: They were brought up together with the children of his German bailiff.

title: The Idiot
text: Very soon, however, there was only one of them left—Nastasia Philipovna—for the other little one died of whooping-cough.

title: The Idiot
text: Totski, who was living abroad at this time, very soon forgot all about the child; but five years after, returning to Russia, it struck him that he would like to look over his estate and see how matters were going there, and, arrived at his bailiff’s house, he was not long in discovering that among the children of the latter there now dwelt a most lovely little girl of twelve, sweet and intelligent, and bright, and promising to develop beauty of most unusual quality—as to which last Totski was an undoubted authority.

title: The Idiot
text: He only stayed at his country seat a few days on this occasion, but he had time to make his arrangements.

title: The Idiot
text: Great changes took place in the child’s education; a good governess was engaged, a Swiss lady of experience and culture.

title: The Idiot
text: For four years this lady resided in the house with little Nastia, and then the education was considered complete.

title: The Idiot
text: The governess took her departure, and another lady came down to fetch Nastia, by Totski’s instructions.

title: The Idiot
text: The child was now transported to another of Totski’s estates in a distant part of the country.

title: The Idiot
text: Here she found a delightful little house, just built, and prepared for her reception with great care and taste; and here she took up her abode together with the lady who had accompanied her from her old home.

title: The Idiot
text: In the house there were two experienced maids, musical instruments of all sorts, a charming “young lady’s library,” pictures, paint-boxes, a lap-dog, and everything to make life agreeable.

title: The Idiot
text: Within a fortnight Totski himself arrived, and from that time he appeared to have taken a great fancy to this part of the world and came down each summer, staying two and three months at a time.

title: The Idiot
text: So passed four years peacefully and happily, in charming surroundings.

title: The Idiot
text: At the end of that time, and about four months after Totski’s last visit (he had stayed but a fortnight on this occasion), a report reached Nastasia Philipovna that he was about to be married in St. Petersburg, to a rich, eminent, and lovely woman.

title: The Idiot
text: The report was only partially true, the marriage project being only in an embryo condition; but a great change now came over Nastasia Philipovna.

title: The Idiot
text: She suddenly displayed unusual decision of character; and without wasting time in thought, she left her country home and came up to St. Petersburg, straight to Totski’s house, all alone.

title: The Idiot
text: The latter, amazed at her conduct, began to express his displeasure; but he very soon became aware that he must change his voice, style, and everything else, with this young lady; the good old times were gone.

title: The Idiot
text: An entirely new and different woman sat before him, between whom and the girl he had left in the country last July there seemed nothing in common.

title: The Idiot
text: In the first place, this new woman understood a good deal more than was usual for young people of her age; so much indeed, that Totski could not help wondering where she had picked up her knowledge.

title: The Idiot
text: Surely not from her “young lady’s library”?

title: The Idiot
text: It even embraced legal matters, and the “world” in general, to a considerable extent.

title: The Idiot
text: Her character was absolutely changed.

title: The Idiot
text: No more of the girlish alternations of timidity and petulance, the adorable naivete, the reveries, the tears, the playfulness...

title: The Idiot
text: It was an entirely new and hitherto unknown being who now sat and laughed at him, and informed him to his face that she had never had the faintest feeling for him of any kind, except loathing and contempt—contempt which had followed closely upon her sensations of surprise and bewilderment after her first acquaintance with him.

title: The Idiot
text: This new woman gave him further to understand that though it was absolutely the same to her whom he married, yet she had decided to prevent this marriage—for no particular reason, but that she chose to do so, and because she wished to amuse herself at his expense for that it was “quite her turn to laugh a little now!”

title: The Idiot
text: Such were her words—very likely she did not give her real reason for this eccentric conduct; but, at all events, that was all the explanation she deigned to offer.

title: The Idiot
text: Meanwhile, Totski thought the matter over as well as his scattered ideas would permit.

title: The Idiot
text: His meditations lasted a fortnight, however, and at the end of that time his resolution was taken.

title: The Idiot
text: The fact was, Totski was at that time a man of fifty years of age; his position was solid and respectable; his place in society had long been firmly fixed upon safe foundations; he loved himself, his personal comforts, and his position better than all the world, as every respectable gentleman should!

title: The Idiot
text: At the same time his grasp of things in general soon showed Totski that he now had to deal with a being who was outside the pale of the ordinary rules of traditional behaviour, and who would not only threaten mischief but would undoubtedly carry it out, and stop for no one.

title: The Idiot
text: There was evidently, he concluded, something at work here; some storm of the mind, some paroxysm of romantic anger, goodness knows against whom or what, some insatiable contempt—in a word, something altogether absurd and impossible, but at the same time most dangerous to be met with by any respectable person with a position in society to keep up.

title: The Idiot
text: For a man of Totski’s wealth and standing, it would, of course, have been the simplest possible matter to take steps which would rid him at once from all annoyance; while it was obviously impossible for Nastasia Philipovna to harm him in any way, either legally or by stirring up a scandal, for, in case of the latter danger, he could so easily remove her to a sphere of safety.

title: The Idiot
text: However, these arguments would only hold good in case of Nastasia acting as others might in such an emergency.

title: The Idiot
text: She was much more likely to overstep the bounds of reasonable conduct by some extraordinary eccentricity.

title: The Idiot
text: Here the sound judgment of Totski stood him in good stead.

title: The Idiot
text: He realized that Nastasia Philipovna must be well aware that she could do nothing by legal means to injure him, and that her flashing eyes betrayed some entirely different intention.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia Philipovna was quite capable of ruining herself, and even of perpetrating something which would send her to Siberia, for the mere pleasure of injuring a man for whom she had developed so inhuman a sense of loathing and contempt.

title: The Idiot
text: He had sufficient insight to understand that she valued nothing in the world—herself least of all—and he made no attempt to conceal the fact that he was a coward in some respects.

title: The Idiot
text: For instance, if he had been told that he would be stabbed at the altar, or publicly insulted, he would undoubtedly have been frightened; but not so much at the idea of being murdered, or wounded, or insulted, as at the thought that if such things were to happen he would be made to look ridiculous in the eyes of society.

title: The Idiot
text: He knew well that Nastasia thoroughly understood him and where to wound him and how, and therefore, as the marriage was still only in embryo, Totski decided to conciliate her by giving it up.

title: The Idiot
text: His decision was strengthened by the fact that Nastasia Philipovna had curiously altered of late.

title: The Idiot
text: It would be difficult to conceive how different she was physically, at the present time, to the girl of a few years ago.

title: The Idiot
text: She was pretty then... but now!

title: The Idiot
text: Totski laughed angrily when he thought how short-sighted he had been.

title: The Idiot
text: In days gone by he remembered how he had looked at her beautiful eyes, how even then he had marvelled at their dark mysterious depths, and at their wondering gaze which seemed to seek an answer to some unknown riddle.

title: The Idiot
text: Her complexion also had altered.

title: The Idiot
text: She was now exceedingly pale, but, curiously, this change only made her more beautiful.

title: The Idiot
text: Like most men of the world, Totski had rather despised such a cheaply-bought conquest, but of late years he had begun to think differently about it.

title: The Idiot
text: It had struck him as long ago as last spring that he ought to be finding a good match for Nastasia; for instance, some respectable and reasonable young fellow serving in a government office in another part of the country.

title: The Idiot
text: How maliciously Nastasia laughed at the idea of such a thing, now!

title: The Idiot
text: However, it appeared to Totski that he might make use of her in another way; and he determined to establish her in St. Petersburg, surrounding her with all the comforts and luxuries that his wealth could command.

title: The Idiot
text: In this way he might gain glory in certain circles.

title: The Idiot
text: Five years of this Petersburg life went by, and, of course, during that time a great deal happened.

title: The Idiot
text: Totski’s position was very uncomfortable; having “funked” once, he could not totally regain his ease.

title: The Idiot
text: He was afraid, he did not know why, but he was simply afraid of Nastasia Philipovna.

title: The Idiot
text: For the first two years or so he had suspected that she wished to marry him herself, and that only her vanity prevented her telling him so.

title: The Idiot
text: He thought that she wanted him to approach her with a humble proposal from his own side.

title: The Idiot
text: But to his great, and not entirely pleasurable amazement, he discovered that this was by no means the case, and that were he to offer himself he would be refused.

title: The Idiot
text: He could not understand such a state of things, and was obliged to conclude that it was pride, the pride of an injured and imaginative woman, which had gone to such lengths that it preferred to sit and nurse its contempt and hatred in solitude rather than mount to heights of hitherto unattainable splendour.

title: The Idiot
text: To make matters worse, she was quite impervious to mercenary considerations, and could not be bribed in any way.

title: The Idiot
text: Finally, Totski took cunning means to try to break his chains and be free.

title: The Idiot
text: He tried to tempt her in various ways to lose her heart; he invited princes, hussars, secretaries of embassies, poets, novelists, even Socialists, to see her; but not one of them all made the faintest impression upon Nastasia.

title: The Idiot
text: It was as though she had a pebble in place of a heart, as though her feelings and affections were dried up and withered for ever.

title: The Idiot
text: She lived almost entirely alone; she read, she studied, she loved music.

title: The Idiot
text: Her principal acquaintances were poor women of various grades, a couple of actresses, and the family of a poor schoolteacher.

title: The Idiot
text: Among these people she was much beloved.

title: The Idiot
text: She received four or five friends sometimes, of an evening.

title: The Idiot
text: Totski often came.

title: The Idiot
text: Lately, too, General Epanchin had been enabled with great difficulty to introduce himself into her circle.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania made her acquaintance also, and others were Ferdishenko, an ill-bred, and would-be witty, young clerk, and Ptitsin, a money-lender of modest and polished manners, who had risen from poverty.

title: The Idiot
text: In fact, Nastasia Philipovna’s beauty became a thing known to all the town; but not a single man could boast of anything more than his own admiration for her; and this reputation of hers, and her wit and culture and grace, all confirmed Totski in the plan he had now prepared.

title: The Idiot
text: And it was at this moment that General Epanchin began to play so large and important a part in the story.

title: The Idiot
text: When Totski had approached the general with his request for friendly counsel as to a marriage with one of his daughters, he had made a full and candid confession.

title: The Idiot
text: He had said that he intended to stop at no means to obtain his freedom; even if Nastasia were to promise to leave him entirely alone in future, he would not (he said) believe and trust her; words were not enough for him; he must have solid guarantees of some sort.

title: The Idiot
text: So he and the general determined to try what an attempt to appeal to her heart would effect.

title: The Idiot
text: Having arrived at Nastasia’s house one day, with Epanchin, Totski immediately began to speak of the intolerable torment of his position.

title: The Idiot
text: He admitted that he was to blame for all, but candidly confessed that he could not bring himself to feel any remorse for his original guilt towards herself, because he was a man of sensual passions which were inborn and ineradicable, and that he had no power over himself in this respect; but that he wished, seriously, to marry at last, and that the whole fate of the most desirable social union which he contemplated, was in her hands; in a word, he confided his all to her generosity of heart.

title: The Idiot
text: General Epanchin took up his part and spoke in the character of father of a family; he spoke sensibly, and without wasting words over any attempt at sentimentality, he merely recorded his full admission of her right to be the arbiter of Totski’s destiny at this moment.

title: The Idiot
text: He then pointed out that the fate of his daughter, and very likely of both his other daughters, now hung upon her reply.

title: The Idiot
text: To Nastasia’s question as to what they wished her to do, Totski confessed that he had been so frightened by her, five years ago, that he could never now be entirely comfortable until she herself married.

title: The Idiot
text: He immediately added that such a suggestion from him would, of course, be absurd, unless accompanied by remarks of a more pointed nature.

title: The Idiot
text: He very well knew, he said, that a certain young gentleman of good family, namely, Gavrila Ardalionovitch Ivolgin, with whom she was acquainted, and whom she received at her house, had long loved her passionately, and would give his life for some response from her.

title: The Idiot
text: The young fellow had confessed this love of his to him (Totski) and had also admitted it in the hearing of his benefactor, General Epanchin.

title: The Idiot
text: Lastly, he could not help being of opinion that Nastasia must be aware of Gania’s love for her, and if he (Totski) mistook not, she had looked with some favour upon it, being often lonely, and rather tired of her present life.

title: The Idiot
text: Having remarked how difficult it was for him, of all people, to speak to her of these matters, Totski concluded by saying that he trusted Nastasia Philipovna would not look with contempt upon him if he now expressed his sincere desire to guarantee her future by a gift of seventy-five thousand roubles.

title: The Idiot
text: He added that the sum would have been left her all the same in his will, and that therefore she must not consider the gift as in any way an indemnification to her for anything, but that there was no reason, after all, why a man should not be allowed to entertain a natural desire to lighten his conscience, etc., etc.

title: The Idiot
text: ; in fact, all that would naturally be said under the circumstances.

title: The Idiot
text: Totski was very eloquent all through, and, in conclusion, just touched on the fact that not a soul in the world, not even General Epanchin, had ever heard a word about the above seventy-five thousand roubles, and that this was the first time he had ever given expression to his intentions in respect to them.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia Philipovna’s reply to this long rigmarole astonished both the friends considerably.

title: The Idiot
text: Not only was there no trace of her former irony, of her old hatred and enmity, and of that dreadful laughter, the very recollection of which sent a cold chill down Totski’s back to this very day; but she seemed charmed and really glad to have the opportunity of talking seriously with him for once in a way.

title: The Idiot
text: She confessed that she had long wished to have a frank and free conversation and to ask for friendly advice, but that pride had hitherto prevented her; now, however, that the ice was broken, nothing could be more welcome to her than this opportunity.

title: The Idiot
text: First, with a sad smile, and then with a twinkle of merriment in her eyes, she admitted that such a storm as that of five years ago was now quite out of the question.

title: The Idiot
text: She said that she had long since changed her views of things, and recognized that facts must be taken into consideration in spite of the feelings of the heart.

title: The Idiot
text: What was done was done and ended, and she could not understand why Totski should still feel alarmed.

title: The Idiot
text: She next turned to General Epanchin and observed, most courteously, that she had long since known of his daughters, and that she had heard none but good report; that she had learned to think of them with deep and sincere respect.

title: The Idiot
text: The idea alone that she could in any way serve them, would be to her both a pride and a source of real happiness.

title: The Idiot
text: It was true that she was lonely in her present life; Totski had judged her thoughts aright.

title: The Idiot
text: She longed to rise, if not to love, at least to family life and new hopes and objects, but as to Gavrila Ardalionovitch, she could not as yet say much.

title: The Idiot
text: She thought it must be the case that he loved her; she felt that she too might learn to love him, if she could be sure of the firmness of his attachment to herself; but he was very young, and it was a difficult question to decide.

title: The Idiot
text: What she specially liked about him was that he worked, and supported his family by his toil.

title: The Idiot
text: She had heard that he was proud and ambitious; she had heard much that was interesting of his mother and sister, she had heard of them from Mr. Ptitsin, and would much like to make their acquaintance, but—another question!

title: The Idiot
text: —would they like to receive her into their house?

title: The Idiot
text: At all events, though she did not reject the idea of this marriage, she desired not to be hurried.

title: The Idiot
text: As for the seventy-five thousand roubles, Mr. Totski need not have found any difficulty or awkwardness about the matter; she quite understood the value of money, and would, of course, accept the gift.

title: The Idiot
text: She thanked him for his delicacy, however, but saw no reason why Gavrila Ardalionovitch should not know about it.

title: The Idiot
text: She would not marry the latter, she said, until she felt persuaded that neither on his part nor on the part of his family did there exist any sort of concealed suspicions as to herself.

title: The Idiot
text: She did not intend to ask forgiveness for anything in the past, which fact she desired to be known.

title: The Idiot
text: She did not consider herself to blame for anything that had happened in former years, and she thought that Gavrila Ardalionovitch should be informed as to the relations which had existed between herself and Totski during the last five years.

title: The Idiot
text: If she accepted this money it was not to be considered as indemnification for her misfortune as a young girl, which had not been in any degree her own fault, but merely as compensation for her ruined life.

title: The Idiot
text: She became so excited and agitated during all these explanations and confessions that General Epanchin was highly gratified, and considered the matter satisfactorily arranged once for all.

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot

title: The Idiot
text: Before long Nastasia and Gania had talked the matter over.

title: The Idiot
text: But she recognized his love, on the understanding that she bound herself to nothing whatever, and that she reserved the right to say “no” up to the very hour of the marriage ceremony.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania was to have the same right of refusal at the last moment.

title: The Idiot
text: It soon became clear to Gania, after scenes of wrath and quarrellings at the domestic hearth, that his family were seriously opposed to the match, and that Nastasia was aware of this fact was equally evident.

title: The Idiot
text: She said nothing about it, though he daily expected her to do so.

title: The Idiot
text: There were several rumours afloat, before long, which upset Totski’s equanimity a good deal, but we will not now stop to describe them; merely mentioning an instance or two.

title: The Idiot
text: One was that Nastasia had entered into close and secret relations with the Epanchin girls—a most unlikely rumour; another was that Nastasia had long satisfied herself of the fact that Gania was merely marrying her for money, and that his nature was gloomy and greedy, impatient and selfish, to an extraordinary degree; and that although he had been keen enough in his desire to achieve a conquest before, yet since the two friends had agreed to exploit his passion for their own purposes, it was clear enough that he had begun to consider the whole thing a nuisance and a nightmare.

title: The Idiot
text: In his heart passion and hate seemed to hold divided sway, and although he had at last given his consent to marry the woman (as he said), under the stress of circumstances, yet he promised himself that he would “take it out of her,” after marriage.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia seemed to Totski to have divined all this, and to be preparing something on her own account, which frightened him to such an extent that he did not dare communicate his views even to the general.

title: The Idiot
text: But at times he would pluck up his courage and be full of hope and good spirits again, acting, in fact, as weak men do act in such circumstances.

title: The Idiot
text: However, both the friends felt that the thing looked rosy indeed when one day Nastasia informed them that she would give her final answer on the evening of her birthday, which anniversary was due in a very short time.

title: The Idiot
text: A strange rumour began to circulate, meanwhile; no less than that the respectable and highly respected General Epanchin was himself so fascinated by Nastasia Philipovna that his feeling for her amounted almost to passion.

title: The Idiot
text: What he thought to gain by Gania’s marriage to the girl it was difficult to imagine.

title: The Idiot
text: Possibly he counted on Gania’s complaisance; for Totski had long suspected that there existed some secret understanding between the general and his secretary.

title: The Idiot
text: At all events the fact was known that he had prepared a magnificent present of pearls for Nastasia’s birthday, and that he was looking forward to the occasion when he should present his gift with the greatest excitement and impatience.

title: The Idiot
text: The day before her birthday he was in a fever of agitation.

title: The Idiot
text: Mrs. Epanchin, long accustomed to her husband’s infidelities, had heard of the pearls, and the rumour excited her liveliest curiosity and interest.

title: The Idiot
text: The general remarked her suspicions, and felt that a grand explanation must shortly take place—which fact alarmed him much.

title: The Idiot
text: This is the reason why he was so unwilling to take lunch (on the morning upon which we took up this narrative) with the rest of his family.

title: The Idiot
text: Before the prince’s arrival he had made up his mind to plead business, and “cut” the meal; which simply meant running away.

title: The Idiot
text: He was particularly anxious that this one day should be passed—especially the evening—without unpleasantness between himself and his family; and just at the right moment the prince turned up—“as though Heaven had sent him on purpose,” said the general to himself, as he left the study to seek out the wife of his bosom.

title: The Idiot
text: Mrs. General Epanchin was a proud woman by nature.

title: The Idiot
text: What must her feelings have been when she heard that Prince Muishkin, the last of his and her line, had arrived in beggar’s guise, a wretched idiot, a recipient of charity—all of which details the general gave out for greater effect!

title: The Idiot
text: He was anxious to steal her interest at the first swoop, so as to distract her thoughts from other matters nearer home.

title: The Idiot
text: Mrs. Epanchin was in the habit of holding herself very straight, and staring before her, without speaking, in moments of excitement.

title: The Idiot
text: She was a fine woman of the same age as her husband, with a slightly hooked nose, a high, narrow forehead, thick hair turning a little grey, and a sallow complexion.

title: The Idiot
text: Her eyes were grey and wore a very curious expression at times.

title: The Idiot
text: She believed them to be most effective—a belief that nothing could alter.

title: The Idiot
text: “What, receive him! Now, at once?” asked Mrs. Epanchin, gazing vaguely at her husband as he stood fidgeting before her.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, dear me, I assure you there is no need to stand on ceremony with him,” the general explained hastily.

title: The Idiot
text: “He is quite a child, not to say a pathetic-looking creature. He has fits of some sort, and has just arrived from Switzerland, straight from the station, dressed like a German and without a farthing in his pocket. I gave him twenty-five roubles to go on with, and am going to find him some easy place in one of the government offices. I should like you to ply him well with the victuals, my dears, for I should think he must be very hungry.”

title: The Idiot
text: “You astonish me,” said the lady, gazing as before.

title: The Idiot
text: “Fits, and hungry too! What sort of fits?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, they don’t come on frequently, besides, he’s a regular child, though he seems to be fairly educated. I should like you, if possible, my dears,” the general added, making slowly for the door, “to put him through his paces a bit, and see what he is good for. I think you should be kind to him; it is a good deed, you know—however, just as you like, of course—but he is a sort of relation, remember, and I thought it might interest you to see the young fellow, seeing that this is so.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, of course, mamma, if we needn’t stand on ceremony with him, we must give the poor fellow something to eat after his journey; especially as he has not the least idea where to go to,” said Alexandra, the eldest of the girls.

title: The Idiot
text: “Besides, he’s quite a child; we can entertain him with a little hide-and-seek, in case of need,” said Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “Hide-and-seek? What do you mean?” inquired Mrs. Epanchin.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, do stop pretending, mamma,” cried Aglaya, in vexation.

title: The Idiot
text: “Send him up, father; mother allows.”

title: The Idiot
text: The general rang the bell and gave orders that the prince should be shown in.

title: The Idiot
text: “Only on condition that he has a napkin under his chin at lunch, then,” said Mrs. Epanchin, “and let Fedor, or Mavra, stand behind him while he eats. Is he quiet when he has these fits? He doesn’t show violence, does he?”

title: The Idiot
text: “On the contrary, he seems to be very well brought up. His manners are excellent—but here he is himself. Here you are, prince—let me introduce you, the last of the Muishkins, a relative of your own, my dear, or at least of the same name. Receive him kindly, please. They’ll bring in lunch directly, prince; you must stop and have some, but you must excuse me. I’m in a hurry, I must be off—”

title: The Idiot
text: “We all know where you must be off to!” said Mrs. Epanchin, in a meaning voice.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, yes—I must hurry away, I’m late! Look here, dears, let him write you something in your albums; you’ve no idea what a wonderful caligraphist he is, wonderful talent! He has just written out ‘Abbot Pafnute signed this’ for me. Well, au revoir!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Stop a minute; where are you off to? Who is this abbot?” cried Mrs. Epanchin to her retreating husband in a tone of excited annoyance.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, my dear, it was an old abbot of that name—I must be off to see the count, he’s waiting for me, I’m late—Good-bye! Au revoir, prince!”—and the general bolted at full speed.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, yes—I know what count you’re going to see!” remarked his wife in a cutting manner, as she turned her angry eyes on the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Now then, what’s all this about?—What abbot—Who’s Pafnute?” she added, brusquely.

title: The Idiot
text: “Mamma!” said Alexandra, shocked at her rudeness.

title: The Idiot
text: Aglaya stamped her foot.

title: The Idiot
text: “Nonsense! Let me alone!” said the angry mother.

title: The Idiot
text: “Now then, prince, sit down here, no, nearer, come nearer the light! I want to have a good look at you. So, now then, who is this abbot?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Abbot Pafnute,” said our friend, seriously and with deference.

title: The Idiot
text: “Pafnute, yes. And who was he?”

title: The Idiot
text: Mrs. Epanchin put these questions hastily and brusquely, and when the prince answered she nodded her head sagely at each word he said.

title: The Idiot
text: “The Abbot Pafnute lived in the fourteenth century,” began the prince; “he was in charge of one of the monasteries on the Volga, about where our present Kostroma government lies. He went to Oreol and helped in the great matters then going on in the religious world; he signed an edict there, and I have seen a print of his signature; it struck me, so I copied it. When the general asked me, in his study, to write something for him, to show my handwriting, I wrote ‘The Abbot Pafnute signed this,’ in the exact handwriting of the abbot. The general liked it very much, and that’s why he recalled it just now.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Aglaya, make a note of ‘Pafnute,’ or we shall forget him. H’m! and where is this signature?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I think it was left on the general’s table.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Let it be sent for at once!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, I’ll write you a new one in half a minute,” said the prince, “if you like!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Of course, mamma!” said Alexandra.

title: The Idiot
text: “But let’s have lunch now, we are all hungry!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes; come along, prince,” said the mother, “are you very hungry?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes; I must say that I am pretty hungry, thanks very much.”

title: The Idiot
text: “H’m! I like to see that you know your manners; and you are by no means such a person as the general thought fit to describe you. Come along; you sit here, opposite to me,” she continued, “I wish to be able to see your face. Alexandra, Adelaida, look after the prince! He doesn’t seem so very ill, does he? I don’t think he requires a napkin under his chin, after all; are you accustomed to having one on, prince?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Formerly, when I was seven years old or so. I believe I wore one; but now I usually hold my napkin on my knee when I eat.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Of course, of course! And about your fits?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Fits?” asked the prince, slightly surprised.

title: The Idiot
text: “I very seldom have fits nowadays. I don’t know how it may be here, though; they say the climate may be bad for me.”

title: The Idiot
text: “He talks very well, you know!” said Mrs. Epanchin, who still continued to nod at each word the prince spoke.

title: The Idiot
text: “I really did not expect it at all; in fact, I suppose it was all stuff and nonsense on the general’s part, as usual. Eat away, prince, and tell me where you were born, and where you were brought up. I wish to know all about you, you interest me very much!”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince expressed his thanks once more, and eating heartily the while, recommenced the narrative of his life in Switzerland, all of which we have heard before.

title: The Idiot
text: Mrs. Epanchin became more and more pleased with her guest; the girls, too, listened with considerable attention.

title: The Idiot
text: In talking over the question of relationship it turned out that the prince was very well up in the matter and knew his pedigree off by heart.

title: The Idiot
text: It was found that scarcely any connection existed between himself and Mrs. Epanchin, but the talk, and the opportunity of conversing about her family tree, gratified the latter exceedingly, and she rose from the table in great good humour.

title: The Idiot
text: “Let’s all go to my boudoir,” she said, “and they shall bring some coffee in there. That’s the room where we all assemble and busy ourselves as we like best,” she explained.

title: The Idiot
text: “Alexandra, my eldest, here, plays the piano, or reads or sews; Adelaida paints landscapes and portraits (but never finishes any); and Aglaya sits and does nothing. I don’t work too much, either. Here we are, now; sit down, prince, near the fire and talk to us. I want to hear you relate something. I wish to make sure of you first and then tell my old friend, Princess Bielokonski, about you. I wish you to know all the good people and to interest them. Now then, begin!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Mamma, it’s rather a strange order, that!” said Adelaida, who was fussing among her paints and paint-brushes at the easel.

title: The Idiot
text: Aglaya and Alexandra had settled themselves with folded hands on a sofa, evidently meaning to be listeners.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince felt that the general attention was concentrated upon himself.

title: The Idiot
text: “I should refuse to say a word if I were ordered to tell a story like that!” observed Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why? what’s there strange about it? He has a tongue. Why shouldn’t he tell us something? I want to judge whether he is a good story-teller; anything you like, prince—how you liked Switzerland, what was your first impression, anything. You’ll see, he’ll begin directly and tell us all about it beautifully.”

title: The Idiot
text: “The impression was forcible—” the prince began.

title: The Idiot
text: “There, you see, girls,” said the impatient lady, “he has begun, you see.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, then, let him talk, mamma,” said Alexandra.

title: The Idiot
text: “This prince is a great humbug and by no means an idiot,” she whispered to Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, I saw that at once,” replied the latter.

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t think it at all nice of him to play a part. What does he wish to gain by it, I wonder?”

title: The Idiot
text: “My first impression was a very strong one,” repeated the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “When they took me away from Russia, I remember I passed through many German towns and looked out of the windows, but did not trouble so much as to ask questions about them. This was after a long series of fits. I always used to fall into a sort of torpid condition after such a series, and lost my memory almost entirely; and though I was not altogether without reason at such times, yet I had no logical power of thought. This would continue for three or four days, and then I would recover myself again. I remember my melancholy was intolerable; I felt inclined to cry; I sat and wondered and wondered uncomfortably; the consciousness that everything was strange weighed terribly upon me; I could understand that it was all foreign and strange. I recollect I awoke from this state for the first time at Basle, one evening; the bray of a donkey aroused me, a donkey in the town market. I saw the donkey and was extremely pleased with it, and from that moment my head seemed to clear.”

title: The Idiot
text: “A donkey? How strange! Yet it is not strange. Anyone of us might fall in love with a donkey! It happened in mythological times,” said Madame Epanchin, looking wrathfully at her daughters, who had begun to laugh.

title: The Idiot
text: “Go on, prince.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Since that evening I have been specially fond of donkeys. I began to ask questions about them, for I had never seen one before; and I at once came to the conclusion that this must be one of the most useful of animals—strong, willing, patient, cheap; and, thanks to this donkey, I began to like the whole country I was travelling through; and my melancholy passed away.”

title: The Idiot
text: “All this is very strange and interesting,” said Mrs. Epanchin.

title: The Idiot
text: “Now let’s leave the donkey and go on to other matters. What are you laughing at, Aglaya? and you too, Adelaida? The prince told us his experiences very cleverly; he saw the donkey himself, and what have you ever seen? You have never been abroad.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I have seen a donkey though, mamma!” said Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “And I’ve heard one!” said Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: All three of the girls laughed out loud, and the prince laughed with them.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, it’s too bad of you,” said mamma.

title: The Idiot
text: “You must forgive them, prince; they are good girls. I am very fond of them, though I often have to be scolding them; they are all as silly and mad as march hares.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, why shouldn’t they laugh?” said the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “I shouldn’t have let the chance go by in their place, I know. But I stick up for the donkey, all the same; he’s a patient, good-natured fellow.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Are you a patient man, prince? I ask out of curiosity,” said Mrs. Epanchin.

title: The Idiot
text: All laughed again.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, that wretched donkey again, I see!” cried the lady.

title: The Idiot
text: “I assure you, prince, I was not guilty of the least—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Insinuation?

title: The Idiot
text: Oh!

title: The Idiot
text: I assure you, I take your word for it.

title: The Idiot
text: And the prince continued laughing merrily.

title: The Idiot
text: “I must say it’s very nice of you to laugh. I see you really are a kind-hearted fellow,” said Mrs. Epanchin.

title: The Idiot
text: “I’m not always kind, though.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I am kind myself, and always kind too, if you please!” she retorted, unexpectedly; “and that is my chief fault, for one ought not to be always kind. I am often angry with these girls and their father; but the worst of it is, I am always kindest when I am cross. I was very angry just before you came, and Aglaya there read me a lesson—thanks, Aglaya, dear—come and kiss me—there—that’s enough” she added, as Aglaya came forward and kissed her lips and then her hand.

title: The Idiot
text: “Now then, go on, prince. Perhaps you can think of something more exciting than about the donkey, eh?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I must say, again, I can’t understand how you can expect anyone to tell you stories straight away, so,” said Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “I know I never could!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, but the prince can, because he is clever—cleverer than you are by ten or twenty times, if you like. There, that’s so, prince; and seriously, let’s drop the donkey now—what else did you see abroad, besides the donkey?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, but the prince told us about the donkey very cleverly, all the same,” said Alexandra.

title: The Idiot
text: “I have always been most interested to hear how people go mad and get well again, and that sort of thing. Especially when it happens suddenly.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Quite so, quite so!” cried Mrs. Epanchin, delighted.

title: The Idiot
text: “I see you can be sensible now and then, Alexandra. You were speaking of Switzerland, prince?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes. We came to Lucerne, and I was taken out in a boat. I felt how lovely it was, but the loveliness weighed upon me somehow or other, and made me feel melancholy.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why?” asked Alexandra.

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t know; I always feel like that when I look at the beauties of nature for the first time; but then, I was ill at that time, of course!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, but I should like to see it!” said Adelaida; “and I don’t know when we shall ever go abroad. I’ve been two years looking out for a good subject for a picture. I’ve done all I know. ‘The North and South I know by heart,’ as our poet observes. Do help me to a subject, prince.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, but I know nothing about painting. It seems to me one only has to look, and paint what one sees.”

title: The Idiot
text: “But I don’t know how to see!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Nonsense, what rubbish you talk!” the mother struck in.

title: The Idiot
text: “Not know how to see! Open your eyes and look! If you can’t see here, you won’t see abroad either. Tell us what you saw yourself, prince!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, that’s better,” said Adelaida; “the prince learned to see abroad.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, I hardly know! You see, I only went to restore my health. I don’t know whether I learned to see, exactly. I was very happy, however, nearly all the time.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Happy! you can be happy?” cried Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “Then how can you say you did not learn to see? I should think you could teach us to see!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! do teach us,” laughed Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! I can’t do that,” said the prince, laughing too.

title: The Idiot
text: “I lived almost all the while in one little Swiss village; what can I teach you? At first I was only just not absolutely dull; then my health began to improve—then every day became dearer and more precious to me, and the longer I stayed, the dearer became the time to me; so much so that I could not help observing it; but why this was so, it would be difficult to say.”

title: The Idiot
text: “So that you didn’t care to go away anywhere else?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, at first I did; I was restless; I didn’t know however I should manage to support life—you know there are such moments, especially in solitude. There was a waterfall near us, such a lovely thin streak of water, like a thread but white and moving. It fell from a great height, but it looked quite low, and it was half a mile away, though it did not seem fifty paces. I loved to listen to it at night, but it was then that I became so restless. Sometimes I went and climbed the mountain and stood there in the midst of the tall pines, all alone in the terrible silence, with our little village in the distance, and the sky so blue, and the sun so bright, and an old ruined castle on the mountain-side, far away. I used to watch the line where earth and sky met, and longed to go and seek there the key of all mysteries, thinking that I might find there a new life, perhaps some great city where life should be grander and richer—and then it struck me that life may be grand enough even in a prison.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I read that last most praiseworthy thought in my manual, when I was twelve years old,” said Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “All this is pure philosophy,” said Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “You are a philosopher, prince, and have come here to instruct us in your views.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Perhaps you are right,” said the prince, smiling.

title: The Idiot
text: “I think I am a philosopher, perhaps, and who knows, perhaps I do wish to teach my views of things to those I meet with?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Your philosophy is rather like that of an old woman we know, who is rich and yet does nothing but try how little she can spend. She talks of nothing but money all day. Your great philosophical idea of a grand life in a prison and your four happy years in that Swiss village are like this, rather,” said Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “As to life in a prison, of course there may be two opinions,” said the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “I once heard the story of a man who lived twelve years in a prison—I heard it from the man himself.

title: The Idiot
text: He was one of the persons under treatment with my professor; he had fits, and attacks of melancholy, then he would weep, and once he tried to commit suicide.

title: The Idiot
text: His life in prison was sad enough; his only acquaintances were spiders and a tree that grew outside his grating—but I think I had better tell you of another man I met last year.

title: The Idiot
text: There was a very strange feature in this case, strange because of its extremely rare occurrence.

title: The Idiot
text: This man had once been brought to the scaffold in company with several others, and had had the sentence of death by shooting passed upon him for some political crime.

title: The Idiot
text: Twenty minutes later he had been reprieved and some other punishment substituted; but the interval between the two sentences, twenty minutes, or at least a quarter of an hour, had been passed in the certainty that within a few minutes he must die.

title: The Idiot
text: I was very anxious to hear him speak of his impressions during that dreadful time, and I several times inquired of him as to what he thought and felt.

title: The Idiot
text: He remembered everything with the most accurate and extraordinary distinctness, and declared that he would never forget a single iota of the experience.

title: The Idiot
text: “About twenty paces from the scaffold, where he had stood to hear the sentence, were three posts, fixed in the ground, to which to fasten the criminals (of whom there were several).

title: The Idiot
text: The first three criminals were taken to the posts, dressed in long white tunics, with white caps drawn over their faces, so that they could not see the rifles pointed at them.

title: The Idiot
text: Then a group of soldiers took their stand opposite to each post.

title: The Idiot
text: My friend was the eighth on the list, and therefore he would have been among the third lot to go up.

title: The Idiot
text: A priest went about among them with a cross: and there was about five minutes of time left for him to live.

title: The Idiot
text: “He said that those five minutes seemed to him to be a most interminable period, an enormous wealth of time; he seemed to be living, in these minutes, so many lives that there was no need as yet to think of that last moment, so that he made several arrangements, dividing up the time into portions—one for saying farewell to his companions, two minutes for that; then a couple more for thinking over his own life and career and all about himself; and another minute for a last look around.

title: The Idiot
text: He remembered having divided his time like this quite well.

title: The Idiot
text: While saying good-bye to his friends he recollected asking one of them some very usual everyday question, and being much interested in the answer.

title: The Idiot
text: Then having bade farewell, he embarked upon those two minutes which he had allotted to looking into himself; he knew beforehand what he was going to think about.

title: The Idiot
text: He wished to put it to himself as quickly and clearly as possible, that here was he, a living, thinking man, and that in three minutes he would be nobody; or if somebody or something, then what and where?

title: The Idiot
text: He thought he would decide this question once for all in these last three minutes.

title: The Idiot
text: A little way off there stood a church, and its gilded spire glittered in the sun.

title: The Idiot
text: He remembered staring stubbornly at this spire, and at the rays of light sparkling from it.

title: The Idiot
text: He could not tear his eyes from these rays of light; he got the idea that these rays were his new nature, and that in three minutes he would become one of them, amalgamated somehow with them.

title: The Idiot
text: “The repugnance to what must ensue almost immediately, and the uncertainty, were dreadful, he said; but worst of all was the idea, ‘What should I do if I were not to die now? What if I were to return to life again? What an eternity of days, and all mine! How I should grudge and count up every minute of it, so as to waste not a single instant! He said that this thought weighed so upon him and became such a terrible burden upon his brain that he could not bear it, and wished they would shoot him quickly and have done with it.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince paused and all waited, expecting him to go on again and finish the story.

title: The Idiot
text: “Is that all?” asked Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “All? Yes,” said the prince, emerging from a momentary reverie.

title: The Idiot
text: “And why did you tell us this?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, I happened to recall it, that’s all! It fitted into the conversation—”

title: The Idiot
text: “You probably wish to deduce, prince,” said Alexandra, “that moments of time cannot be reckoned by money value, and that sometimes five minutes are worth priceless treasures. All this is very praiseworthy; but may I ask about this friend of yours, who told you the terrible experience of his life? He was reprieved, you say; in other words, they did restore to him that ‘eternity of days. What did he do with these riches of time? Did he keep careful account of his minutes?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh no, he didn’t! I asked him myself. He said that he had not lived a bit as he had intended, and had wasted many, and many a minute.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Very well, then there’s an experiment, and the thing is proved; one cannot live and count each moment; say what you like, but one cannot.”

title: The Idiot
text: “That is true,” said the prince, “I have thought so myself. And yet, why shouldn’t one do it?”

title: The Idiot
text: “You think, then, that you could live more wisely than other people?” said Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “I have had that idea.”

title: The Idiot
text: “And you have it still?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes—I have it still,” the prince replied.

title: The Idiot
text: He had contemplated Aglaya until now, with a pleasant though rather timid smile, but as the last words fell from his lips he began to laugh, and looked at her merrily.

title: The Idiot
text: “You are not very modest!” said she.

title: The Idiot
text: “But how brave you are!” said he.

title: The Idiot
text: “You are laughing, and I—that man’s tale impressed me so much, that I dreamt of it afterwards; yes, I dreamt of those five minutes...”

title: The Idiot
text: He looked at his listeners again with that same serious, searching expression.

title: The Idiot
text: “You are not angry with me?” he asked suddenly, and with a kind of nervous hurry, although he looked them straight in the face.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why should we be angry?” they cried.

title: The Idiot
text: “Only because I seem to be giving you a lecture, all the time!”

title: The Idiot
text: At this they laughed heartily.

title: The Idiot
text: “Please don’t be angry with me,” continued the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “I know very well that I have seen less of life than other people, and have less knowledge of it. I must appear to speak strangely sometimes...”

title: The Idiot
text: He said the last words nervously.

title: The Idiot
text: “You say you have been happy, and that proves you have lived, not less, but more than other people. Why make all these excuses?” interrupted Aglaya in a mocking tone of voice.

title: The Idiot
text: “Besides, you need not mind about lecturing us; you have nothing to boast of. With your quietism, one could live happily for a hundred years at least. One might show you the execution of a felon, or show you one’s little finger. You could draw a moral from either, and be quite satisfied. That sort of existence is easy enough.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I can’t understand why you always fly into a temper,” said Mrs. Epanchin, who had been listening to the conversation and examining the faces of the speakers in turn.

title: The Idiot
text: “I do not understand what you mean. What has your little finger to do with it? The prince talks well, though he is not amusing. He began all right, but now he seems sad.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Never mind, mamma! Prince, I wish you had seen an execution,” said Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “I should like to ask you a question about that, if you had.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I have seen an execution,” said the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “You have!” cried Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “I might have guessed it. That’s a fitting crown to the rest of the story. If you have seen an execution, how can you say you lived happily all the while?”

title: The Idiot
text: “But is there capital punishment where you were?” asked Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “I saw it at Lyons. Schneider took us there, and as soon as we arrived we came in for that.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, and did you like it very much? Was it very edifying and instructive?” asked Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “No, I didn’t like it at all, and was ill after seeing it; but I confess I stared as though my eyes were fixed to the sight. I could not tear them away.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I, too, should have been unable to tear my eyes away,” said Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “They do not at all approve of women going to see an execution there. The women who do go are condemned for it afterwards in the newspapers.”

title: The Idiot
text: “That is, by contending that it is not a sight for women they admit that it is a sight for men. I congratulate them on the deduction. I suppose you quite agree with them, prince?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Tell us about the execution,” put in Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “I would much rather not, just now,” said the prince, a little disturbed and frowning slightly.

title: The Idiot
text: “You don’t seem to want to tell us,” said Aglaya, with a mocking air.

title: The Idiot
text: “No,—the thing is, I was telling all about the execution a little while ago, and—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Whom did you tell about it?”

title: The Idiot
text: “The man-servant, while I was waiting to see the general.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Our man-servant?” exclaimed several voices at once.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, the one who waits in the entrance hall, a greyish, red-faced man—”

title: The Idiot
text: “The prince is clearly a democrat,” remarked Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, if you could tell Aleksey about it, surely you can tell us too.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I do so want to hear about it,” repeated Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “Just now, I confess,” began the prince, with more animation, “when you asked me for a subject for a picture, I confess I had serious thoughts of giving you one. I thought of asking you to draw the face of a criminal, one minute before the fall of the guillotine, while the wretched man is still standing on the scaffold, preparatory to placing his neck on the block.”

title: The Idiot
text: “What, his face? only his face?” asked Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “That would be a strange subject indeed. And what sort of a picture would that make?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, why not?” the prince insisted, with some warmth.

title: The Idiot
text: “When I was in Basle I saw a picture very much in that style—I should like to tell you about it; I will some time or other; it struck me very forcibly.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, you shall tell us about the Basle picture another time; now we must have all about the execution,” said Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “Tell us about that face as it appeared to your imagination—how should it be drawn?—just the face alone, do you mean?”

title: The Idiot
text: “It was just a minute before the execution,” began the prince, readily, carried away by the recollection and evidently forgetting everything else in a moment; “just at the instant when he stepped off the ladder on to the scaffold.

title: The Idiot
text: He happened to look in my direction: I saw his eyes and understood all, at once—but how am I to describe it?

title: The Idiot
text: I do so wish you or somebody else could draw it, you, if possible.

title: The Idiot
text: I thought at the time what a picture it would make.

title: The Idiot
text: You must imagine all that went before, of course, all—all.

title: The Idiot
text: He had lived in the prison for some time and had not expected that the execution would take place for at least a week yet—he had counted on all the formalities and so on taking time; but it so happened that his papers had been got ready quickly.

title: The Idiot
text: At five o’clock in the morning he was asleep—it was October, and at five in the morning it was cold and dark.

title: The Idiot
text: The governor of the prison comes in on tip-toe and touches the sleeping man’s shoulder gently.

title: The Idiot
text: He starts up.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘What is it?’ he says.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘The execution is fixed for ten o’clock. He was only just awake, and would not believe at first, but began to argue that his papers would not be out for a week, and so on. When he was wide awake and realized the truth, he became very silent and argued no more—so they say; but after a bit he said: ‘It comes very hard on one so suddenly’ and then he was silent again and said nothing.

title: The Idiot
text: “The three or four hours went by, of course, in necessary preparations—the priest, breakfast, (coffee, meat, and some wine they gave him; doesn’t it seem ridiculous?) And yet I believe these people give them a good breakfast out of pure kindness of heart, and believe that they are doing a good action.

title: The Idiot
text: Then he is dressed, and then begins the procession through the town to the scaffold.

title: The Idiot
text: I think he, too, must feel that he has an age to live still while they cart him along.

title: The Idiot
text: Probably he thought, on the way, ‘Oh, I have a long, long time yet. Three streets of life yet! When we’ve passed this street there’ll be that other one; and then that one where the baker’s shop is on the right; and when shall we get there? It’s ages, ages!

title: The Idiot
text: Around him are crowds shouting, yelling—ten thousand faces, twenty thousand eyes.

title: The Idiot
text: All this has to be endured, and especially the thought: ‘Here are ten thousand men, and not one of them is going to be executed, and yet I am to die.

title: The Idiot
text: Well, all that is preparatory.

title: The Idiot
text: “At the scaffold there is a ladder, and just there he burst into tears—and this was a strong man, and a terribly wicked one, they say!

title: The Idiot
text: There was a priest with him the whole time, talking; even in the cart as they drove along, he talked and talked.

title: The Idiot
text: Probably the other heard nothing; he would begin to listen now and then, and at the third word or so he had forgotten all about it.

title: The Idiot
text: “At last he began to mount the steps; his legs were tied, so that he had to take very small steps.

title: The Idiot
text: The priest, who seemed to be a wise man, had stopped talking now, and only held the cross for the wretched fellow to kiss.

title: The Idiot
text: At the foot of the ladder he had been pale enough; but when he set foot on the scaffold at the top, his face suddenly became the colour of paper, positively like white notepaper.

title: The Idiot
text: His legs must have become suddenly feeble and helpless, and he felt a choking in his throat—you know the sudden feeling one has in moments of terrible fear, when one does not lose one’s wits, but is absolutely powerless to move?

title: The Idiot
text: If some dreadful thing were suddenly to happen; if a house were just about to fall on one;—don’t you know how one would long to sit down and shut one’s eyes and wait, and wait?

title: The Idiot
text: Well, when this terrible feeling came over him, the priest quickly pressed the cross to his lips, without a word—a little silver cross it was—and he kept on pressing it to the man’s lips every second.

title: The Idiot
text: And whenever the cross touched his lips, the eyes would open for a moment, and the legs moved once, and he kissed the cross greedily, hurriedly—just as though he were anxious to catch hold of something in case of its being useful to him afterwards, though he could hardly have had any connected religious thoughts at the time.

title: The Idiot
text: And so up to the very block.

title: The Idiot
text: “How strange that criminals seldom swoon at such a moment!

title: The Idiot
text: On the contrary, the brain is especially active, and works incessantly—probably hard, hard, hard—like an engine at full pressure.

title: The Idiot
