text: I imagine that various thoughts must beat loud and fast through his head—all unfinished ones, and strange, funny thoughts, very likely!

title: The Idiot
text: —like this, for instance: ‘That man is looking at me, and he has a wart on his forehead! and the executioner has burst one of his buttons, and the lowest one is all rusty! And meanwhile he notices and remembers everything. There is one point that cannot be forgotten, round which everything else dances and turns about; and because of this point he cannot faint, and this lasts until the very final quarter of a second, when the wretched neck is on the block and the victim listens and waits and knows—that’s the point, he knows that he is just now about to die, and listens for the rasp of the iron over his head.

title: The Idiot
text: If I lay there, I should certainly listen for that grating sound, and hear it, too!

title: The Idiot
text: There would probably be but the tenth part of an instant left to hear it in, but one would certainly hear it.

title: The Idiot
text: And imagine, some people declare that when the head flies off it is conscious of having flown off!

title: The Idiot
text: Just imagine what a thing to realize!

title: The Idiot
text: Fancy if consciousness were to last for even five seconds!

title: The Idiot
text: “Draw the scaffold so that only the top step of the ladder comes in clearly.

title: The Idiot
text: The criminal must be just stepping on to it, his face as white as note-paper.

title: The Idiot
text: The priest is holding the cross to his blue lips, and the criminal kisses it, and knows and sees and understands everything.

title: The Idiot
text: The cross and the head—there’s your picture; the priest and the executioner, with his two assistants, and a few heads and eyes below.

title: The Idiot
text: Those might come in as subordinate accessories—a sort of mist.

title: The Idiot
text: There’s a picture for you.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince paused, and looked around.

title: The Idiot
text: “Certainly that isn’t much like quietism,” murmured Alexandra, half to herself.

title: The Idiot
text: “Now tell us about your love affairs,” said Adelaida, after a moment’s pause.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince gazed at her in amazement.

title: The Idiot
text: “You know,” Adelaida continued, “you owe us a description of the Basle picture; but first I wish to hear how you fell in love. Don’t deny the fact, for you did, of course. Besides, you stop philosophizing when you are telling about anything.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why are you ashamed of your stories the moment after you have told them?” asked Aglaya, suddenly.

title: The Idiot
text: “How silly you are!” said Mrs. Epanchin, looking indignantly towards the last speaker.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, that wasn’t a clever remark,” said Alexandra.

title: The Idiot
text: “Don’t listen to her, prince,” said Mrs. Epanchin; “she says that sort of thing out of mischief. Don’t think anything of their nonsense, it means nothing. They love to chaff, but they like you. I can see it in their faces—I know their faces.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I know their faces, too,” said the prince, with a peculiar stress on the words.

title: The Idiot
text: “How so?” asked Adelaida, with curiosity.

title: The Idiot
text: “What do you know about our faces?” exclaimed the other two, in chorus.

title: The Idiot
text: But the prince was silent and serious.

title: The Idiot
text: All awaited his reply.

title: The Idiot
text: “I’ll tell you afterwards,” he said quietly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Ah, you want to arouse our curiosity!” said Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “And how terribly solemn you are about it!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Very well,” interrupted Adelaida, “then if you can read faces so well, you must have been in love. Come now; I’ve guessed—let’s have the secret!”

title: The Idiot
text: “I have not been in love,” said the prince, as quietly and seriously as before.

title: The Idiot
text: “I have been happy in another way.”

title: The Idiot
text: “How, how?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, I’ll tell you,” said the prince, apparently in a deep reverie.

title: The Idiot
text: “Here you all are,” began the prince, “settling yourselves down to listen to me with so much curiosity, that if I do not satisfy you you will probably be angry with me. No, no! I’m only joking!” he added, hastily, with a smile.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, then—they were all children there, and I was always among children and only with children.

title: The Idiot
text: They were the children of the village in which I lived, and they went to the school there—all of them.

title: The Idiot
text: I did not teach them, oh no; there was a master for that, one Jules Thibaut.

title: The Idiot
text: I may have taught them some things, but I was among them just as an outsider, and I passed all four years of my life there among them.

title: The Idiot
text: I wished for nothing better; I used to tell them everything and hid nothing from them.

title: The Idiot
text: Their fathers and relations were very angry with me, because the children could do nothing without me at last, and used to throng after me at all times.

title: The Idiot
text: The schoolmaster was my greatest enemy in the end!

title: The Idiot
text: I had many enemies, and all because of the children.

title: The Idiot
text: Even Schneider reproached me.

title: The Idiot
text: What were they afraid of?

title: The Idiot
text: One can tell a child everything, anything.

title: The Idiot
text: I have often been struck by the fact that parents know their children so little.

title: The Idiot
text: They should not conceal so much from them.

title: The Idiot
text: How well even little children understand that their parents conceal things from them, because they consider them too young to understand!

title: The Idiot
text: Children are capable of giving advice in the most important matters.

title: The Idiot
text: How can one deceive these dear little birds, when they look at one so sweetly and confidingly?

title: The Idiot
text: I call them birds because there is nothing in the world better than birds!

title: The Idiot
text: “However, most of the people were angry with me about one and the same thing; but Thibaut simply was jealous of me.

title: The Idiot
text: At first he had wagged his head and wondered how it was that the children understood what I told them so well, and could not learn from him; and he laughed like anything when I replied that neither he nor I could teach them very much, but that they might teach us a good deal.

title: The Idiot
text: “How he could hate me and tell scandalous stories about me, living among children as he did, is what I cannot understand.

title: The Idiot
text: Children soothe and heal the wounded heart.

title: The Idiot
text: I remember there was one poor fellow at our professor’s who was being treated for madness, and you have no idea what those children did for him, eventually.

title: The Idiot
text: I don’t think he was mad, but only terribly unhappy.

title: The Idiot
text: But I’ll tell you all about him another day.

title: The Idiot
text: Now I must get on with this story.

title: The Idiot
text: “The children did not love me at first; I was such a sickly, awkward kind of a fellow then—and I know I am ugly.

title: The Idiot
text: Besides, I was a foreigner.

title: The Idiot
text: The children used to laugh at me, at first; and they even went so far as to throw stones at me, when they saw me kiss Marie.

title: The Idiot
text: I only kissed her once in my life—no, no, don’t laugh!

title: The Idiot
text: The prince hastened to suppress the smiles of his audience at this point.

title: The Idiot
text: “It was not a matter of love at all!

title: The Idiot
text: If only you knew what a miserable creature she was, you would have pitied her, just as I did.

title: The Idiot
text: She belonged to our village.

title: The Idiot
text: Her mother was an old, old woman, and they used to sell string and thread, and soap and tobacco, out of the window of their little house, and lived on the pittance they gained by this trade.

title: The Idiot
text: The old woman was ill and very old, and could hardly move.

title: The Idiot
text: Marie was her daughter, a girl of twenty, weak and thin and consumptive; but still she did heavy work at the houses around, day by day.

title: The Idiot
text: Well, one fine day a commercial traveller betrayed her and carried her off; and a week later he deserted her.

title: The Idiot
text: She came home dirty, draggled, and shoeless; she had walked for a whole week without shoes; she had slept in the fields, and caught a terrible cold; her feet were swollen and sore, and her hands torn and scratched all over.

title: The Idiot
text: She never had been pretty even before; but her eyes were quiet, innocent, kind eyes.

title: The Idiot
text: “She was very quiet always—and I remember once, when she had suddenly begun singing at her work, everyone said, ‘Marie tried to sing today!’ and she got so chaffed that she was silent for ever after.

title: The Idiot
text: She had been treated kindly in the place before; but when she came back now—ill and shunned and miserable—not one of them all had the slightest sympathy for her.

title: The Idiot
text: Cruel people!

title: The Idiot
text: Oh, what hazy understandings they have on such matters!

title: The Idiot
text: Her mother was the first to show the way.

title: The Idiot
text: She received her wrathfully, unkindly, and with contempt.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘You have disgraced me,’ she said.

title: The Idiot
text: She was the first to cast her into ignominy; but when they all heard that Marie had returned to the village, they ran out to see her and crowded into the little cottage—old men, children, women, girls—such a hurrying, stamping, greedy crowd.

title: The Idiot
text: Marie was lying on the floor at the old woman’s feet, hungry, torn, draggled, crying, miserable.

title: The Idiot
text: “When everyone crowded into the room she hid her face in her dishevelled hair and lay cowering on the floor.

title: The Idiot
text: Everyone looked at her as though she were a piece of dirt off the road.

title: The Idiot
text: The old men scolded and condemned, and the young ones laughed at her.

title: The Idiot
text: The women condemned her too, and looked at her contemptuously, just as though she were some loathsome insect.

title: The Idiot
text: “Her mother allowed all this to go on, and nodded her head and encouraged them.

title: The Idiot
text: The old woman was very ill at that time, and knew she was dying (she really did die a couple of months later), and though she felt the end approaching she never thought of forgiving her daughter, to the very day of her death.

title: The Idiot
text: She would not even speak to her.

title: The Idiot
text: She made her sleep on straw in a shed, and hardly gave her food enough to support life.

title: The Idiot
text: “Marie was very gentle to her mother, and nursed her, and did everything for her; but the old woman accepted all her services without a word and never showed her the slightest kindness.

title: The Idiot
text: Marie bore all this; and I could see when I got to know her that she thought it quite right and fitting, considering herself the lowest and meanest of creatures.

title: The Idiot
text: “When the old woman took to her bed finally, the other old women in the village sat with her by turns, as the custom is there; and then Marie was quite driven out of the house.

title: The Idiot
text: They gave her no food at all, and she could not get any work in the village; none would employ her.

title: The Idiot
text: The men seemed to consider her no longer a woman, they said such dreadful things to her.

title: The Idiot
text: Sometimes on Sundays, if they were drunk enough, they used to throw her a penny or two, into the mud, and Marie would silently pick up the money.

title: The Idiot
text: She had began to spit blood at that time.

title: The Idiot
text: “At last her rags became so tattered and torn that she was ashamed of appearing in the village any longer.

title: The Idiot
text: The children used to pelt her with mud; so she begged to be taken on as assistant cowherd, but the cowherd would not have her.

title: The Idiot
text: Then she took to helping him without leave; and he saw how valuable her assistance was to him, and did not drive her away again; on the contrary, he occasionally gave her the remnants of his dinner, bread and cheese.

title: The Idiot
text: He considered that he was being very kind.

title: The Idiot
text: When the mother died, the village parson was not ashamed to hold Marie up to public derision and shame.

title: The Idiot
text: Marie was standing at the coffin’s head, in all her rags, crying.

title: The Idiot
text: “A crowd of people had collected to see how she would cry.

title: The Idiot
text: The parson, a young fellow ambitious of becoming a great preacher, began his sermon and pointed to Marie.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘There,’ he said, ‘there is the cause of the death of this venerable woman’—(which was a lie, because she had been ill for at least two years)—‘there she stands before you, and dares not lift her eyes from the ground, because she knows that the finger of God is upon her.

title: The Idiot
text: Look at her tatters and rags—the badge of those who lose their virtue.

title: The Idiot
text: Who is she?

title: The Idiot
text: her daughter!

title: The Idiot
text: ’ and so on to the end.

title: The Idiot
text: “And just fancy, this infamy pleased them, all of them, nearly.

title: The Idiot
text: Only the children had altered—for then they were all on my side and had learned to love Marie.

title: The Idiot
text: “This is how it was: I had wished to do something for Marie; I longed to give her some money, but I never had a farthing while I was there.

title: The Idiot
text: But I had a little diamond pin, and this I sold to a travelling pedlar; he gave me eight francs for it—it was worth at least forty.

title: The Idiot
text: “I long sought to meet Marie alone; and at last I did meet her, on the hillside beyond the village.

title: The Idiot
text: I gave her the eight francs and asked her to take care of the money because I could get no more; and then I kissed her and said that she was not to suppose I kissed her with any evil motives or because I was in love with her, for that I did so solely out of pity for her, and because from the first I had not accounted her as guilty so much as unfortunate.

title: The Idiot
text: I longed to console and encourage her somehow, and to assure her that she was not the low, base thing which she and others strove to make out; but I don’t think she understood me.

title: The Idiot
text: She stood before me, dreadfully ashamed of herself, and with downcast eyes; and when I had finished she kissed my hand.

title: The Idiot
text: I would have kissed hers, but she drew it away.

title: The Idiot
text: Just at this moment the whole troop of children saw us.

title: The Idiot
text: (I found out afterwards that they had long kept a watch upon me.)

title: The Idiot
text: They all began whistling and clapping their hands, and laughing at us.

title: The Idiot
text: Marie ran away at once; and when I tried to talk to them, they threw stones at me.

title: The Idiot
text: All the village heard of it the same day, and Marie’s position became worse than ever.

title: The Idiot
text: The children would not let her pass now in the streets, but annoyed her and threw dirt at her more than before.

title: The Idiot
text: They used to run after her—she racing away with her poor feeble lungs panting and gasping, and they pelting her and shouting abuse at her.

title: The Idiot
text: “Once I had to interfere by force; and after that I took to speaking to them every day and whenever I could.

title: The Idiot
text: Occasionally they stopped and listened; but they teased Marie all the same.

title: The Idiot
text: “I told them how unhappy Marie was, and after a while they stopped their abuse of her, and let her go by silently.

title: The Idiot
text: Little by little we got into the way of conversing together, the children and I.

title: The Idiot
text: I concealed nothing from them, I told them all.

title: The Idiot
text: They listened very attentively and soon began to be sorry for Marie.

title: The Idiot
text: At last some of them took to saying ‘Good-morning’ to her, kindly, when they met her.

title: The Idiot
text: It is the custom there to salute anyone you meet with ‘Good-morning’ whether acquainted or not.

title: The Idiot
text: I can imagine how astonished Marie was at these first greetings from the children.

title: The Idiot
text: “Once two little girls got hold of some food and took it to her, and came back and told me.

title: The Idiot
text: They said she had burst into tears, and that they loved her very much now.

title: The Idiot
text: Very soon after that they all became fond of Marie, and at the same time they began to develop the greatest affection for myself.

title: The Idiot
text: They often came to me and begged me to tell them stories.

title: The Idiot
text: I think I must have told stories well, for they did so love to hear them.

title: The Idiot
text: At last I took to reading up interesting things on purpose to pass them on to the little ones, and this went on for all the rest of my time there, three years.

title: The Idiot
text: Later, when everyone—even Schneider—was angry with me for hiding nothing from the children, I pointed out how foolish it was, for they always knew things, only they learnt them in a way that soiled their minds but not so from me.

title: The Idiot
text: One has only to remember one’s own childhood to admit the truth of this.

title: The Idiot
text: But nobody was convinced...

title: The Idiot
text: It was two weeks before her mother died that I had kissed Marie; and when the clergyman preached that sermon the children were all on my side.

title: The Idiot
text: “When I told them what a shame it was of the parson to talk as he had done, and explained my reason, they were so angry that some of them went and broke his windows with stones.

title: The Idiot
text: Of course I stopped them, for that was not right, but all the village heard of it, and how I caught it for spoiling the children!

title: The Idiot
text: Everyone discovered now that the little ones had taken to being fond of Marie, and their parents were terribly alarmed; but Marie was so happy.

title: The Idiot
text: The children were forbidden to meet her; but they used to run out of the village to the herd and take her food and things; and sometimes just ran off there and kissed her, and said, ‘Je vous aime, Marie!’ and then trotted back again.

title: The Idiot
text: They imagined that I was in love with Marie, and this was the only point on which I did not undeceive them, for they got such enjoyment out of it.

title: The Idiot
text: And what delicacy and tenderness they showed!

title: The Idiot
text: “In the evening I used to walk to the waterfall.

title: The Idiot
text: There was a spot there which was quite closed in and hidden from view by large trees; and to this spot the children used to come to me.

title: The Idiot
text: They could not bear that their dear Leon should love a poor girl without shoes to her feet and dressed all in rags and tatters.

title: The Idiot
text: So, would you believe it, they actually clubbed together, somehow, and bought her shoes and stockings, and some linen, and even a dress!

title: The Idiot
text: I can’t understand how they managed it, but they did it, all together.

title: The Idiot
text: When I asked them about it they only laughed and shouted, and the little girls clapped their hands and kissed me. I sometimes went to see Marie secretly, too.

title: The Idiot
text: She had become very ill, and could hardly walk.

title: The Idiot
text: She still went with the herd, but could not help the herdsman any longer.

title: The Idiot
text: She used to sit on a stone near, and wait there almost motionless all day, till the herd went home.

title: The Idiot
text: Her consumption was so advanced, and she was so weak, that she used to sit with closed eyes, breathing heavily.

title: The Idiot
text: Her face was as thin as a skeleton’s, and sweat used to stand on her white brow in large drops.

title: The Idiot
text: I always found her sitting just like that.

title: The Idiot
text: I used to come up quietly to look at her; but Marie would hear me, open her eyes, and tremble violently as she kissed my hands.

title: The Idiot
text: I did not take my hand away because it made her happy to have it, and so she would sit and cry quietly.

title: The Idiot
text: Sometimes she tried to speak; but it was very difficult to understand her.

title: The Idiot
text: She was almost like a madwoman, with excitement and ecstasy, whenever I came.

title: The Idiot
text: Occasionally the children came with me; when they did so, they would stand some way off and keep guard over us, so as to tell me if anybody came near.

title: The Idiot
text: This was a great pleasure to them.

title: The Idiot
text: “When we left her, Marie used to relapse at once into her old condition, and sit with closed eyes and motionless limbs.

title: The Idiot
text: One day she could not go out at all, and remained at home all alone in the empty hut; but the children very soon became aware of the fact, and nearly all of them visited her that day as she lay alone and helpless in her miserable bed.

title: The Idiot
text: “For two days the children looked after her, and then, when the village people got to know that Marie was really dying, some of the old women came and took it in turns to sit by her and look after her a bit.

title: The Idiot
text: I think they began to be a little sorry for her in the village at last; at all events they did not interfere with the children any more, on her account.

title: The Idiot
text: “Marie lay in a state of uncomfortable delirium the whole while; she coughed dreadfully.

title: The Idiot
text: The old women would not let the children stay in the room; but they all collected outside the window each morning, if only for a moment, and shouted ‘Bon jour, notre bonne Marie!’ and Marie no sooner caught sight of, or heard them, and she became quite animated at once, and, in spite of the old women, would try to sit up and nod her head and smile at them, and thank them.

title: The Idiot
text: The little ones used to bring her nice things and sweets to eat, but she could hardly touch anything.

title: The Idiot
text: Thanks to them, I assure you, the girl died almost perfectly happy.

title: The Idiot
text: She almost forgot her misery, and seemed to accept their love as a sort of symbol of pardon for her offence, though she never ceased to consider herself a dreadful sinner.

title: The Idiot
text: They used to flutter at her window just like little birds, calling out: ‘Nous t’aimons, Marie!’

title: The Idiot
text: “She died very soon; I had thought she would live much longer.

title: The Idiot
text: The day before her death I went to see her for the last time, just before sunset.

title: The Idiot
text: I think she recognized me, for she pressed my hand.

title: The Idiot
text: “Next morning they came and told me that Marie was dead.

title: The Idiot
text: The children could not be restrained now; they went and covered her coffin with flowers, and put a wreath of lovely blossoms on her head.

title: The Idiot
text: The pastor did not throw any more shameful words at the poor dead woman; but there were very few people at the funeral.

title: The Idiot
text: However, when it came to carrying the coffin, all the children rushed up, to carry it themselves.

title: The Idiot
text: Of course they could not do it alone, but they insisted on helping, and walked alongside and behind, crying.

title: The Idiot
text: “They have planted roses all round her grave, and every year they look after the flowers and make Marie’s resting-place as beautiful as they can.

title: The Idiot
text: I was in ill odour after all this with the parents of the children, and especially with the parson and schoolmaster.

title: The Idiot
text: Schneider was obliged to promise that I should not meet them and talk to them; but we conversed from a distance by signs, and they used to write me sweet little notes.

title: The Idiot
text: Afterwards I came closer than ever to those little souls, but even then it was very dear to me, to have them so fond of me.

title: The Idiot
text: “Schneider said that I did the children great harm by my pernicious ‘system’; what nonsense that was!

title: The Idiot
text: And what did he mean by my system?

title: The Idiot
text: He said afterwards that he believed I was a child myself—just before I came away.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘You have the form and face of an adult’ he said, ‘but as regards soul, and character, and perhaps even intelligence, you are a child in the completest sense of the word, and always will be, if you live to be sixty. I laughed very much, for of course that is nonsense. But it is a fact that I do not care to be among grown-up people and much prefer the society of children. However kind people may be to me, I never feel quite at home with them, and am always glad to get back to my little companions. Now my companions have always been children, not because I was a child myself once, but because young things attract me. On one of the first days of my stay in Switzerland, I was strolling about alone and miserable, when I came upon the children rushing noisily out of school, with their slates and bags, and books, their games, their laughter and shouts—and my soul went out to them. I stopped and laughed happily as I watched their little feet moving so quickly. Girls and boys, laughing and crying; for as they went home many of them found time to fight and make peace, to weep and play. I forgot my troubles in looking at them. And then, all those three years, I tried to understand why men should be for ever tormenting themselves. I lived the life of a child there, and thought I should never leave the little village; indeed, I was far from thinking that I should ever return to Russia. But at last I recognized the fact that Schneider could not keep me any longer. And then something so important happened, that Schneider himself urged me to depart. I am going to see now if can get good advice about it. Perhaps my lot in life will be changed; but that is not the principal thing. The principal thing is the entire change that has already come over me. I left many things behind me—too many. They have gone. On the journey I said to myself, ‘I am going into the world of men. I don’t know much, perhaps, but a new life has begun for me. I made up my mind to be honest, and steadfast in accomplishing my task.

title: The Idiot
text: Perhaps I shall meet with troubles and many disappointments, but I have made up my mind to be polite and sincere to everyone; more cannot be asked of me.

title: The Idiot
text: People may consider me a child if they like.

title: The Idiot
text: I am often called an idiot, and at one time I certainly was so ill that I was nearly as bad as an idiot; but I am not an idiot now.

title: The Idiot
text: How can I possibly be so when I know myself that I am considered one?

title: The Idiot
text: “When I received a letter from those dear little souls, while passing through Berlin, I only then realized how much I loved them.

title: The Idiot
text: It was very, very painful, getting that first little letter.

title: The Idiot
text: How melancholy they had been when they saw me off!

title: The Idiot
text: For a month before, they had been talking of my departure and sorrowing over it; and at the waterfall, of an evening, when we parted for the night, they would hug me so tight and kiss me so warmly, far more so than before.

title: The Idiot
text: And every now and then they would turn up one by one when I was alone, just to give me a kiss and a hug, to show their love for me.

title: The Idiot
text: The whole flock went with me to the station, which was about a mile from the village, and every now and then one of them would stop to throw his arms round me, and all the little girls had tears in their voices, though they tried hard not to cry.

title: The Idiot
text: As the train steamed out of the station, I saw them all standing on the platform waving to me and crying ‘Hurrah!’ till they were lost in the distance.

title: The Idiot
text: “I assure you, when I came in here just now and saw your kind faces (I can read faces well) my heart felt light for the first time since that moment of parting.

title: The Idiot
text: I think I must be one of those who are born to be in luck, for one does not often meet with people whom one feels he can love from the first sight of their faces; and yet, no sooner do I step out of the railway carriage than I happen upon you!

title: The Idiot
text: “I know it is more or less a shamefaced thing to speak of one’s feelings before others; and yet here am I talking like this to you, and am not a bit ashamed or shy.

title: The Idiot
text: I am an unsociable sort of fellow and shall very likely not come to see you again for some time; but don’t think the worse of me for that.

title: The Idiot
text: It is not that I do not value your society; and you must never suppose that I have taken offence at anything.

title: The Idiot
text: “You asked me about your faces, and what I could read in them; I will tell you with the greatest pleasure.

title: The Idiot
text: You, Adelaida Ivanovna, have a very happy face; it is the most sympathetic of the three.

title: The Idiot
text: Not to speak of your natural beauty, one can look at your face and say to one’s self, ‘She has the face of a kind sister. You are simple and merry, but you can see into another’s heart very quickly. That’s what I read in your face.

title: The Idiot
text: “You too, Alexandra Ivanovna, have a very lovely face; but I think you may have some secret sorrow.

title: The Idiot
text: Your heart is undoubtedly a kind, good one, but you are not merry.

title: The Idiot
text: There is a certain suspicion of ‘shadow’ in your face, like in that of Holbein’s Madonna in Dresden.

title: The Idiot
text: So much for your face.

title: The Idiot
text: Have I guessed right?

title: The Idiot
text: “As for your face, Lizabetha Prokofievna, I not only think, but am perfectly sure, that you are an absolute child—in all, in all, mind, both good and bad—and in spite of your years. Don’t be angry with me for saying so; you know what my feelings for children are. And do not suppose that I am so candid out of pure simplicity of soul. Oh dear no, it is by no means the case! Perhaps I have my own very profound object in view.”

title: The Idiot
text: When the prince ceased speaking all were gazing merrily at him—even Aglaya; but Lizabetha Prokofievna looked the jolliest of all.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well!” she cried, “we have ‘put him through his paces,’ with a vengeance! My dears, you imagined, I believe, that you were about to patronize this young gentleman, like some poor protégé picked up somewhere, and taken under your magnificent protection. What fools we were, and what a specially big fool is your father! Well done, prince! I assure you the general actually asked me to put you through your paces, and examine you. As to what you said about my face, you are absolutely correct in your judgment. I am a child, and know it. I knew it long before you said so; you have expressed my own thoughts. I think your nature and mine must be extremely alike, and I am very glad of it. We are like two drops of water, only you are a man and I a woman, and I’ve not been to Switzerland, and that is all the difference between us.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Don’t be in a hurry, mother; the prince says that he has some motive behind his simplicity,” cried Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, yes, so he does,” laughed the others.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, don’t you begin bantering him,” said mamma.

title: The Idiot
text: “He is probably a good deal cleverer than all three of you girls put together. We shall see. Only you haven’t told us anything about Aglaya yet, prince; and Aglaya and I are both waiting to hear.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I cannot say anything at present. I’ll tell you afterwards.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why? Her face is clear enough, isn’t it?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh yes, of course. You are very beautiful, Aglaya Ivanovna, so beautiful that one is afraid to look at you.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Is that all? What about her character?” persisted Mrs. Epanchin.

title: The Idiot
text: “It is difficult to judge when such beauty is concerned. I have not prepared my judgment. Beauty is a riddle.”

title: The Idiot
text: “That means that you have set Aglaya a riddle!” said Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “Guess it, Aglaya! But she’s pretty, prince, isn’t she?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Most wonderfully so,” said the latter, warmly, gazing at Aglaya with admiration.

title: The Idiot
text: “Almost as lovely as Nastasia Philipovna, but quite a different type.”

title: The Idiot
text: All present exchanged looks of surprise.

title: The Idiot
text: “As lovely as who?” said Mrs. Epanchin.

title: The Idiot
text: “As Nastasia Philipovna? Where have you seen Nastasia Philipovna? What Nastasia Philipovna?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Gavrila Ardalionovitch showed the general her portrait just now.”

title: The Idiot
text: “How so? Did he bring the portrait for my husband?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Only to show it. Nastasia Philipovna gave it to Gavrila Ardalionovitch today, and the latter brought it here to show to the general.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I must see it!” cried Mrs. Epanchin.

title: The Idiot
text: “Where is the portrait? If she gave it to him, he must have it; and he is still in the study. He never leaves before four o’clock on Wednesdays. Send for Gavrila Ardalionovitch at once. No, I don’t long to see him so much. Look here, dear prince, be so kind, will you? Just step to the study and fetch this portrait! Say we want to look at it. Please do this for me, will you?”

title: The Idiot
text: “He is a nice fellow, but a little too simple,” said Adelaida, as the prince left the room.

title: The Idiot
text: “He is, indeed,” said Alexandra; “almost laughably so at times.”

title: The Idiot
text: Neither one nor the other seemed to give expression to her full thoughts.

title: The Idiot
text: “He got out of it very neatly about our faces, though,” said Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: “He flattered us all round, even mamma.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Nonsense!” cried the latter.

title: The Idiot
text: “He did not flatter me. It was I who found his appreciation flattering. I think you are a great deal more foolish than he is. He is simple, of course, but also very knowing. Just like myself.”

title: The Idiot
text: “How stupid of me to speak of the portrait,” thought the prince as he entered the study, with a feeling of guilt at his heart, “and yet, perhaps I was right after all.

title: The Idiot
text: He had an idea, unformed as yet, but a strange idea.

title: The Idiot
text: Gavrila Ardalionovitch was still sitting in the study, buried in a mass of papers.

title: The Idiot
text: He looked as though he did not take his salary from the public company, whose servant he was, for a sinecure.

title: The Idiot
text: He grew very wroth and confused when the prince asked for the portrait, and explained how it came about that he had spoken of it.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, curse it all,” he said; “what on earth must you go blabbing for? You know nothing about the thing, and yet—idiot!” he added, muttering the last word to himself in irrepressible rage.

title: The Idiot
text: “I am very sorry; I was not thinking at the time. I merely said that Aglaya was almost as beautiful as Nastasia Philipovna.”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania asked for further details; and the prince once more repeated the conversation.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania looked at him with ironical contempt the while.

title: The Idiot
text: “Nastasia Philipovna,” he began, and there paused; he was clearly much agitated and annoyed.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince reminded him of the portrait.

title: The Idiot
text: “Listen, prince,” said Gania, as though an idea had just struck him, “I wish to ask you a great favour, and yet I really don’t know—”

title: The Idiot
text: He paused again, he was trying to make up his mind to something, and was turning the matter over.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince waited quietly.

title: The Idiot
text: Once more Gania fixed him with intent and questioning eyes.

title: The Idiot
text: “Prince,” he began again, “they are rather angry with me, in there, owing to a circumstance which I need not explain, so that I do not care to go in at present without an invitation. I particularly wish to speak to Aglaya, but I have written a few words in case I shall not have the chance of seeing her” (here the prince observed a small note in his hand), “and I do not know how to get my communication to her. Don’t you think you could undertake to give it to her at once, but only to her, mind, and so that no one else should see you give it? It isn’t much of a secret, but still—Well, will you do it?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t quite like it,” replied the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, but it is absolutely necessary for me,” Gania entreated.

title: The Idiot
text: “Believe me, if it were not so, I would not ask you; how else am I to get it to her? It is most important, dreadfully important!”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania was evidently much alarmed at the idea that the prince would not consent to take his note, and he looked at him now with an expression of absolute entreaty.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, I will take it then.”

title: The Idiot
text: “But mind, nobody is to see!” cried the delighted Gania “And of course I may rely on your word of honour, eh?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I won’t show it to anyone,” said the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “The letter is not sealed—” continued Gania, and paused in confusion.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, I won’t read it,” said the prince, quite simply.

title: The Idiot
text: He took up the portrait, and went out of the room.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania, left alone, clutched his head with his hands.

title: The Idiot
text: “One word from her,” he said, “one word from her, and I may yet be free.”

title: The Idiot
text: He could not settle himself to his papers again, for agitation and excitement, but began walking up and down the room from corner to corner.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince walked along, musing.

title: The Idiot
text: He did not like his commission, and disliked the idea of Gania sending a note to Aglaya at all; but when he was two rooms distant from the drawing-room, where they all were, he stopped as though recalling something; went to the window, nearer the light, and began to examine the portrait in his hand.

title: The Idiot
text: He longed to solve the mystery of something in the face of Nastasia Philipovna, something which had struck him as he looked at the portrait for the first time; the impression had not left him.

title: The Idiot
text: It was partly the fact of her marvellous beauty that struck him, and partly something else.

title: The Idiot
text: There was a suggestion of immense pride and disdain in the face almost of hatred, and at the same time something confiding and very full of simplicity.

title: The Idiot
text: The contrast aroused a deep sympathy in his heart as he looked at the lovely face.

title: The Idiot
text: The blinding loveliness of it was almost intolerable, this pale thin face with its flaming eyes; it was a strange beauty.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince gazed at it for a minute or two, then glanced around him, and hurriedly raised the portrait to his lips.

title: The Idiot
text: When, a minute after, he reached the drawing-room door, his face was quite composed.

title: The Idiot
text: But just as he reached the door he met Aglaya coming out alone.

title: The Idiot
text: “Gavrila Ardalionovitch begged me to give you this,” he said, handing her the note.

title: The Idiot
text: Aglaya stopped, took the letter, and gazed strangely into the prince’s eyes.

title: The Idiot
text: There was no confusion in her face; a little surprise, perhaps, but that was all.

title: The Idiot
text: By her look she seemed merely to challenge the prince to an explanation as to how he and Gania happened to be connected in this matter.

title: The Idiot
text: But her expression was perfectly cool and quiet, and even condescending.

title: The Idiot
text: So they stood for a moment or two, confronting one another.

title: The Idiot
text: At length a faint smile passed over her face, and she passed by him without a word.

title: The Idiot
text: Mrs. Epanchin examined the portrait of Nastasia Philipovna for some little while, holding it critically at arm’s length.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, she is pretty,” she said at last, “even very pretty. I have seen her twice, but only at a distance. So you admire this kind of beauty, do you?” she asked the prince, suddenly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, I do—this kind.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Do you mean especially this kind?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, especially this kind.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why?”

title: The Idiot
text: “There is much suffering in this face,” murmured the prince, more as though talking to himself than answering the question.

title: The Idiot
text: “I think you are wandering a little, prince,” Mrs. Epanchin decided, after a lengthened survey of his face; and she tossed the portrait on to the table, haughtily.

title: The Idiot
text: Alexandra took it, and Adelaida came up, and both the girls examined the photograph.

title: The Idiot
text: Just then Aglaya entered the room.

title: The Idiot
text: “What a power!” cried Adelaida suddenly, as she earnestly examined the portrait over her sister’s shoulder.

title: The Idiot
text: “Whom? What power?” asked her mother, crossly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Such beauty is real power,” said Adelaida.

title: The Idiot
text: “With such beauty as that one might overthrow the world.

title: The Idiot
text: She returned to her easel thoughtfully.

title: The Idiot
text: Aglaya merely glanced at the portrait—frowned, and put out her underlip; then went and sat down on the sofa with folded hands.

title: The Idiot
text: Mrs. Epanchin rang the bell.

title: The Idiot
text: “Ask Gavrila Ardalionovitch to step this way,” said she to the man who answered.

title: The Idiot
text: “Mamma!” cried Alexandra, significantly.

title: The Idiot
text: “I shall just say two words to him, that’s all,” said her mother, silencing all objection by her manner; she was evidently seriously put out.

title: The Idiot
text: “You see, prince, it is all secrets with us, just now—all secrets. It seems to be the etiquette of the house, for some reason or other. Stupid nonsense, and in a matter which ought to be approached with all candour and open-heartedness. There is a marriage being talked of, and I don’t like this marriage—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Mamma, what are you saying?” said Alexandra again, hurriedly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, what, my dear girl? As if you can possibly like it yourself? The heart is the great thing, and the rest is all rubbish—though one must have sense as well. Perhaps sense is really the great thing. Don’t smile like that, Aglaya. I don’t contradict myself. A fool with a heart and no brains is just as unhappy as a fool with brains and no heart. I am one and you are the other, and therefore both of us suffer, both of us are unhappy.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why are you so unhappy, mother?” asked Adelaida, who alone of all the company seemed to have preserved her good temper and spirits up to now.

title: The Idiot
text: “In the first place, because of my carefully brought-up daughters,” said Mrs. Epanchin, cuttingly; “and as that is the best reason I can give you we need not bother about any other at present. Enough of words, now! We shall see how both of you (I don’t count Aglaya) will manage your business, and whether you, most revered Alexandra Ivanovna, will be happy with your fine mate.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Ah!” she added, as Gania suddenly entered the room, “here’s another marrying subject. How do you do?” she continued, in response to Gania’s bow; but she did not invite him to sit down.

title: The Idiot
text: “You are going to be married?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Married? how—what marriage?” murmured Gania, overwhelmed with confusion.

title: The Idiot
text: “Are you about to take a wife? I ask,—if you prefer that expression.”

title: The Idiot
text: “No, no I—I—no!” said Gania, bringing out his lie with a tell-tale blush of shame.

title: The Idiot
text: He glanced keenly at Aglaya, who was sitting some way off, and dropped his eyes immediately.

title: The Idiot
text: Aglaya gazed coldly, intently, and composedly at him, without taking her eyes off his face, and watched his confusion.

title: The Idiot
text: “No? You say no, do you?” continued the pitiless Mrs. General.

title: The Idiot
text: “Very well, I shall remember that you told me this Wednesday morning, in answer to my question, that you are not going to be married. What day is it, Wednesday, isn’t it?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, I think so!” said Adelaida.

title: The Idiot

text: “Ferdishenko,” he said, gazing intently and inquiringly into the prince’s eyes.

text: “Very well, what next?” said the latter, almost laughing in his face.

title: The Idiot
text: “A lodger here,” continued the other, staring as before.

title: The Idiot
text: “Do you wish to make acquaintance?” asked the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Ah!” said the visitor, passing his fingers through his hair and sighing.

title: The Idiot
text: He then looked over to the other side of the room and around it.

title: The Idiot
text: “Got any money?” he asked, suddenly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Not much.”

title: The Idiot
text: “How much?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Twenty-five roubles.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Let’s see it.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince took his banknote out and showed it to Ferdishenko.

title: The Idiot
text: The latter unfolded it and looked at it; then he turned it round and examined the other side; then he held it up to the light.

title: The Idiot
text: “How strange that it should have browned so,” he said, reflectively.

title: The Idiot
text: “These twenty-five rouble notes brown in a most extraordinary way, while other notes often grow paler. Take it.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince took his note.

title: The Idiot
text: Ferdishenko rose.

title: The Idiot
text: “I came here to warn you,” he said.

title: The Idiot
text: “In the first place, don’t lend me any money, for I shall certainly ask you to.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Very well.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Shall you pay here?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, I intend to.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! I don’t intend to. Thanks. I live here, next door to you; you noticed a room, did you? Don’t come to me very often; I shall see you here quite often enough. Have you seen the general?”

title: The Idiot
text: “No.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Nor heard him?”

title: The Idiot
text: “No; of course not.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, you’ll both hear and see him soon; he even tries to borrow money from me. Avis au lecteur. Good-bye; do you think a man can possibly live with a name like Ferdishenko?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why not?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Good-bye.”

title: The Idiot
text: And so he departed.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince found out afterwards that this gentleman made it his business to amaze people with his originality and wit, but that it did not as a rule “come off.

title: The Idiot
text: He even produced a bad impression on some people, which grieved him sorely; but he did not change his ways for all that.

title: The Idiot
text: As he went out of the prince’s room, he collided with yet another visitor coming in.

title: The Idiot
text: Ferdishenko took the opportunity of making several warning gestures to the prince from behind the new arrival’s back, and left the room in conscious pride.

title: The Idiot
text: This next arrival was a tall red-faced man of about fifty-five, with greyish hair and whiskers, and large eyes which stood out of their sockets.

title: The Idiot
text: His appearance would have been distinguished had it not been that he gave the idea of being rather dirty.

title: The Idiot
text: He was dressed in an old coat, and he smelled of vodka when he came near.

title: The Idiot
text: His walk was effective, and he clearly did his best to appear dignified, and to impress people by his manner.

title: The Idiot
text: This gentleman now approached the prince slowly, and with a most courteous smile; silently took his hand and held it in his own, as he examined the prince’s features as though searching for familiar traits therein.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘Tis he, ‘tis he!” he said at last, quietly, but with much solemnity.

title: The Idiot
text: “As though he were alive once more. I heard the familiar name—the dear familiar name—and, oh! how it reminded me of the irrevocable past—Prince Muishkin, I believe?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Exactly so.”

title: The Idiot
text: “General Ivolgin—retired and unfortunate. May I ask your Christian and generic names?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Lef Nicolaievitch.”

title: The Idiot
text: “So, so—the son of my old, I may say my childhood’s friend, Nicolai Petrovitch.”

title: The Idiot
text: “My father’s name was Nicolai Lvovitch.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Lvovitch,” repeated the general without the slightest haste, and with perfect confidence, just as though he had not committed himself the least in the world, but merely made a little slip of the tongue.

title: The Idiot
text: He sat down, and taking the prince’s hand, drew him to a seat next to himself.

title: The Idiot
text: “I carried you in my arms as a baby,” he observed.

title: The Idiot
text: “Really?” asked the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why, it’s twenty years since my father died.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, yes—twenty years and three months. We were educated together; I went straight into the army, and he—”

title: The Idiot
text: “My father went into the army, too. He was a sub-lieutenant in the Vasiliefsky regiment.”

title: The Idiot
text: “No, sir—in the Bielomirsky; he changed into the latter shortly before his death. I was at his bedside when he died, and gave him my blessing for eternity. Your mother—”

title: The Idiot
text: The general paused, as though overcome with emotion.

title: The Idiot
text: “She died a few months later, from a cold,” said the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, not cold—believe an old man—not from a cold, but from grief for her prince. Oh—your mother, your mother! heigh-ho! Youth—youth! Your father and I—old friends as we were—nearly murdered each other for her sake.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince began to be a little incredulous.

title: The Idiot
text: “I was passionately in love with her when she was engaged—engaged to my friend. The prince noticed the fact and was furious. He came and woke me at seven o’clock one morning. I rise and dress in amazement; silence on both sides. I understand it all. He takes a couple of pistols out of his pocket—across a handkerchief—without witnesses. Why invite witnesses when both of us would be walking in eternity in a couple of minutes? The pistols are loaded; we stretch the handkerchief and stand opposite one another. We aim the pistols at each other’s hearts. Suddenly tears start to our eyes, our hands shake; we weep, we embrace—the battle is one of self-sacrifice now! The prince shouts, ‘She is yours;’ I cry, ‘She is yours—’ in a word, in a word—You’ve come to live with us, hey?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes—yes—for a while, I think,” stammered the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Prince, mother begs you to come to her,” said Colia, appearing at the door.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince rose to go, but the general once more laid his hand in a friendly manner on his shoulder, and dragged him down on to the sofa.

title: The Idiot
text: “As the true friend of your father, I wish to say a few words to you,” he began.

title: The Idiot
text: “I have suffered—there was a catastrophe. I suffered without a trial; I had no trial. Nina Alexandrovna my wife, is an excellent woman, so is my daughter Varvara. We have to let lodgings because we are poor—a dreadful, unheard-of come-down for us—for me, who should have been a governor-general; but we are very glad to have you, at all events. Meanwhile there is a tragedy in the house.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince looked inquiringly at the other.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, a marriage is being arranged—a marriage between a questionable woman and a young fellow who might be a flunkey. They wish to bring this woman into the house where my wife and daughter reside, but while I live and breathe she shall never enter my doors. I shall lie at the threshold, and she shall trample me underfoot if she does. I hardly talk to Gania now, and avoid him as much as I can. I warn you of this beforehand, but you cannot fail to observe it. But you are the son of my old friend, and I hope—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Prince, be so kind as to come to me for a moment in the drawing-room,” said Nina Alexandrovna herself, appearing at the door.

title: The Idiot
text: “Imagine, my dear,” cried the general, “it turns out that I have nursed the prince on my knee in the old days.

title: The Idiot
text: His wife looked searchingly at him, and glanced at the prince, but said nothing.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince rose and followed her; but hardly had they reached the drawing-room, and Nina Alexandrovna had begun to talk hurriedly, when in came the general.

title: The Idiot
text: She immediately relapsed into silence.

title: The Idiot
text: The master of the house may have observed this, but at all events he did not take any notice of it; he was in high good humour.

title: The Idiot
text: “A son of my old friend, dear,” he cried; “surely you must remember Prince Nicolai Lvovitch? You saw him at—at Tver.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t remember any Nicolai Lvovitch. Was that your father?” she inquired of the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, but he died at Elizabethgrad, not at Tver,” said the prince, rather timidly.

title: The Idiot
text: “So Pavlicheff told me.”

title: The Idiot
text: “No, Tver,” insisted the general; “he removed just before his death. You were very small and cannot remember; and Pavlicheff, though an excellent fellow, may have made a mistake.”

title: The Idiot
text: “You knew Pavlicheff then?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, yes—a wonderful fellow; but I was present myself. I gave him my blessing.”

title: The Idiot
text: “My father was just about to be tried when he died,” said the prince, “although I never knew of what he was accused. He died in hospital.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! it was the Kolpakoff business, and of course he would have been acquitted.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes? Do you know that for a fact?” asked the prince, whose curiosity was aroused by the general’s words.

title: The Idiot
text: “I should think so indeed!” cried the latter.

title: The Idiot
text: “The court-martial came to no decision. It was a mysterious, an impossible business, one might say! Captain Larionoff, commander of the company, had died; his command was handed over to the prince for the moment. Very well. This soldier, Kolpakoff, stole some leather from one of his comrades, intending to sell it, and spent the money on drink. Well! The prince—you understand that what follows took place in the presence of the sergeant-major, and a corporal—the prince rated Kolpakoff soundly, and threatened to have him flogged. Well, Kolpakoff went back to the barracks, lay down on a camp bedstead, and in a quarter of an hour was dead: you quite understand? It was, as I said, a strange, almost impossible, affair. In due course Kolpakoff was buried; the prince wrote his report, the deceased’s name was removed from the roll. All as it should be, is it not? But exactly three months later at the inspection of the brigade, the man Kolpakoff was found in the third company of the second battalion of infantry, Novozemlianski division, just as if nothing had happened!”

title: The Idiot
text: “What?” said the prince, much astonished.

title: The Idiot
text: “It did not occur—it’s a mistake!” said Nina Alexandrovna quickly, looking, at the prince rather anxiously.

title: The Idiot
text: “Mon mari se trompe,” she added, speaking in French.

title: The Idiot
text: “My dear, ‘se trompe’ is easily said. Do you remember any case at all like it? Everybody was at their wits’ end. I should be the first to say ‘qu’on se trompe,’ but unfortunately I was an eye-witness, and was also on the commission of inquiry. Everything proved that it was really he, the very same soldier Kolpakoff who had been given the usual military funeral to the sound of the drum. It is of course a most curious case—nearly an impossible one. I recognize that... but—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Father, your dinner is ready,” said Varvara at this point, putting her head in at the door.

title: The Idiot
text: “Very glad, I’m particularly hungry. Yes, yes, a strange coincidence—almost a psychological—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Your soup’ll be cold; do come.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Coming, coming,” said the general.

title: The Idiot
text: “Son of my old friend—” he was heard muttering as he went down the passage.

title: The Idiot
text: “You will have to excuse very much in my husband, if you stay with us,” said Nina Alexandrovna; “but he will not disturb you often. He dines alone. Everyone has his little peculiarities, you know, and some people perhaps have more than those who are most pointed at and laughed at. One thing I must beg of you—if my husband applies to you for payment for board and lodging, tell him that you have already paid me. Of course anything paid by you to the general would be as fully settled as if paid to me, so far as you are concerned; but I wish it to be so, if you please, for convenience’ sake. What is it, Varia?”

title: The Idiot
text: Varia had quietly entered the room, and was holding out the portrait of Nastasia Philipovna to her mother.

title: The Idiot
text: Nina Alexandrovna started, and examined the photograph intently, gazing at it long and sadly.

title: The Idiot
text: At last she looked up inquiringly at Varia.

title: The Idiot
text: “It’s a present from herself to him,” said Varia; “the question is to be finally decided this evening.”

title: The Idiot
text: “This evening!” repeated her mother in a tone of despair, but softly, as though to herself.

title: The Idiot
text: “Then it’s all settled, of course, and there’s no hope left to us. She has anticipated her answer by the present of her portrait. Did he show it you himself?” she added, in some surprise.

title: The Idiot
text: “You know we have hardly spoken to each other for a whole month. Ptitsin told me all about it; and the photo was lying under the table, and I picked it up.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Prince,” asked Nina Alexandrovna, “I wanted to inquire whether you have known my son long? I think he said that you had only arrived today from somewhere.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince gave a short narrative of what we have heard before, leaving out the greater part.

title: The Idiot
text: The two ladies listened intently.

title: The Idiot
text: “I did not ask about Gania out of curiosity,” said the elder, at last.

title: The Idiot
text: “I wish to know how much you know about him, because he said just now that we need not stand on ceremony with you. What, exactly, does that mean?”

title: The Idiot
text: At this moment Gania and Ptitsin entered the room together, and Nina Alexandrovna immediately became silent again.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince remained seated next to her, but Varia moved to the other end of the room; the portrait of Nastasia Philipovna remained lying as before on the work-table.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania observed it there, and with a frown of annoyance snatched it up and threw it across to his writing-table, which stood at the other end of the room.

title: The Idiot
text: “Is it today, Gania?” asked Nina Alexandrovna, at last.

title: The Idiot
text: “Is what today?” cried the former.

title: The Idiot
text: Then suddenly recollecting himself, he turned sharply on the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh,” he growled, “I see, you are here, that explains it! Is it a disease, or what, that you can’t hold your tongue? Look here, understand once for all, prince—”

title: The Idiot
text: “I am to blame in this, Gania—no one else,” said Ptitsin.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania glanced inquiringly at the speaker.

title: The Idiot
text: “It’s better so, you know, Gania—especially as, from one point of view, the matter may be considered as settled,” said Ptitsin; and sitting down a little way from the table he began to study a paper covered with pencil writing.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania stood and frowned, he expected a family scene.

title: The Idiot
text: He never thought of apologizing to the prince, however.

title: The Idiot
text: “If it’s all settled, Gania, then of course Mr. Ptitsin is right,” said Nina Alexandrovna.

title: The Idiot
text: “Don’t frown.

title: The Idiot
text: You need not worry yourself, Gania; I shall ask you no questions.

title: The Idiot
text: You need not tell me anything you don’t like.

title: The Idiot
text: I assure you I have quite submitted to your will.

title: The Idiot
text: She said all this, knitting away the while as though perfectly calm and composed.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania was surprised, but cautiously kept silence and looked at his mother, hoping that she would express herself more clearly.

title: The Idiot
text: Nina Alexandrovna observed his cautiousness and added, with a bitter smile:

title: The Idiot
text: “You are still suspicious, I see, and do not believe me; but you may be quite at your ease. There shall be no more tears, nor questions—not from my side, at all events. All I wish is that you may be happy, you know that. I have submitted to my fate; but my heart will always be with you, whether we remain united, or whether we part. Of course I only answer for myself—you can hardly expect your sister—”

title: The Idiot
text: “My sister again,” cried Gania, looking at her with contempt and almost hate.

title: The Idiot
text: “Look here, mother, I have already given you my word that I shall always respect you fully and absolutely, and so shall everyone else in this house, be it who it may, who shall cross this threshold.”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania was so much relieved that he gazed at his mother almost affectionately.

title: The Idiot
text: “I was not at all afraid for myself, Gania, as you know well. It was not for my own sake that I have been so anxious and worried all this time! They say it is all to be settled to-day. What is to be settled?”

title: The Idiot
text: “She has promised to tell me tonight at her own house whether she consents or not,” replied Gania.

title: The Idiot
text: “We have been silent on this subject for three weeks,” said his mother, “and it was better so; and now I will only ask you one question. How can she give her consent and make you a present of her portrait when you do not love her? How can such a—such a—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Practised hand—eh?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I was not going to express myself so. But how could you so blind her?”

title: The Idiot
text: Nina Alexandrovna’s question betrayed intense annoyance.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania waited a moment and then said, without taking the trouble to conceal the irony of his tone:

title: The Idiot
text: “There you are, mother, you are always like that. You begin by promising that there are to be no reproaches or insinuations or questions, and here you are beginning them at once. We had better drop the subject—we had, really. I shall never leave you, mother; any other man would cut and run from such a sister as this. See how she is looking at me at this moment! Besides, how do you know that I am blinding Nastasia Philipovna? As for Varia, I don’t care—she can do just as she pleases. There, that’s quite enough!”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania’s irritation increased with every word he uttered, as he walked up and down the room.

title: The Idiot
text: These conversations always touched the family sores before long.

title: The Idiot
text: “I have said already that the moment she comes in I go out, and I shall keep my word,” remarked Varia.

title: The Idiot
text: “Out of obstinacy” shouted Gania.

title: The Idiot
text: “You haven’t married, either, thanks to your obstinacy. Oh, you needn’t frown at me, Varvara! You can go at once for all I care; I am sick enough of your company. What, you are going to leave us are you, too?” he cried, turning to the prince, who was rising from his chair.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania’s voice was full of the most uncontrolled and uncontrollable irritation.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince turned at the door to say something, but perceiving in Gania’s expression that there was but that one drop wanting to make the cup overflow, he changed his mind and left the room without a word.

title: The Idiot
text: A few minutes later he was aware from the noisy voices in the drawing room, that the conversation had become more quarrelsome than ever after his departure.

title: The Idiot
text: He crossed the salon and the entrance-hall, so as to pass down the corridor into his own room.

title: The Idiot
text: As he came near the front door he heard someone outside vainly endeavouring to ring the bell, which was evidently broken, and only shook a little, without emitting any sound.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince took down the chain and opened the door.

title: The Idiot
text: He started back in amazement—for there stood Nastasia Philipovna.

title: The Idiot
text: He knew her at once from her photograph.

title: The Idiot
text: Her eyes blazed with anger as she looked at him.

title: The Idiot
text: She quickly pushed by him into the hall, shouldering him out of her way, and said, furiously, as she threw off her fur cloak:

title: The Idiot
text: “If you are too lazy to mend your bell, you should at least wait in the hall to let people in when they rattle the bell handle. There, now, you’ve dropped my fur cloak—dummy!”

title: The Idiot
text: Sure enough the cloak was lying on the ground.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia had thrown it off her towards the prince, expecting him to catch it, but the prince had missed it.

title: The Idiot
text: “Now then—announce me, quick!”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince wanted to say something, but was so confused and astonished that he could not.

title: The Idiot
text: However, he moved off towards the drawing-room with the cloak over his arm.

title: The Idiot
text: “Now then, where are you taking my cloak to? Ha, ha, ha! Are you mad?”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince turned and came back, more confused than ever.

title: The Idiot
text: When she burst out laughing, he smiled, but his tongue could not form a word as yet.

title: The Idiot
text: At first, when he had opened the door and saw her standing before him, he had become as pale as death; but now the red blood had rushed back to his cheeks in a torrent.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why, what an idiot it is!” cried Nastasia, stamping her foot with irritation.

title: The Idiot
text: “Go on, do! Whom are you going to announce?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Nastasia Philipovna,” murmured the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “And how do you know that?” she asked him, sharply.

title: The Idiot
text: “I have never seen you before!”

title: The Idiot
text: “Go on, announce me—what’s that noise?”

title: The Idiot
text: “They are quarrelling,” said the prince, and entered the drawing-room, just as matters in there had almost reached a crisis.

title: The Idiot
text: Nina Alexandrovna had forgotten that she had “submitted to everything!

title: The Idiot
text: She was defending Varia.

title: The Idiot
text: Ptitsin was taking her part, too.

title: The Idiot
text: Not that Varia was afraid of standing up for herself.

title: The Idiot
text: She was by no means that sort of a girl; but her brother was becoming ruder and more intolerable every moment.

title: The Idiot
text: Her usual practice in such cases as the present was to say nothing, but stare at him, without taking her eyes off his face for an instant.

title: The Idiot
text: This manoeuvre, as she well knew, could drive Gania distracted.

title: The Idiot
text: Just at this moment the door opened and the prince entered, announcing:

title: The Idiot
text: “Nastasia Philipovna!”

title: The Idiot
text: Silence immediately fell on the room; all looked at the prince as though they neither understood, nor hoped to understand.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania was motionless with horror.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia’s arrival was a most unexpected and overwhelming event to all parties.

title: The Idiot
text: In the first place, she had never been before.

title: The Idiot
text: Up to now she had been so haughty that she had never even asked Gania to introduce her to his parents.

title: The Idiot
text: Of late she had not so much as mentioned them.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania was partly glad of this; but still he had put it to her debit in the account to be settled after marriage.

title: The Idiot
text: He would have borne anything from her rather than this visit.

title: The Idiot
text: But one thing seemed to him quite clear—her visit now, and the present of her portrait on this particular day, pointed out plainly enough which way she intended to make her decision!

title: The Idiot
text: The incredulous amazement with which all regarded the prince did not last long, for Nastasia herself appeared at the door and passed in, pushing by the prince again.

title: The Idiot
text: “At last I’ve stormed the citadel! Why do you tie up your bell?” she said, merrily, as she pressed Gania’s hand, the latter having rushed up to her as soon as she made her appearance.

title: The Idiot
text: “What are you looking so upset about? Introduce me, please!”

title: The Idiot
text: The bewildered Gania introduced her first to Varia, and both women, before shaking hands, exchanged looks of strange import.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia, however, smiled amiably; but Varia did not try to look amiable, and kept her gloomy expression.

title: The Idiot
text: She did not even vouchsafe the usual courteous smile of etiquette.

title: The Idiot
text: Gania darted a terrible glance of wrath at her for this, but Nina Alexandrovna mended matters a little when Gania introduced her at last.

title: The Idiot
text: Hardly, however, had the old lady begun about her “highly gratified feelings,” and so on, when Nastasia left her, and flounced into a chair by Gania’s side in the corner by the window, and cried: “Where’s your study? and where are the—the lodgers? You do take in lodgers, don’t you?”

title: The Idiot
text: Gania looked dreadfully put out, and tried to say something in reply, but Nastasia interrupted him:

title: The Idiot
text: “Why, where are you going to squeeze lodgers in here? Don’t you use a study? Does this sort of thing pay?” she added, turning to Nina Alexandrovna.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, it is troublesome, rather,” said the latter; “but I suppose it will ‘pay’ pretty well. We have only just begun, however—”

title: The Idiot
text: Again Nastasia Philipovna did not hear the sentence out.

title: The Idiot
text: She glanced at Gania, and cried, laughing, “What a face! My goodness, what a face you have on at this moment!”

title: The Idiot
text: Indeed, Gania did not look in the least like himself.

title: The Idiot
text: His bewilderment and his alarmed perplexity passed off, however, and his lips now twitched with rage as he continued to stare evilly at his laughing guest, while his countenance became absolutely livid.

title: The Idiot
text: There was another witness, who, though standing at the door motionless and bewildered himself, still managed to remark Gania’s death-like pallor, and the dreadful change that had come over his face.

title: The Idiot
text: This witness was the prince, who now advanced in alarm and muttered to Gania:

title: The Idiot
text: “Drink some water, and don’t look like that!”

title: The Idiot
text: It was clear that he came out with these words quite spontaneously, on the spur of the moment.

title: The Idiot
text: But his speech was productive of much—for it appeared that all Gania’s rage now overflowed upon the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: He seized him by the shoulder and gazed with an intensity of loathing and revenge at him, but said nothing—as though his feelings were too strong to permit of words.

title: The Idiot
text: General agitation prevailed.

title: The Idiot
text: Nina Alexandrovna gave a little cry of anxiety; Ptitsin took a step forward in alarm; Colia and Ferdishenko stood stock still at the door in amazement;—only Varia remained coolly watching the scene from under her eyelashes.

title: The Idiot
text: She did not sit down, but stood by her mother with folded hands.

title: The Idiot
text: However, Gania recollected himself almost immediately.

title: The Idiot
text: He let go of the prince and burst out laughing.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why, are you a doctor, prince, or what?” he asked, as naturally as possible.

title: The Idiot
text: “I declare you quite frightened me! Nastasia Philipovna, let me introduce this interesting character to you—though I have only known him myself since the morning.”

title: The Idiot
