title: The Idiot
text: “Hippolyte,” said the prince, “give me the papers, and go to bed like a sensible fellow. We’ll have a good talk tomorrow, but you really mustn’t go on with this reading; it is not good for you!”

title: The Idiot
text: “How can I? How can I?” cried Hippolyte, looking at him in amazement.

title: The Idiot
text: “Gentlemen! I was a fool! I won’t break off again. Listen, everyone who wants to!”

title: The Idiot
text: He gulped down some water out of a glass standing near, bent over the table, in order to hide his face from the audience, and recommenced.

title: The Idiot
text: “The idea that it is not worth while living for a few weeks took possession of me a month ago, when I was told that I had four weeks to live, but only partially so at that time.

title: The Idiot
text: The idea quite overmastered me three days since, that evening at Pavlofsk.

title: The Idiot
text: The first time that I felt really impressed with this thought was on the terrace at the prince’s, at the very moment when I had taken it into my head to make a last trial of life.

title: The Idiot
text: I wanted to see people and trees (I believe I said so myself), I got excited, I maintained Burdovsky’s rights, ‘my neighbour!’—I dreamt that one and all would open their arms, and embrace me, that there would be an indescribable exchange of forgiveness between us all!

title: The Idiot
text: In a word, I behaved like a fool, and then, at that very same instant, I felt my ‘last conviction.

title: The Idiot
text: I ask myself now how I could have waited six months for that conviction!

title: The Idiot
text: I knew that I had a disease that spares no one, and I really had no illusions; but the more I realized my condition, the more I clung to life; I wanted to live at any price.

title: The Idiot
text: I confess I might well have resented that blind, deaf fate, which, with no apparent reason, seemed to have decided to crush me like a fly; but why did I not stop at resentment?

title: The Idiot
text: Why did I begin to live, knowing that it was not worthwhile to begin?

title: The Idiot
text: Why did I attempt to do what I knew to be an impossibility?

title: The Idiot
text: And yet I could not even read a book to the end; I had given up reading.

title: The Idiot
text: What is the good of reading, what is the good of learning anything, for just six months?

title: The Idiot
text: That thought has made me throw aside a book more than once.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, that wall of Meyer’s could tell a tale if it liked.

title: The Idiot
text: There was no spot on its dirty surface that I did not know by heart.

title: The Idiot
text: Accursed wall! and yet it is dearer to me than all the Pavlofsk trees!

title: The Idiot
text: —That is—it would be dearer if it were not all the same to me, now!

title: The Idiot
text: “I remember now with what hungry interest I began to watch the lives of other people—interest that I had never felt before!

title: The Idiot
text: I used to wait for Colia’s arrival impatiently, for I was so ill myself, then, that I could not leave the house.

title: The Idiot
text: I so threw myself into every little detail of news, and took so much interest in every report and rumour, that I believe I became a regular gossip!

title: The Idiot
text: I could not understand, among other things, how all these people—with so much life in and before them—do not become rich—and I don’t understand it now.

title: The Idiot
text: I remember being told of a poor wretch I once knew, who had died of hunger.

title: The Idiot
text: I was almost beside myself with rage!

title: The Idiot
text: I believe if I could have resuscitated him I would have done so for the sole purpose of murdering him!

title: The Idiot
text: “Occasionally I was so much better that I could go out; but the streets used to put me in such a rage that I would lock myself up for days rather than go out, even if I were well enough to do so!

title: The Idiot
text: I could not bear to see all those preoccupied, anxious-looking creatures continuously surging along the streets past me!

title: The Idiot
text: Why are they always anxious?

title: The Idiot
text: What is the meaning of their eternal care and worry?

title: The Idiot
text: It is their wickedness, their perpetual detestable malice—that’s what it is—they are all full of malice, malice!

title: The Idiot
text: “Whose fault is it that they are all miserable, that they don’t know how to live, though they have fifty or sixty years of life before them?

title: The Idiot
text: Why did that fool allow himself to die of hunger with sixty years of unlived life before him?

title: The Idiot
text: “And everyone of them shows his rags, his toil-worn hands, and yells in his wrath: ‘Here are we, working like cattle all our lives, and always as hungry as dogs, and there are others who do not work, and are fat and rich! The eternal refrain! And side by side with them trots along some wretched fellow who has known better days, doing light porter’s work from morn to night for a living, always blubbering and saying that ‘his wife died because he had no money to buy medicine with,’ and his children dying of cold and hunger, and his eldest daughter gone to the bad, and so on.

title: The Idiot
text: Oh!

title: The Idiot
text: I have no pity and no patience for these fools of people.

title: The Idiot
text: Why can’t they be Rothschilds?

title: The Idiot
text: Whose fault is it that a man has not got millions of money like Rothschild?

title: The Idiot
text: If he has life, all this must be in his power!

title: The Idiot
text: Whose fault is it that he does not know how to live his life?

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh! it’s all the same to me now—now!

title: The Idiot
text: But at that time I would soak my pillow at night with tears of mortification, and tear at my blanket in my rage and fury.

title: The Idiot
text: Oh, how I longed at that time to be turned out—me, eighteen years old, poor, half-clothed, turned out into the street, quite alone, without lodging, without work, without a crust of bread, without relations, without a single acquaintance, in some large town—hungry, beaten (if you like), but in good health—and then I would show them—

title: The Idiot
text: “What would I show them?

title: The Idiot
text: “Oh, don’t think that I have no sense of my own humiliation!

title: The Idiot
text: I have suffered already in reading so far.

title: The Idiot
text: Which of you all does not think me a fool at this moment—a young fool who knows nothing of life—forgetting that to live as I have lived these last six months is to live longer than grey-haired old men.

title: The Idiot
text: Well, let them laugh, and say it is all nonsense, if they please.

title: The Idiot
text: They may say it is all fairy-tales, if they like; and I have spent whole nights telling myself fairy-tales.

title: The Idiot
text: I remember them all.

title: The Idiot
text: But how can I tell fairy-tales now?

title: The Idiot
text: The time for them is over.

title: The Idiot
text: They amused me when I found that there was not even time for me to learn the Greek grammar, as I wanted to do.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘I shall die before I get to the syntax,’ I thought at the first page—and threw the book under the table.

title: The Idiot
text: It is there still, for I forbade anyone to pick it up.

title: The Idiot
text: “If this ‘Explanation’ gets into anybody’s hands, and they have patience to read it through, they may consider me a madman, or a schoolboy, or, more likely, a man condemned to die, who thought it only natural to conclude that all men, excepting himself, esteem life far too lightly, live it far too carelessly and lazily, and are, therefore, one and all, unworthy of it.

title: The Idiot
text: Well, I affirm that my reader is wrong again, for my convictions have nothing to do with my sentence of death.

title: The Idiot
text: Ask them, ask any one of them, or all of them, what they mean by happiness!

title: The Idiot
text: Oh, you may be perfectly sure that if Columbus was happy, it was not after he had discovered America, but when he was discovering it!

title: The Idiot
text: You may be quite sure that he reached the culminating point of his happiness three days before he saw the New World with his actual eyes, when his mutinous sailors wanted to tack about, and return to Europe!

title: The Idiot
text: What did the New World matter after all?

title: The Idiot
text: Columbus had hardly seen it when he died, and in reality he was entirely ignorant of what he had discovered.

title: The Idiot
text: The important thing is life—life and nothing else!

title: The Idiot
text: What is any ‘discovery’ whatever compared with the incessant, eternal discovery of life?

title: The Idiot
text: “But what is the use of talking?

title: The Idiot
text: I’m afraid all this is so commonplace that my confession will be taken for a schoolboy exercise—the work of some ambitious lad writing in the hope of his work ‘seeing the light’; or perhaps my readers will say that ‘I had perhaps something to say, but did not know how to express it.’

title: The Idiot
text: “Let me add to this that in every idea emanating from genius, or even in every serious human idea—born in the human brain—there always remains something—some sediment—which cannot be expressed to others, though one wrote volumes and lectured upon it for five-and-thirty years.

title: The Idiot
text: There is always a something, a remnant, which will never come out from your brain, but will remain there with you, and you alone, for ever and ever, and you will die, perhaps, without having imparted what may be the very essence of your idea to a single living soul.

title: The Idiot
text: “So that if I cannot now impart all that has tormented me for the last six months, at all events you will understand that, having reached my ‘last convictions,’ I must have paid a very dear price for them.

title: The Idiot
text: That is what I wished, for reasons of my own, to make a point of in this my ‘Explanation.’

title: The Idiot
text: “But let me resume.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I will not deceive you.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘Reality’ got me so entrapped in its meshes now and again during the past six months, that I forgot my ‘sentence’ (or perhaps I did not wish to think of it), and actually busied myself with affairs.

title: The Idiot
text: “A word as to my circumstances.

title: The Idiot
text: When, eight months since, I became very ill, I threw up all my old connections and dropped all my old companions.

title: The Idiot
text: As I was always a gloomy, morose sort of individual, my friends easily forgot me; of course, they would have forgotten me all the same, without that excuse.

title: The Idiot
text: My position at home was solitary enough.

title: The Idiot
text: Five months ago I separated myself entirely from the family, and no one dared enter my room except at stated times, to clean and tidy it, and so on, and to bring me my meals.

title: The Idiot
text: My mother dared not disobey me; she kept the children quiet, for my sake, and beat them if they dared to make any noise and disturb me. I so often complained of them that I should think they must be very fond, indeed, of me by this time.

title: The Idiot
text: I think I must have tormented ‘my faithful Colia’ (as I called him) a good deal too.

title: The Idiot
text: He tormented me of late; I could see that he always bore my tempers as though he had determined to ‘spare the poor invalid. This annoyed me, naturally. He seemed to have taken it into his head to imitate the prince in Christian meekness! Surikoff, who lived above us, annoyed me, too. He was so miserably poor, and I used to prove to him that he had no one to blame but himself for his poverty. I used to be so angry that I think I frightened him eventually, for he stopped coming to see me. He was a most meek and humble fellow, was Surikoff. (N.B.—They say that meekness is a great power. I must ask the prince about this, for the expression is his.) But I remember one day in March, when I went up to his lodgings to see whether it was true that one of his children had been starved and frozen to death, I began to hold forth to him about his poverty being his own fault, and, in the course of my remarks, I accidentally smiled at the corpse of his child. Well, the poor wretch’s lips began to tremble, and he caught me by the shoulder, and pushed me to the door. ‘Go out,’ he said, in a whisper.

title: The Idiot
text: I went out, of course, and I declare I liked it.

title: The Idiot
text: I liked it at the very moment when I was turned out.

title: The Idiot
text: But his words filled me with a strange sort of feeling of disdainful pity for him whenever I thought of them—a feeling which I did not in the least desire to entertain.

title: The Idiot
text: At the very moment of the insult (for I admit that I did insult him, though I did not mean to), this man could not lose his temper.

title: The Idiot
text: His lips had trembled, but I swear it was not with rage.

title: The Idiot
text: He had taken me by the arm, and said, ‘Go out,’ without the least anger.

title: The Idiot
text: There was dignity, a great deal of dignity, about him, and it was so inconsistent with the look of him that, I assure you, it was quite comical.

title: The Idiot
text: But there was no anger.

title: The Idiot
text: Perhaps he merely began to despise me at that moment.

title: The Idiot
text: “Since that time he has always taken off his hat to me on the stairs, whenever I met him, which is a thing he never did before; but he always gets away from me as quickly as he can, as though he felt confused.

title: The Idiot
text: If he did despise me, he despised me ‘meekly,’ after his own fashion.

title: The Idiot
text: “I dare say he only took his hat off out of fear, as it were, to the son of his creditor; for he always owed my mother money.

title: The Idiot
text: I thought of having an explanation with him, but I knew that if I did, he would begin to apologize in a minute or two, so I decided to let him alone.

title: The Idiot
text: “Just about that time, that is, the middle of March, I suddenly felt very much better; this continued for a couple of weeks.

title: The Idiot
text: I used to go out at dusk.

title: The Idiot
text: I like the dusk, especially in March, when the night frost begins to harden the day’s puddles, and the gas is burning.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, one night in the Shestilavochnaya, a man passed me with a paper parcel under his arm.

title: The Idiot
text: I did not take stock of him very carefully, but he seemed to be dressed in some shabby summer dust-coat, much too light for the season.

title: The Idiot
text: When he was opposite the lamp-post, some ten yards away, I observed something fall out of his pocket.

title: The Idiot
text: I hurried forward to pick it up, just in time, for an old wretch in a long kaftan rushed up too.

title: The Idiot
text: He did not dispute the matter, but glanced at what was in my hand and disappeared.

title: The Idiot
text: “It was a large old-fashioned pocket-book, stuffed full; but I guessed, at a glance, that it had anything in the world inside it, except money.

title: The Idiot
text: “The owner was now some forty yards ahead of me, and was very soon lost in the crowd.

title: The Idiot
text: I ran after him, and began calling out; but as I knew nothing to say excepting ‘hey!’ he did not turn round.

title: The Idiot
text: Suddenly he turned into the gate of a house to the left; and when I darted in after him, the gateway was so dark that I could see nothing whatever.

title: The Idiot
text: It was one of those large houses built in small tenements, of which there must have been at least a hundred.

title: The Idiot
text: “When I entered the yard I thought I saw a man going along on the far side of it; but it was so dark I could not make out his figure.

title: The Idiot
text: “I crossed to that corner and found a dirty dark staircase.

title: The Idiot
text: I heard a man mounting up above me, some way higher than I was, and thinking I should catch him before his door would be opened to him, I rushed after him.

title: The Idiot
text: I heard a door open and shut on the fifth storey, as I panted along; the stairs were narrow, and the steps innumerable, but at last I reached the door I thought the right one.

title: The Idiot
text: Some moments passed before I found the bell and got it to ring.

title: The Idiot
text: “An old peasant woman opened the door; she was busy lighting the ‘samovar’ in a tiny kitchen.

title: The Idiot
text: She listened silently to my questions, did not understand a word, of course, and opened another door leading into a little bit of a room, low and scarcely furnished at all, but with a large, wide bed in it, hung with curtains.

title: The Idiot
text: On this bed lay one Terentich, as the woman called him, drunk, it appeared to me.

title: The Idiot
text: On the table was an end of candle in an iron candlestick, and a half-bottle of vodka, nearly finished.

title: The Idiot
text: Terentich muttered something to me, and signed towards the next room.

title: The Idiot
text: The old woman had disappeared, so there was nothing for me to do but to open the door indicated.

title: The Idiot
text: I did so, and entered the next room.

title: The Idiot
text: “This was still smaller than the other, so cramped that I could scarcely turn round; a narrow single bed at one side took up nearly all the room.

title: The Idiot
text: Besides the bed there were only three common chairs, and a wretched old kitchen-table standing before a small sofa.

title: The Idiot
text: One could hardly squeeze through between the table and the bed.

title: The Idiot
text: “On the table, as in the other room, burned a tallow candle-end in an iron candlestick; and on the bed there whined a baby of scarcely three weeks old.

title: The Idiot
text: A pale-looking woman was dressing the child, probably the mother; she looked as though she had not as yet got over the trouble of childbirth, she seemed so weak and was so carelessly dressed.

title: The Idiot
text: Another child, a little girl of about three years old, lay on the sofa, covered over with what looked like a man’s old dress-coat.

title: The Idiot
text: “At the table stood a man in his shirt sleeves; he had thrown off his coat; it lay upon the bed; and he was unfolding a blue paper parcel in which were a couple of pounds of bread, and some little sausages.

title: The Idiot
text: “On the table along with these things were a few old bits of black bread, and some tea in a pot.

title: The Idiot
text: From under the bed there protruded an open portmanteau full of bundles of rags.

title: The Idiot
text: In a word, the confusion and untidiness of the room were indescribable.

title: The Idiot
text: “It appeared to me, at the first glance, that both the man and the woman were respectable people, but brought to that pitch of poverty where untidiness seems to get the better of every effort to cope with it, till at last they take a sort of bitter satisfaction in it.

title: The Idiot
text: When I entered the room, the man, who had entered but a moment before me, and was still unpacking his parcels, was saying something to his wife in an excited manner.

title: The Idiot
text: The news was apparently bad, as usual, for the woman began whimpering.

title: The Idiot
text: The man’s face seemed to me to be refined and even pleasant.

title: The Idiot
text: He was dark-complexioned, and about twenty-eight years of age; he wore black whiskers, and his lip and chin were shaved.

title: The Idiot
text: He looked morose, but with a sort of pride of expression.

title: The Idiot
text: A curious scene followed.

title: The Idiot
text: “There are people who find satisfaction in their own touchy feelings, especially when they have just taken the deepest offence; at such moments they feel that they would rather be offended than not.

title: The Idiot
text: These easily-ignited natures, if they are wise, are always full of remorse afterwards, when they reflect that they have been ten times as angry as they need have been.

title: The Idiot
text: “The gentleman before me gazed at me for some seconds in amazement, and his wife in terror; as though there was something alarmingly extraordinary in the fact that anyone could come to see them.

title: The Idiot
text: But suddenly he fell upon me almost with fury; I had had no time to mutter more than a couple of words; but he had doubtless observed that I was decently dressed and, therefore, took deep offence because I had dared enter his den so unceremoniously, and spy out the squalor and untidiness of it.

title: The Idiot
text: “Of course he was delighted to get hold of someone upon whom to vent his rage against things in general.

title: The Idiot
text: “For a moment I thought he would assault me; he grew so pale that he looked like a woman about to have hysterics; his wife was dreadfully alarmed.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘How dare you come in so?

title: The Idiot
text: Be off!

title: The Idiot
text: ’ he shouted, trembling all over with rage and scarcely able to articulate the words.

title: The Idiot
text: Suddenly, however, he observed his pocketbook in my hand.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘I think you dropped this,’ I remarked, as quietly and drily as I could.

title: The Idiot
text: (I thought it best to treat him so.)

title: The Idiot
text: For some while he stood before me in downright terror, and seemed unable to understand.

title: The Idiot
text: He then suddenly grabbed at his side-pocket, opened his mouth in alarm, and beat his forehead with his hand.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘My God!

title: The Idiot
text: ’ he cried, ‘where did you find it?

title: The Idiot
text: How?

title: The Idiot
text: I explained in as few words as I could, and as drily as possible, how I had seen it and picked it up; how I had run after him, and called out to him, and how I had followed him upstairs and groped my way to his door.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘Gracious Heaven!

title: The Idiot
text: ’ he cried, ‘all our papers are in it! My dear sir, you little know what you have done for us. I should have been lost—lost!’

title: The Idiot
text: “I had taken hold of the door-handle meanwhile, intending to leave the room without reply; but I was panting with my run upstairs, and my exhaustion came to a climax in a violent fit of coughing, so bad that I could hardly stand.

title: The Idiot
text: “I saw how the man dashed about the room to find me an empty chair, how he kicked the rags off a chair which was covered up by them, brought it to me, and helped me to sit down; but my cough went on for another three minutes or so.

title: The Idiot
text: When I came to myself he was sitting by me on another chair, which he had also cleared of the rubbish by throwing it all over the floor, and was watching me intently.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘I’m afraid you are ill?

title: The Idiot
text: ’ he remarked, in the tone which doctors use when they address a patient.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘I am myself a medical man’ (he did not say ‘doctor’), with which words he waved his hands towards the room and its contents as though in protest at his present condition.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘I see that you—’

title: The Idiot
text: “‘I’m in consumption,’ I said laconically, rising from my seat.

title: The Idiot
text: “He jumped up, too.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘Perhaps you are exaggerating—if you were to take proper measures perhaps—”

title: The Idiot
text: “He was terribly confused and did not seem able to collect his scattered senses; the pocket-book was still in his left hand.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘Oh, don’t mind me,’ I said.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘Dr. B—— saw me last week’ (I lugged him in again), ‘and my hash is quite settled; pardon me—’ I took hold of the door-handle again.

title: The Idiot
text: I was on the point of opening the door and leaving my grateful but confused medical friend to himself and his shame, when my damnable cough got hold of me again.

title: The Idiot
text: “My doctor insisted on my sitting down again to get my breath.

title: The Idiot
text: He now said something to his wife who, without leaving her place, addressed a few words of gratitude and courtesy to me.

title: The Idiot
text: She seemed very shy over it, and her sickly face flushed up with confusion.

title: The Idiot
text: I remained, but with the air of a man who knows he is intruding and is anxious to get away.

title: The Idiot
text: The doctor’s remorse at last seemed to need a vent, I could see.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘If I—’ he began, breaking off abruptly every other moment, and starting another sentence.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘I—I am so very grateful to you, and I am so much to blame in your eyes, I feel sure, I—you see—’ (he pointed to the room again) ‘at this moment I am in such a position—’

title: The Idiot
text: “‘Oh!

title: The Idiot
text: I said, ‘there’s nothing to see; it’s quite a clear case—you’ve lost your post and have come up to make explanations and get another, if you can!’

title: The Idiot
text: “‘How do you know that?

title: The Idiot
text: ’ he asked in amazement.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘Oh, it was evident at the first glance,’ I said ironically, but not intentionally so.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘There are lots of people who come up from the provinces full of hope, and run about town, and have to live as best they can.’

title: The Idiot
text: “He began to talk at once excitedly and with trembling lips; he began complaining and telling me his story.

title: The Idiot
text: He interested me, I confess; I sat there nearly an hour.

title: The Idiot
text: His story was a very ordinary one.

title: The Idiot
text: He had been a provincial doctor; he had a civil appointment, and had no sooner taken it up than intrigues began.

title: The Idiot
text: Even his wife was dragged into these.

title: The Idiot
text: He was proud, and flew into a passion; there was a change of local government which acted in favour of his opponents; his position was undermined, complaints were made against him; he lost his post and came up to Petersburg with his last remaining money, in order to appeal to higher authorities.

title: The Idiot
text: Of course nobody would listen to him for a long time; he would come and tell his story one day and be refused promptly; another day he would be fed on false promises; again he would be treated harshly; then he would be told to sign some documents; then he would sign the paper and hand it in, and they would refuse to receive it, and tell him to file a formal petition.

title: The Idiot
text: In a word he had been driven about from office to office for five months and had spent every farthing he had; his wife’s last rags had just been pawned; and meanwhile a child had been born to them and—and today I have a final refusal to my petition, and I have hardly a crumb of bread left—I have nothing left; my wife has had a baby lately—and I—I—’

title: The Idiot
text: “He sprang up from his chair and turned away.

title: The Idiot
text: His wife was crying in the corner; the child had begun to moan again.

title: The Idiot
text: I pulled out my note-book and began writing in it.

title: The Idiot
text: When I had finished and rose from my chair he was standing before me with an expression of alarmed curiosity.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘I have jotted down your name,’ I told him, ‘and all the rest of it—the place you served at, the district, the date, and all. I have a friend, Bachmatoff, whose uncle is a councillor of state and has to do with these matters, one Peter Matveyevitch Bachmatoff.’

title: The Idiot
text: “‘Peter Matveyevitch Bachmatoff!

title: The Idiot
text: ’ he cried, trembling all over with excitement.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘Why, nearly everything depends on that very man!’

title: The Idiot
text: “It is very curious, this story of the medical man, and my visit, and the happy termination to which I contributed by accident!

title: The Idiot
text: Everything fitted in, as in a novel.

title: The Idiot
text: I told the poor people not to put much hope in me, because I was but a poor schoolboy myself—(I am not really, but I humiliated myself as much as possible in order to make them less hopeful)—but that I would go at once to the Vassili Ostroff and see my friend; and that as I knew for certain that his uncle adored him, and was absolutely devoted to him as the last hope and branch of the family, perhaps the old man might do something to oblige his nephew.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘If only they would allow me to explain all to his excellency! If I could but be permitted to tell my tale to him!” he cried, trembling with feverish agitation, and his eyes flashing with excitement.

title: The Idiot
text: I repeated once more that I could not hold out much hope—that it would probably end in smoke, and if I did not turn up next morning they must make up their minds that there was no more to be done in the matter.

title: The Idiot
text: “They showed me out with bows and every kind of respect; they seemed quite beside themselves.

title: The Idiot
text: I shall never forget the expression of their faces!

title: The Idiot
text: “I took a droshky and drove over to the Vassili Ostroff at once.

title: The Idiot
text: For some years I had been at enmity with this young Bachmatoff, at school.

title: The Idiot
text: We considered him an aristocrat; at all events I called him one.

title: The Idiot
text: He used to dress smartly, and always drove to school in a private trap.

title: The Idiot
text: He was a good companion, and was always merry and jolly, sometimes even witty, though he was not very intellectual, in spite of the fact that he was always top of the class; I myself was never top in anything!

title: The Idiot
text: All his companions were very fond of him, excepting myself.

title: The Idiot
text: He had several times during those years come up to me and tried to make friends; but I had always turned sulkily away and refused to have anything to do with him.

title: The Idiot
text: I had not seen him for a whole year now; he was at the university.

title: The Idiot
text: When, at nine o’clock, or so, this evening, I arrived and was shown up to him with great ceremony, he first received me with astonishment, and not too affably, but he soon cheered up, and suddenly gazed intently at me and burst out laughing.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘Why, what on earth can have possessed you to come and see me, Terentieff?

title: The Idiot
text: ’ he cried, with his usual pleasant, sometimes audacious, but never offensive familiarity, which I liked in reality, but for which I also detested him.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘Why what’s the matter?’ he cried in alarm.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘Are you ill?’

title: The Idiot
text: “That confounded cough of mine had come on again; I fell into a chair, and with difficulty recovered my breath.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘It’s all right, it’s only consumption’ I said.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘I have come to you with a petition!’

title: The Idiot
text: “He sat down in amazement, and I lost no time in telling him the medical man’s history; and explained that he, with the influence which he possessed over his uncle, might do some good to the poor fellow.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘I’ll do it—I’ll do it, of course!

title: The Idiot
text: ’ he said.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘I shall attack my uncle about it tomorrow morning, and I’m very glad you told me the story. But how was it that you thought of coming to me about it, Terentieff?’

title: The Idiot
text: “‘So much depends upon your uncle,’ I said.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘And besides we have always been enemies, Bachmatoff; and as you are a generous sort of fellow, I thought you would not refuse my request because I was your enemy!

title: The Idiot
text: I added with irony.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘Like Napoleon going to England, eh?

title: The Idiot
text: ’ cried he, laughing.

title: The Idiot
text: ‘I’ll do it though—of course, and at once, if I can!’ he added, seeing that I rose seriously from my chair at this point.

title: The Idiot
text: “And sure enough the matter ended as satisfactorily as possible.

title: The Idiot
text: A month or so later my medical friend was appointed to another post.

title: The Idiot
text: He got his travelling expenses paid, and something to help him to start life with once more.

title: The Idiot
text: I think Bachmatoff must have persuaded the doctor to accept a loan from himself.

title: The Idiot
text: I saw Bachmatoff two or three times, about this period, the third time being when he gave a farewell dinner to the doctor and his wife before their departure, a champagne dinner.

title: The Idiot
text: “Bachmatoff saw me home after the dinner and we crossed the Nicolai bridge.

title: The Idiot
text: We were both a little drunk.

title: The Idiot
text: He told me of his joy, the joyful feeling of having done a good action; he said that it was all thanks to myself that he could feel this satisfaction; and held forth about the foolishness of the theory that individual charity is useless.

title: The Idiot
text: “I, too, was burning to have my say!

title: The Idiot
text: “‘In Moscow,’ I said, ‘there was an old state counsellor, a civil general, who, all his life, had been in the habit of visiting the prisons and speaking to criminals. Every party of convicts on its way to Siberia knew beforehand that on the Vorobeef Hills the “old general” would pay them a visit.

title: The Idiot
text: He did all he undertook seriously and devotedly.

title: The Idiot
text: He would walk down the rows of the unfortunate prisoners, stop before each individual and ask after his needs—he never sermonized them; he spoke kindly to them—he gave them money; he brought them all sorts of necessaries for the journey, and gave them devotional books, choosing those who could read, under the firm conviction that they would read to those who could not, as they went along.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘He scarcely ever talked about the particular crimes of any of them, but listened if any volunteered information on that point.

title: The Idiot
text: All the convicts were equal for him, and he made no distinction.

title: The Idiot
text: He spoke to all as to brothers, and every one of them looked upon him as a father.

title: The Idiot
text: When he observed among the exiles some poor woman with a child, he would always come forward and fondle the little one, and make it laugh.

title: The Idiot
text: He continued these acts of mercy up to his very death; and by that time all the criminals, all over Russia and Siberia, knew him!

title: The Idiot
text: “‘A man I knew who had been to Siberia and returned, told me that he himself had been a witness of how the very most hardened criminals remembered the old general, though, in point of fact, he could never, of course, have distributed more than a few pence to each member of a party.

title: The Idiot
text: Their recollection of him was not sentimental or particularly devoted.

title: The Idiot
text: Some wretch, for instance, who had been a murderer—cutting the throat of a dozen fellow-creatures, for instance; or stabbing six little children for his own amusement (there have been such men!)—would perhaps, without rhyme or reason, suddenly give a sigh and say, “I wonder whether that old general is alive still!

title: The Idiot
text: Although perhaps he had not thought of mentioning him for a dozen years before!

title: The Idiot
text: How can one say what seed of good may have been dropped into his soul, never to die?

title: The Idiot
text: “I continued in that strain for a long while, pointing out to Bachmatoff how impossible it is to follow up the effects of any isolated good deed one may do, in all its influences and subtle workings upon the heart and after-actions of others.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘And to think that you are to be cut off from life!

title: The Idiot
text: ’ remarked Bachmatoff, in a tone of reproach, as though he would like to find someone to pitch into on my account.

title: The Idiot
text: “We were leaning over the balustrade of the bridge, looking into the Neva at this moment.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘Do you know what has suddenly come into my head?

title: The Idiot
text: ’ said I, suddenly—leaning further and further over the rail.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘Surely not to throw yourself into the river?

title: The Idiot
text: ’ cried Bachmatoff in alarm.

title: The Idiot
text: Perhaps he read my thought in my face.

title: The Idiot
text: “‘No, not yet. At present nothing but the following consideration. You see I have some two or three months left me to live—perhaps four; well, supposing that when I have but a month or two more, I take a fancy for some “good deed” that needs both trouble and time, like this business of our doctor friend, for instance: why, I shall have to give up the idea of it and take to something else—some little good deed, more within my means, eh?

title: The Idiot
text: Isn’t that an amusing idea!

title: The Idiot
text: “Poor Bachmatoff was much impressed—painfully so.

title: The Idiot
text: He took me all the way home; not attempting to console me, but behaving with the greatest delicacy.

title: The Idiot
text: On taking leave he pressed my hand warmly and asked permission to come and see me. I replied that if he came to me as a ‘comforter,’ so to speak (for he would be in that capacity whether he spoke to me in a soothing manner or only kept silence, as I pointed out to him), he would but remind me each time of my approaching death!

title: The Idiot
text: He shrugged his shoulders, but quite agreed with me; and we parted better friends than I had expected.

title: The Idiot
text: “But that evening and that night were sown the first seeds of my ‘last conviction.

title: The Idiot
text: I seized greedily on my new idea; I thirstily drank in all its different aspects (I did not sleep a wink that night!), and the deeper I went into it the more my being seemed to merge itself in it, and the more alarmed I became.

title: The Idiot
text: A dreadful terror came over me at last, and did not leave me all next day.

title: The Idiot
text: “Sometimes, thinking over this, I became quite numb with the terror of it; and I might well have deduced from this fact, that my ‘last conviction’ was eating into my being too fast and too seriously, and would undoubtedly come to its climax before long.

title: The Idiot
text: And for the climax I needed greater determination than I yet possessed.

title: The Idiot
text: “However, within three weeks my determination was taken, owing to a very strange circumstance.

title: The Idiot
text: “Here on my paper, I make a note of all the figures and dates that come into my explanation.

title: The Idiot
text: Of course, it is all the same to me, but just now—and perhaps only at this moment—I desire that all those who are to judge of my action should see clearly out of how logical a sequence of deductions has at length proceeded my ‘last conviction.’

title: The Idiot
text: “I have said above that the determination needed by me for the accomplishment of my final resolve, came to hand not through any sequence of causes, but thanks to a certain strange circumstance which had perhaps no connection whatever with the matter at issue.

title: The Idiot
text: Ten days ago Rogojin called upon me about certain business of his own with which I have nothing to do at present.

title: The Idiot
text: I had never seen Rogojin before, but had often heard about him.

title: The Idiot
text: “I gave him all the information he needed, and he very soon took his departure; so that, since he only came for the purpose of gaining the information, the matter might have been expected to end there.

title: The Idiot
text: “But he interested me too much, and all that day I was under the influence of strange thoughts connected with him, and I determined to return his visit the next day.

title: The Idiot
text: “Rogojin was evidently by no means pleased to see me, and hinted, delicately, that he saw no reason why our acquaintance should continue.

title: The Idiot
text: For all that, however, I spent a very interesting hour, and so, I dare say, did he.

title: The Idiot
text: There was so great a contrast between us that I am sure we must both have felt it; anyhow, I felt it acutely.

title: The Idiot
text: Here was I, with my days numbered, and he, a man in the full vigour of life, living in the present, without the slightest thought for ‘final convictions,’ or numbers, or days, or, in fact, for anything but that which-which—well, which he was mad about, if he will excuse me the expression—as a feeble author who cannot express his ideas properly.

title: The Idiot
text: “In spite of his lack of amiability, I could not help seeing, in Rogojin a man of intellect and sense; and although, perhaps, there was little in the outside world which was of interest to him, still he was clearly a man with eyes to see.

title: The Idiot
text: “I hinted nothing to him about my ‘final conviction,’ but it appeared to me that he had guessed it from my words.

title: The Idiot
text: He remained silent—he is a terribly silent man. I remarked to him, as I rose to depart, that, in spite of the contrast and the wide differences between us two, les extremites se touchent (‘extremes meet,’ as I explained to him in Russian); so that maybe he was not so far from my final conviction as appeared.

title: The Idiot
text: “His only reply to this was a sour grimace.

title: The Idiot
text: He rose and looked for my cap, and placed it in my hand, and led me out of the house—that dreadful gloomy house of his—to all appearances, of course, as though I were leaving of my own accord, and he were simply seeing me to the door out of politeness.

title: The Idiot
text: His house impressed me much; it is like a burial-ground, he seems to like it, which is, however, quite natural.

title: The Idiot
text: Such a full life as he leads is so overflowing with absorbing interests that he has little need of assistance from his surroundings.

title: The Idiot
text: “The visit to Rogojin exhausted me terribly.

title: The Idiot
text: Besides, I had felt ill since the morning; and by evening I was so weak that I took to my bed, and was in high fever at intervals, and even delirious.

title: The Idiot
text: Colia sat with me until eleven o’clock.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yet I remember all he talked about, and every word we said, though whenever my eyes closed for a moment I could picture nothing but the image of Surikoff just in the act of finding a million roubles.

title: The Idiot
text: He could not make up his mind what to do with the money, and tore his hair over it.

title: The Idiot
text: He trembled with fear that somebody would rob him, and at last he decided to bury it in the ground.

title: The Idiot
text: I persuaded him that, instead of putting it all away uselessly underground, he had better melt it down and make a golden coffin out of it for his starved child, and then dig up the little one and put her into the golden coffin.

title: The Idiot
text: Surikoff accepted this suggestion, I thought, with tears of gratitude, and immediately commenced to carry out my design.

title: The Idiot
text: “I thought I spat on the ground and left him in disgust.

title: The Idiot
text: Colia told me, when I quite recovered my senses, that I had not been asleep for a moment, but that I had spoken to him about Surikoff the whole while.

title: The Idiot
text: “At moments I was in a state of dreadful weakness and misery, so that Colia was greatly disturbed when he left me.

title: The Idiot
text: “When I arose to lock the door after him, I suddenly called to mind a picture I had noticed at Rogojin’s in one of his gloomiest rooms, over the door.

title: The Idiot
text: He had pointed it out to me himself as we walked past it, and I believe I must have stood a good five minutes in front of it.

title: The Idiot
text: There was nothing artistic about it, but the picture made me feel strangely uncomfortable.

title: The Idiot
text: It represented Christ just taken down from the cross.

title: The Idiot
text: It seems to me that painters as a rule represent the Saviour, both on the cross and taken down from it, with great beauty still upon His face.

title: The Idiot
text: This marvellous beauty they strive to preserve even in His moments of deepest agony and passion.

title: The Idiot
text: But there was no such beauty in Rogojin’s picture.

title: The Idiot
text: This was the presentment of a poor mangled body which had evidently suffered unbearable anguish even before its crucifixion, full of wounds and bruises, marks of the violence of soldiers and people, and of the bitterness of the moment when He had fallen with the cross—all this combined with the anguish of the actual crucifixion.

title: The Idiot
text: “The face was depicted as though still suffering; as though the body, only just dead, was still almost quivering with agony.

title: The Idiot
