text: Muishkin remembered the doctor’s visit quite well.

title: The Idiot
text: He remembered that Lebedeff had said that he looked ill, and had better see a doctor; and although the prince scouted the idea, Lebedeff had turned up almost immediately with his old friend, explaining that they had just met at the bedside of Hippolyte, who was very ill, and that the doctor had something to tell the prince about the sick man.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince had, of course, at once received him, and had plunged into a conversation about Hippolyte.

title: The Idiot
text: He had given the doctor an account of Hippolyte’s attempted suicide; and had proceeded thereafter to talk of his own malady,—of Switzerland, of Schneider, and so on; and so deeply was the old man interested by the prince’s conversation and his description of Schneider’s system, that he sat on for two hours.

title: The Idiot
text: Muishkin gave him excellent cigars to smoke, and Lebedeff, for his part, regaled him with liqueurs, brought in by Vera, to whom the doctor—a married man and the father of a family—addressed such compliments that she was filled with indignation.

title: The Idiot
text: They parted friends, and, after leaving the prince, the doctor said to Lebedeff: “If all such people were put under restraint, there would be no one left for keepers.

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff then, in tragic tones, told of the approaching marriage, whereupon the other nodded his head and replied that, after all, marriages like that were not so rare; that he had heard that the lady was very fascinating and of extraordinary beauty, which was enough to explain the infatuation of a wealthy man; that, further, thanks to the liberality of Totski and of Rogojin, she possessed—so he had heard—not only money, but pearls, diamonds, shawls, and furniture, and consequently she could not be considered a bad match.

title: The Idiot
text: In brief, it seemed to the doctor that the prince’s choice, far from being a sign of foolishness, denoted, on the contrary, a shrewd, calculating, and practical mind.

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff had been much struck by this point of view, and he terminated his confession by assuring the prince that he was ready, if need be, to shed his very life’s blood for him.

title: The Idiot
text: Hippolyte, too, was a source of some distraction to the prince at this time; he would send for him at any and every hour of the day.

title: The Idiot
text: They lived,—Hippolyte and his mother and the children,—in a small house not far off, and the little ones were happy, if only because they were able to escape from the invalid into the garden.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince had enough to do in keeping the peace between the irritable Hippolyte and his mother, and eventually the former became so malicious and sarcastic on the subject of the approaching wedding, that Muishkin took offence at last, and refused to continue his visits.

title: The Idiot
text: A couple of days later, however, Hippolyte’s mother came with tears in her eyes, and begged the prince to come back, “or he would eat her up bodily. She added that Hippolyte had a great secret to disclose. Of course the prince went. There was no secret, however, unless we reckon certain pantings and agitated glances around (probably all put on) as the invalid begged his visitor to “beware of Rogojin.”

title: The Idiot
text: “He is the sort of man,” he continued, “who won’t give up his object, you know; he is not like you and me, prince—he belongs to quite a different order of beings. If he sets his heart on a thing he won’t be afraid of anything—” and so on.

title: The Idiot
text: Hippolyte was very ill, and looked as though he could not long survive.

title: The Idiot
text: He was tearful at first, but grew more and more sarcastic and malicious as the interview proceeded.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince questioned him in detail as to his hints about Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: He was anxious to seize upon some facts which might confirm Hippolyte’s vague warnings; but there were none; only Hippolyte’s own private impressions and feelings.

title: The Idiot
text: However, the invalid—to his immense satisfaction—ended by seriously alarming the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: At first Muishkin had not cared to make any reply to his sundry questions, and only smiled in response to Hippolyte’s advice to “run for his life—abroad, if necessary. There are Russian priests everywhere, and one can get married all over the world.”

title: The Idiot
text: But it was Hippolyte’s last idea which upset him.

title: The Idiot
text: “What I am really alarmed about, though,” he said, “is Aglaya Ivanovna. Rogojin knows how you love her. Love for love. You took Nastasia Philipovna from him. He will murder Aglaya Ivanovna; for though she is not yours, of course, now, still such an act would pain you,—wouldn’t it?”

title: The Idiot
text: He had attained his end.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince left the house beside himself with terror.

title: The Idiot
text: These warnings about Rogojin were expressed on the day before the wedding.

title: The Idiot
text: That evening the prince saw Nastasia Philipovna for the last time before they were to meet at the altar; but Nastasia was not in a position to give him any comfort or consolation.

title: The Idiot
text: On the contrary, she only added to his mental perturbation as the evening went on.

title: The Idiot
text: Up to this time she had invariably done her best to cheer him—she was afraid of his looking melancholy; she would try singing to him, and telling him every sort of funny story or reminiscence that she could recall.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince nearly always pretended to be amused, whether he were so actually or no; but often enough he laughed sincerely, delighted by the brilliancy of her wit when she was carried away by her narrative, as she very often was.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia would be wild with joy to see the impression she had made, and to hear his laugh of real amusement; and she would remain the whole evening in a state of pride and happiness.

title: The Idiot
text: But this evening her melancholy and thoughtfulness grew with every hour.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince had told Evgenie Pavlovitch with perfect sincerity that he loved Nastasia Philipovna with all his soul.

title: The Idiot
text: In his love for her there was the sort of tenderness one feels for a sick, unhappy child which cannot be left alone.

title: The Idiot
text: He never spoke of his feelings for Nastasia to anyone, not even to herself.

title: The Idiot
text: When they were together they never discussed their “feelings,” and there was nothing in their cheerful, animated conversation which an outsider could not have heard.

title: The Idiot
text: Daria Alexeyevna, with whom Nastasia was staying, told afterwards how she had been filled with joy and delight only to look at them, all this time.

title: The Idiot
text: Thanks to the manner in which he regarded Nastasia’s mental and moral condition, the prince was to some extent freed from other perplexities.

title: The Idiot
text: She was now quite different from the woman he had known three months before.

title: The Idiot
text: He was not astonished, for instance, to see her now so impatient to marry him—she who formerly had wept with rage and hurled curses and reproaches at him if he mentioned marriage!

title: The Idiot
text: “It shows that she no longer fears, as she did then, that she would make me unhappy by marrying me,” he thought.

title: The Idiot
text: And he felt sure that so sudden a change could not be a natural one.

title: The Idiot
text: This rapid growth of self-confidence could not be due only to her hatred for Aglaya.

title: The Idiot
text: To suppose that would be to suspect the depth of her feelings.

title: The Idiot
text: Nor could it arise from dread of the fate that awaited her if she married Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: These causes, indeed, as well as others, might have played a part in it, but the true reason, Muishkin decided, was the one he had long suspected—that the poor sick soul had come to the end of its forces.

title: The Idiot
text: Yet this was an explanation that did not procure him any peace of mind.

title: The Idiot
text: At times he seemed to be making violent efforts to think of nothing, and one would have said that he looked on his marriage as an unimportant formality, and on his future happiness as a thing not worth considering.

title: The Idiot
text: As to conversations such as the one held with Evgenie Pavlovitch, he avoided them as far as possible, feeling that there were certain objections to which he could make no answer.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince had observed that Nastasia knew well enough what Aglaya was to him.

title: The Idiot
text: He never spoke of it, but he had seen her face when she had caught him starting off for the Epanchins’ house on several occasions.

title: The Idiot
text: When the Epanchins left Pavlofsk, she had beamed with radiance and happiness.

title: The Idiot
text: Unsuspicious and unobservant as he was, he had feared at that time that Nastasia might have some scheme in her mind for a scene or scandal which would drive Aglaya out of Pavlofsk.

title: The Idiot
text: She had encouraged the rumours and excitement among the inhabitants of the place as to her marriage with the prince, in order to annoy her rival; and, finding it difficult to meet the Epanchins anywhere, she had, on one occasion, taken him for a drive past their house.

title: The Idiot
text: He did not observe what was happening until they were almost passing the windows, when it was too late to do anything.

title: The Idiot
text: He said nothing, but for two days afterwards he was ill.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia did not try that particular experiment again.

title: The Idiot
text: A few days before that fixed for the wedding, she grew grave and thoughtful.

title: The Idiot
text: She always ended by getting the better of her melancholy, and becoming merry and cheerful again, but not quite so unaffectedly happy as she had been some days earlier.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince redoubled his attentive study of her symptoms.

title: The Idiot
text: It was a most curious circumstance, in his opinion, that she never spoke of Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: But once, about five days before the wedding, when the prince was at home, a messenger arrived begging him to come at once, as Nastasia Philipovna was very ill.

title: The Idiot
text: He had found her in a condition approaching to absolute madness.

title: The Idiot
text: She screamed, and trembled, and cried out that Rogojin was hiding out there in the garden—that she had seen him herself—and that he would murder her in the night—that he would cut her throat.

title: The Idiot
text: She was terribly agitated all day.

title: The Idiot
text: But it so happened that the prince called at Hippolyte’s house later on, and heard from his mother that she had been in town all day, and had there received a visit from Rogojin, who had made inquiries about Pavlofsk.

title: The Idiot
text: On inquiry, it turned out that Rogojin visited the old lady in town at almost the same moment when Nastasia declared that she had seen him in the garden; so that the whole thing turned out to be an illusion on her part.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia immediately went across to Hippolyte’s to inquire more accurately, and returned immensely relieved and comforted.

title: The Idiot
text: On the day before the wedding, the prince left Nastasia in a state of great animation.

title: The Idiot
text: Her wedding-dress and all sorts of finery had just arrived from town.

title: The Idiot
text: Muishkin had not imagined that she would be so excited over it, but he praised everything, and his praise rendered her doubly happy.

title: The Idiot
text: But Nastasia could not hide the cause of her intense interest in her wedding splendour.

title: The Idiot
text: She had heard of the indignation in the town, and knew that some of the populace was getting up a sort of charivari with music, that verses had been composed for the occasion, and that the rest of Pavlofsk society more or less encouraged these preparations.

title: The Idiot
text: So, since attempts were being made to humiliate her, she wanted to hold her head even higher than usual, and to overwhelm them all with the beauty and taste of her toilette.

title: The Idiot
text: “Let them shout and whistle, if they dare!

title: The Idiot
text: Her eyes flashed at the thought.

title: The Idiot
text: But, underneath this, she had another motive, of which she did not speak.

title: The Idiot
text: She thought that possibly Aglaya, or at any rate someone sent by her, would be present incognito at the ceremony, or in the crowd, and she wished to be prepared for this eventuality.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince left her at eleven, full of these thoughts, and went home.

title: The Idiot
text: But it was not twelve o’clock when a messenger came to say that Nastasia was very bad, and he must come at once.

title: The Idiot
text: On hurrying back he found his bride locked up in her own room and could hear her hysterical cries and sobs.

title: The Idiot
text: It was some time before she could be made to hear that the prince had come, and then she opened the door only just sufficiently to let him in, and immediately locked it behind him.

title: The Idiot
text: She then fell on her knees at his feet.

title: The Idiot
text: (So at least Dana Alexeyevna reported.)

title: The Idiot
text: “What am I doing? What am I doing to you?” she sobbed convulsively, embracing his knees.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince was a whole hour soothing and comforting her, and left her, at length, pacified and composed.

title: The Idiot
text: He sent another messenger during the night to inquire after her, and two more next morning.

title: The Idiot
text: The last brought back a message that Nastasia was surrounded by a whole army of dressmakers and maids, and was as happy and as busy as such a beauty should be on her wedding morning, and that there was not a vestige of yesterday’s agitation remaining.

title: The Idiot
text: The message concluded with the news that at the moment of the bearer’s departure there was a great confabulation in progress as to which diamonds were to be worn, and how.

title: The Idiot
text: This message entirely calmed the prince’s mind.

title: The Idiot
text: The following report of the proceedings on the wedding day may be depended upon, as coming from eye-witnesses.

title: The Idiot
text: The wedding was fixed for eight o’clock in the evening.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia Philipovna was ready at seven.

title: The Idiot
text: From six o’clock groups of people began to gather at Nastasia’s house, at the prince’s, and at the church door, but more especially at the former place.

title: The Idiot
text: The church began to fill at seven.

title: The Idiot
text: Colia and Vera Lebedeff were very anxious on the prince’s account, but they were so busy over the arrangements for receiving the guests after the wedding, that they had not much time for the indulgence of personal feelings.

title: The Idiot
text: There were to be very few guests besides the best men and so on; only Dana Alexeyevna, the Ptitsins, Gania, and the doctor.

title: The Idiot
text: When the prince asked Lebedeff why he had invited the doctor, who was almost a stranger, Lebedeff replied:

title: The Idiot
text: “Why, he wears an ‘order,’ and it looks so well!”

title: The Idiot
text: This idea amused the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: Keller and Burdovsky looked wonderfully correct in their dress-coats and white kid gloves, although Keller caused the bridegroom some alarm by his undisguisedly hostile glances at the gathering crowd of sight-seers outside.

title: The Idiot
text: At about half-past seven the prince started for the church in his carriage.

title: The Idiot
text: We may remark here that he seemed anxious not to omit a single one of the recognized customs and traditions observed at weddings.

title: The Idiot
text: He wished all to be done as openly as possible, and “in due order.”

title: The Idiot
text: Arrived at the church, Muishkin, under Keller’s guidance, passed through the crowd of spectators, amid continuous whispering and excited exclamations.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince stayed near the altar, while Keller made off once more to fetch the bride.

title: The Idiot
text: On reaching the gate of Daria Alexeyevna’s house, Keller found a far denser crowd than he had encountered at the prince’s.

title: The Idiot
text: The remarks and exclamations of the spectators here were of so irritating a nature that Keller was very near making them a speech on the impropriety of their conduct, but was luckily caught by Burdovsky, in the act of turning to address them, and hurried indoors.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia Philipovna was ready.

title: The Idiot
text: She rose from her seat, looked into the glass and remarked, as Keller told the tale afterwards, that she was “as pale as a corpse.

title: The Idiot
text: She then bent her head reverently, before the ikon in the corner, and left the room.

title: The Idiot
text: A torrent of voices greeted her appearance at the front door.

title: The Idiot
text: The crowd whistled, clapped its hands, and laughed and shouted; but in a moment or two isolated voices were distinguishable.

title: The Idiot
text: “What a beauty!” cried one.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, she isn’t the first in the world, nor the last,” said another.

title: The Idiot
text: “Marriage covers everything,” observed a third.

title: The Idiot
text: “I defy you to find another beauty like that,” said a fourth.

title: The Idiot
text: “She’s a real princess! I’d sell my soul for such a princess as that!”

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia came out of the house looking as white as any handkerchief; but her large dark eyes shone upon the vulgar crowd like blazing coals.

title: The Idiot
text: The spectators’ cries were redoubled, and became more exultant and triumphant every moment.

title: The Idiot
text: The door of the carriage was open, and Keller had given his hand to the bride to help her in, when suddenly with a loud cry she rushed from him, straight into the surging crowd.

title: The Idiot
text: Her friends about her were stupefied with amazement; the crowd parted as she rushed through it, and suddenly, at a distance of five or six yards from the carriage, appeared Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: It was his look that had caught her eyes.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia rushed to him like a madwoman, and seized both his hands.

title: The Idiot
text: “Save me!” she cried.

title: The Idiot
text: “Take me away, anywhere you like, quick!”

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin seized her in his arms and almost carried her to the carriage.

title: The Idiot
text: Then, in a flash, he tore a hundred-rouble note out of his pocket and held it to the coachman.

title: The Idiot
text: “To the station, quick! If you catch the train you shall have another. Quick!”

title: The Idiot
text: He leaped into the carriage after Nastasia and banged the door.

title: The Idiot
text: The coachman did not hesitate a moment; he whipped up the horses, and they were off.

title: The Idiot
text: “One more second and I should have stopped him,” said Keller, afterwards.

title: The Idiot
text: In fact, he and Burdovsky jumped into another carriage and set off in pursuit; but it struck them as they drove along that it was not much use trying to bring Nastasia back by force.

title: The Idiot
text: “Besides,” said Burdovsky, “the prince would not like it, would he?

title: The Idiot
text: So they gave up the pursuit.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin and Nastasia Philipovna reached the station just in time for the train.

title: The Idiot
text: As he jumped out of the carriage and was almost on the point of entering the train, Rogojin accosted a young girl standing on the platform and wearing an old-fashioned, but respectable-looking, black cloak and a silk handkerchief over her head.

title: The Idiot
text: “Take fifty roubles for your cloak?” he shouted, holding the money out to the girl.

title: The Idiot
text: Before the astonished young woman could collect her scattered senses, he pushed the money into her hand, seized the mantle, and threw it and the handkerchief over Nastasia’s head and shoulders.

title: The Idiot
text: The latter’s wedding-array would have attracted too much attention, and it was not until some time later that the girl understood why her old cloak and kerchief had been bought at such a price.

title: The Idiot
text: The news of what had happened reached the church with extraordinary rapidity.

title: The Idiot
text: When Keller arrived, a host of people whom he did not know thronged around to ask him questions.

title: The Idiot
text: There was much excited talking, and shaking of heads, even some laughter; but no one left the church, all being anxious to observe how the now celebrated bridegroom would take the news.

title: The Idiot
text: He grew very pale upon hearing it, but took it quite quietly.

title: The Idiot
text: “I was afraid,” he muttered, scarcely audibly, “but I hardly thought it would come to this. Then after a short silence, he added: “However, in her state, it is quite consistent with the natural order of things.”

title: The Idiot
text: Even Keller admitted afterwards that this was “extraordinarily philosophical” on the prince’s part.

title: The Idiot
text: He left the church quite calm, to all appearances, as many witnesses were found to declare afterwards.

title: The Idiot
text: He seemed anxious to reach home and be left alone as quickly as possible; but this was not to be.

title: The Idiot
text: He was accompanied by nearly all the invited guests, and besides this, the house was almost besieged by excited bands of people, who insisted upon being allowed to enter the verandah.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince heard Keller and Lebedeff remonstrating and quarrelling with these unknown individuals, and soon went out himself.

title: The Idiot
text: He approached the disturbers of his peace, requested courteously to be told what was desired; then politely putting Lebedeff and Keller aside, he addressed an old gentleman who was standing on the verandah steps at the head of the band of would-be guests, and courteously requested him to honour him with a visit.

title: The Idiot
text: The old fellow was quite taken aback by this, but entered, followed by a few more, who tried to appear at their ease.

title: The Idiot
text: The rest remained outside, and presently the whole crowd was censuring those who had accepted the invitation.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince offered seats to his strange visitors, tea was served, and a general conversation sprang up.

title: The Idiot
text: Everything was done most decorously, to the considerable surprise of the intruders.

title: The Idiot
text: A few tentative attempts were made to turn the conversation to the events of the day, and a few indiscreet questions were asked; but Muishkin replied to everybody with such simplicity and good-humour, and at the same time with so much dignity, and showed such confidence in the good breeding of his guests, that the indiscreet talkers were quickly silenced.

title: The Idiot
text: By degrees the conversation became almost serious.

title: The Idiot
text: One gentleman suddenly exclaimed, with great vehemence: “Whatever happens, I shall not sell my property; I shall wait. Enterprise is better than money, and there, sir, you have my whole system of economy, if you wish! He addressed the prince, who warmly commended his sentiments, though Lebedeff whispered in his ear that this gentleman, who talked so much of his “property,” had never had either house or home.

title: The Idiot
text: Nearly an hour passed thus, and when tea was over the visitors seemed to think that it was time to go.

title: The Idiot
text: As they went out, the doctor and the old gentleman bade Muishkin a warm farewell, and all the rest took their leave with hearty protestations of good-will, dropping remarks to the effect that “it was no use worrying,” and that “perhaps all would turn out for the best,” and so on.

title: The Idiot
text: Some of the younger intruders would have asked for champagne, but they were checked by the older ones.

title: The Idiot
text: When all had departed, Keller leaned over to Lebedeff, and said:

title: The Idiot
text: “With you and me there would have been a scene. We should have shouted and fought, and called in the police. But he has simply made some new friends—and such friends, too! I know them!”

title: The Idiot
text: Lebedeff, who was slightly intoxicated, answered with a sigh:

title: The Idiot
text: “Things are hidden from the wise and prudent, and revealed unto babes. I have applied those words to him before, but now I add that God has preserved the babe himself from the abyss, He and all His saints.”

title: The Idiot
text: At last, about half-past ten, the prince was left alone.

title: The Idiot
text: His head ached.

title: The Idiot
text: Colia was the last to go, after having helped him to change his wedding clothes.

title: The Idiot
text: They parted on affectionate terms, and, without speaking of what had happened, Colia promised to come very early the next day.

title: The Idiot
text: He said later that the prince had given no hint of his intentions when they said good-bye, but had hidden them even from him.

title: The Idiot
text: Soon there was hardly anyone left in the house.

title: The Idiot
text: Burdovsky had gone to see Hippolyte; Keller and Lebedeff had wandered off together somewhere.

title: The Idiot
text: Only Vera Lebedeff remained hurriedly rearranging the furniture in the rooms.

title: The Idiot
text: As she left the verandah, she glanced at the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: He was seated at the table, with both elbows upon it, and his head resting on his hands.

title: The Idiot
text: She approached him, and touched his shoulder gently.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince started and looked at her in perplexity; he seemed to be collecting his senses for a minute or so, before he could remember where he was.

title: The Idiot
text: As recollection dawned upon him, he became violently agitated.

title: The Idiot
text: All he did, however, was to ask Vera very earnestly to knock at his door and awake him in time for the first train to Petersburg next morning.

title: The Idiot
text: Vera promised, and the prince entreated her not to tell anyone of his intention.

title: The Idiot
text: She promised this, too; and at last, when she had half-closed the door, he called her back a third time, took her hands in his, kissed them, then kissed her forehead, and in a rather peculiar manner said to her, “Until tomorrow!”

title: The Idiot
text: Such was Vera’s story afterwards.

title: The Idiot
text: She went away in great anxiety about him, but when she saw him in the morning, he seemed to be quite himself again, greeted her with a smile, and told her that he would very likely be back by the evening.

title: The Idiot
text: It appears that he did not consider it necessary to inform anyone excepting Vera of his departure for town.

title: The Idiot
text: An hour later he was in St. Petersburg, and by ten o’clock he had rung the bell at Rogojin’s.

title: The Idiot
text: He had gone to the front door, and was kept waiting a long while before anyone came.

title: The Idiot
text: At last the door of old Mrs. Rogojin’s flat was opened, and an aged servant appeared.

title: The Idiot
text: “Parfen Semionovitch is not at home,” she announced from the doorway.

title: The Idiot
text: “Whom do you want?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Parfen Semionovitch.”

title: The Idiot
text: “He is not in.”

title: The Idiot
text: The old woman examined the prince from head to foot with great curiosity.

title: The Idiot
text: “At all events tell me whether he slept at home last night, and whether he came alone?”

title: The Idiot
text: The old woman continued to stare at him, but said nothing.

title: The Idiot
text: “Was not Nastasia Philipovna here with him, yesterday evening?”

title: The Idiot
text: “And, pray, who are you yourself?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Prince Lef Nicolaievitch Muishkin; he knows me well.”

title: The Idiot
text: “He is not at home.”

title: The Idiot
text: The woman lowered her eyes.

title: The Idiot
text: “And Nastasia Philipovna?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I know nothing about it.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Stop a minute! When will he come back?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t know that either.”

title: The Idiot
text: The door was shut with these words, and the old woman disappeared.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince decided to come back within an hour.

title: The Idiot
text: Passing out of the house, he met the porter.

title: The Idiot
text: “Is Parfen Semionovitch at home?” he asked.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Why did they tell me he was not at home, then?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Where did they tell you so,—at his door?”

title: The Idiot
text: “No, at his mother’s flat; I rang at Parfen Semionovitch’s door and nobody came.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, he may have gone out. I can’t tell. Sometimes he takes the keys with him, and leaves the rooms empty for two or three days.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Do you know for certain that he was at home last night?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, he was.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Was Nastasia Philipovna with him?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t know; she doesn’t come often. I think I should have known if she had come.”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince went out deep in thought, and walked up and down the pavement for some time.

title: The Idiot
text: The windows of all the rooms occupied by Rogojin were closed, those of his mother’s apartments were open.

title: The Idiot
text: It was a hot, bright day.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince crossed the road in order to have a good look at the windows again; not only were Rogojin’s closed, but the white blinds were all down as well.

title: The Idiot
text: He stood there for a minute and then, suddenly and strangely enough, it seemed to him that a little corner of one of the blinds was lifted, and Rogojin’s face appeared for an instant and then vanished.

title: The Idiot
text: He waited another minute, and decided to go and ring the bell once more; however, he thought better of it again and put it off for an hour.

title: The Idiot
text: The chief object in his mind at this moment was to get as quickly as he could to Nastasia Philipovna’s lodging.

title: The Idiot
text: He remembered that, not long since, when she had left Pavlofsk at his request, he had begged her to put up in town at the house of a respectable widow, who had well-furnished rooms to let, near the Ismailofsky barracks.

title: The Idiot
text: Probably Nastasia had kept the rooms when she came down to Pavlofsk this last time; and most likely she would have spent the night in them, Rogojin having taken her straight there from the station.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince took a droshky.

title: The Idiot
text: It struck him as he drove on that he ought to have begun by coming here, since it was most improbable that Rogojin should have taken Nastasia to his own house last night.

title: The Idiot
text: He remembered that the porter said she very rarely came at all, so that it was still less likely that she would have gone there so late at night.

title: The Idiot
text: Vainly trying to comfort himself with these reflections, the prince reached the Ismailofsky barracks more dead than alive.

title: The Idiot
text: To his consternation the good people at the lodgings had not only heard nothing of Nastasia, but all came out to look at him as if he were a marvel of some sort.

title: The Idiot
text: The whole family, of all ages, surrounded him, and he was begged to enter.

title: The Idiot
text: He guessed at once that they knew perfectly well who he was, and that yesterday ought to have been his wedding-day; and further that they were dying to ask about the wedding, and especially about why he should be here now, inquiring for the woman who in all reasonable human probability might have been expected to be with him in Pavlofsk.

title: The Idiot
text: He satisfied their curiosity, in as few words as possible, with regard to the wedding, but their exclamations and sighs were so numerous and sincere that he was obliged to tell the whole story—in a short form, of course.

title: The Idiot
text: The advice of all these agitated ladies was that the prince should go at once and knock at Rogojin’s until he was let in: and when let in insist upon a substantial explanation of everything.

title: The Idiot
text: If Rogojin was really not at home, the prince was advised to go to a certain house, the address of which was given, where lived a German lady, a friend of Nastasia Philipovna’s.

title: The Idiot
text: It was possible that she might have spent the night there in her anxiety to conceal herself.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince rose from his seat in a condition of mental collapse.

title: The Idiot
text: The good ladies reported afterwards that “his pallor was terrible to see, and his legs seemed to give way underneath him.

title: The Idiot
text: With difficulty he was made to understand that his new friends would be glad of his address, in order to act with him if possible.

title: The Idiot
text: After a moment’s thought he gave the address of the small hotel, on the stairs of which he had had a fit some five weeks since.

title: The Idiot
text: He then set off once more for Rogojin’s.

title: The Idiot
text: This time they neither opened the door at Rogojin’s flat nor at the one opposite.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince found the porter with difficulty, but when found, the man would hardly look at him or answer his questions, pretending to be busy.

title: The Idiot
text: Eventually, however, he was persuaded to reply so far as to state that Rogojin had left the house early in the morning and gone to Pavlofsk, and that he would not return today at all.

title: The Idiot
text: “I shall wait; he may come back this evening.”

title: The Idiot
text: “He may not be home for a week.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Then, at all events, he did sleep here, did he?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well—he did sleep here, yes.”

title: The Idiot
text: All this was suspicious and unsatisfactory.

title: The Idiot
text: Very likely the porter had received new instructions during the interval of the prince’s absence; his manner was so different now.

title: The Idiot
text: He had been obliging—now he was as obstinate and silent as a mule.

title: The Idiot
text: However, the prince decided to call again in a couple of hours, and after that to watch the house, in case of need.

title: The Idiot
text: His hope was that he might yet find Nastasia at the address which he had just received.

title: The Idiot
text: To that address he now set off at full speed.

title: The Idiot
text: But alas! at the German lady’s house they did not even appear to understand what he wanted.

title: The Idiot
text: After a while, by means of certain hints, he was able to gather that Nastasia must have had a quarrel with her friend two or three weeks ago, since which date the latter had neither heard nor seen anything of her.

title: The Idiot
text: He was given to understand that the subject of Nastasia’s present whereabouts was not of the slightest interest to her; and that Nastasia might marry all the princes in the world for all she cared!

title: The Idiot
text: So Muishkin took his leave hurriedly.

title: The Idiot
text: It struck him now that she might have gone away to Moscow just as she had done the last time, and that Rogojin had perhaps gone after her, or even with her.

title: The Idiot
text: If only he could find some trace!

title: The Idiot
text: However, he must take his room at the hotel; and he started off in that direction.

title: The Idiot
text: Having engaged his room, he was asked by the waiter whether he would take dinner; replying mechanically in the affirmative, he sat down and waited; but it was not long before it struck him that dining would delay him.

title: The Idiot
text: Enraged at this idea, he started up, crossed the dark passage (which filled him with horrible impressions and gloomy forebodings), and set out once more for Rogojin’s.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin had not returned, and no one came to the door.

title: The Idiot
text: He rang at the old lady’s door opposite, and was informed that Parfen Semionovitch would not return for three days.

title: The Idiot
text: The curiosity with which the old servant stared at him again impressed the prince disagreeably.

title: The Idiot
text: He could not find the porter this time at all.

title: The Idiot
text: As before, he crossed the street and watched the windows from the other side, walking up and down in anguish of soul for half an hour or so in the stifling heat.

title: The Idiot
text: Nothing stirred; the blinds were motionless; indeed, the prince began to think that the apparition of Rogojin’s face could have been nothing but fancy.

title: The Idiot
text: Soothed by this thought, he drove off once more to his friends at the Ismailofsky barracks.

title: The Idiot
text: He was expected there.

title: The Idiot
text: The mother had already been to three or four places to look for Nastasia, but had not found a trace of any kind.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince said nothing, but entered the room, sat down silently, and stared at them, one after the other, with the air of a man who cannot understand what is being said to him.

title: The Idiot
text: It was strange—one moment he seemed to be so observant, the next so absent; his behaviour struck all the family as most remarkable.

title: The Idiot
text: At length he rose from his seat, and begged to be shown Nastasia’s rooms.

title: The Idiot
text: The ladies reported afterwards how he had examined everything in the apartments.

title: The Idiot
text: He observed an open book on the table, Madam Bovary, and requested the leave of the lady of the house to take it with him.

title: The Idiot
text: He had turned down the leaf at the open page, and pocketed it before they could explain that it was a library book.

title: The Idiot
text: He had then seated himself by the open window, and seeing a card-table, he asked who played cards.

title: The Idiot
text: He was informed that Nastasia used to play with Rogojin every evening, either at “preference” or “little fool,” or “whist”; that this had been their practice since her last return from Pavlofsk; that she had taken to this amusement because she did not like to see Rogojin sitting silent and dull for whole evenings at a time; that the day after Nastasia had made a remark to this effect, Rogojin had whipped a pack of cards out of his pocket.

title: The Idiot
text: Nastasia had laughed, but soon they began playing.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince asked where were the cards, but was told that Rogojin used to bring a new pack every day, and always carried it away in his pocket.

title: The Idiot
text: The good ladies recommended the prince to try knocking at Rogojin’s once more—not at once, but in the evening.

title: The Idiot
text: Meanwhile, the mother would go to Pavlofsk to inquire at Dana Alexeyevna’s whether anything had been heard of Nastasia there.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince was to come back at ten o’clock and meet her, to hear her news and arrange plans for the morrow.

title: The Idiot
text: In spite of the kindly-meant consolations of his new friends, the prince walked to his hotel in inexpressible anguish of spirit, through the hot, dusty streets, aimlessly staring at the faces of those who passed him.

title: The Idiot
text: Arrived at his destination, he determined to rest awhile in his room before he started for Rogojin’s once more.

title: The Idiot
text: He sat down, rested his elbows on the table and his head on his hands, and fell to thinking.

title: The Idiot
text: Heaven knows how long and upon what subjects he thought.

title: The Idiot
text: He thought of many things—of Vera Lebedeff, and of her father; of Hippolyte; of Rogojin himself, first at the funeral, then as he had met him in the park, then, suddenly, as they had met in this very passage, outside, when Rogojin had watched in the darkness and awaited him with uplifted knife.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince remembered his enemy’s eyes as they had glared at him in the darkness.

title: The Idiot
text: He shuddered, as a sudden idea struck him.

title: The Idiot
text: This idea was, that if Rogojin were in Petersburg, though he might hide for a time, yet he was quite sure to come to him—the prince—before long, with either good or evil intentions, but probably with the same intention as on that other occasion.

title: The Idiot
text: At all events, if Rogojin were to come at all he would be sure to seek the prince here—he had no other town address—perhaps in this same corridor; he might well seek him here if he needed him.

title: The Idiot
text: And perhaps he did need him.

title: The Idiot
text: This idea seemed quite natural to the prince, though he could not have explained why he should so suddenly have become necessary to Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin would not come if all were well with him, that was part of the thought; he would come if all were not well; and certainly, undoubtedly, all would not be well with him.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince could not bear this new idea; he took his hat and rushed out towards the street.

title: The Idiot
text: It was almost dark in the passage.

title: The Idiot
text: “What if he were to come out of that corner as I go by and—and stop me?” thought the prince, as he approached the familiar spot.

title: The Idiot
text: But no one came out.

title: The Idiot
text: He passed under the gateway and into the street.

title: The Idiot
text: The crowds of people walking about—as is always the case at sunset in Petersburg, during the summer—surprised him, but he walked on in the direction of Rogojin’s house.

title: The Idiot
text: About fifty yards from the hotel, at the first cross-road, as he passed through the crowd of foot-passengers sauntering along, someone touched his shoulder, and said in a whisper into his ear:

title: The Idiot
text: “Lef Nicolaievitch, my friend, come along with me.

title: The Idiot
text: It was Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince immediately began to tell him, eagerly and joyfully, how he had but the moment before expected to see him in the dark passage of the hotel.

title: The Idiot
text: “I was there,” said Rogojin, unexpectedly.

title: The Idiot
text: “Come along.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince was surprised at this answer; but his astonishment increased a couple of minutes afterwards, when he began to consider it.

title: The Idiot
text: Having thought it over, he glanced at Rogojin in alarm.

title: The Idiot
text: The latter was striding along a yard or so ahead, looking straight in front of him, and mechanically making way for anyone he met.

title: The Idiot
text: “Why did you not ask for me at my room if you were in the hotel?” asked the prince, suddenly.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin stopped and looked at him; then reflected, and replied as though he had not heard the question:

title: The Idiot
text: “Look here, Lef Nicolaievitch, you go straight on to the house; I shall walk on the other side. See that we keep together.”

title: The Idiot
text: So saying, Rogojin crossed the road.

title: The Idiot
text: Arrived on the opposite pavement, he looked back to see whether the prince were moving, waved his hand in the direction of the Gorohovaya, and strode on, looking across every moment to see whether Muishkin understood his instructions.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince supposed that Rogojin desired to look out for someone whom he was afraid to miss; but if so, why had he not told him whom to look out for?

title: The Idiot
text: So the two proceeded for half a mile or so.

title: The Idiot
text: Suddenly the prince began to tremble from some unknown cause.

title: The Idiot
text: He could not bear it, and signalled to Rogojin across the road.

title: The Idiot
text: The latter came at once.

title: The Idiot
text: “Is Nastasia Philipovna at your house?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes.”

title: The Idiot
text: “And was it you looked out of the window under the blind this morning?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Then why did—”

title: The Idiot
text: But the prince could not finish his question; he did not know what to say.

title: The Idiot
text: Besides this, his heart was beating so that he found it difficult to speak at all.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin was silent also and looked at him as before, with an expression of deep thoughtfulness.

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, I’m going,” he said, at last, preparing to recross the road.

title: The Idiot
text: “You go along here as before; we will keep to different sides of the road; it’s better so, you’ll see.”

title: The Idiot
text: When they reached the Gorohovaya, and came near the house, the prince’s legs were trembling so that he could hardly walk.

title: The Idiot
text: It was about ten o’clock.

title: The Idiot
text: The old lady’s windows were open, as before; Rogojin’s were all shut, and in the darkness the white blinds showed whiter than ever.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin and the prince each approached the house on his respective side of the road; Rogojin, who was on the near side, beckoned the prince across.

title: The Idiot
text: He went over to the doorway.

title: The Idiot
text: “Even the porter does not know that I have come home now. I told him, and told them at my mother’s too, that I was off to Pavlofsk,” said Rogojin, with a cunning and almost satisfied smile.

title: The Idiot
text: “We’ll go in quietly and nobody will hear us.”

title: The Idiot
text: He had the key in his hand.

title: The Idiot
text: Mounting the staircase he turned and signalled to the prince to go more softly; he opened the door very quietly, let the prince in, followed him, locked the door behind him, and put the key in his pocket.

title: The Idiot
text: “Come along,” he whispered.

title: The Idiot
text: He had spoken in a whisper all the way.

title: The Idiot
text: In spite of his apparent outward composure, he was evidently in a state of great mental agitation.

title: The Idiot
text: Arrived in a large salon, next to the study, he went to the window and cautiously beckoned the prince up to him.

title: The Idiot
text: “When you rang the bell this morning I thought it must be you. I went to the door on tip-toe and heard you talking to the servant opposite. I had told her before that if anyone came and rang—especially you, and I gave her your name—she was not to tell about me. Then I thought, what if he goes and stands opposite and looks up, or waits about to watch the house? So I came to this very window, looked out, and there you were staring straight at me. That’s how it came about.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Where is Nastasia Philipovna?” asked the prince, breathlessly.

title: The Idiot
text: “She’s here,” replied Rogojin, slowly, after a slight pause.

title: The Idiot
text: “Where?”

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin raised his eyes and gazed intently at the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Come,” he said.

title: The Idiot
text: He continued to speak in a whisper, very deliberately as before, and looked strangely thoughtful and dreamy.

title: The Idiot
text: Even while he told the story of how he had peeped through the blind, he gave the impression of wishing to say something else.

title: The Idiot
text: They entered the study.

title: The Idiot
text: In this room some changes had taken place since the prince last saw it.

title: The Idiot
text: It was now divided into two equal parts by a heavy green silk curtain stretched across it, separating the alcove beyond, where stood Rogojin’s bed, from the rest of the room.

title: The Idiot
text: The heavy curtain was drawn now, and it was very dark.

title: The Idiot
text: The bright Petersburg summer nights were already beginning to close in, and but for the full moon, it would have been difficult to distinguish anything in Rogojin’s dismal room, with the drawn blinds.

title: The Idiot
text: They could just see one anothers faces, however, though not in detail.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin’s face was white, as usual.

title: The Idiot
text: His glittering eyes watched the prince with an intent stare.

title: The Idiot
text: “Had you not better light a candle?” said Muishkin.

title: The Idiot
text: “No, I needn’t,” replied Rogojin, and taking the other by the hand he drew him down to a chair.

title: The Idiot
text: He himself took a chair opposite and drew it up so close that he almost pressed against the prince’s knees.

title: The Idiot
text: At their side was a little round table.

title: The Idiot
text: “Sit down,” said Rogojin; “let’s rest a bit.

title: The Idiot
text: There was silence for a moment.

title: The Idiot
text: “I knew you would be at that hotel,” he continued, just as men sometimes commence a serious conversation by discussing any outside subject before leading up to the main point.

title: The Idiot
text: “As I entered the passage it struck me that perhaps you were sitting and waiting for me, just as I was waiting for you. Have you been to the old lady at Ismailofsky barracks?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes,” said the prince, squeezing the word out with difficulty owing to the dreadful beating of his heart.

title: The Idiot
text: “I thought you would. ‘They’ll talk about it,’ I thought; so I determined to go and fetch you to spend the night here—‘We will be together,’ I thought, ‘for this one night—’”

title: The Idiot
text: “Rogojin, where is Nastasia Philipovna?” said the prince, suddenly rising from his seat.

title: The Idiot
text: He was quaking in all his limbs, and his words came in a scarcely audible whisper.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin rose also.

title: The Idiot
text: “There,” he whispered, nodding his head towards the curtain.

title: The Idiot
text: “Asleep?” whispered the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: Rogojin looked intently at him again, as before.

title: The Idiot
text: “Let’s go in—but you mustn’t—well—let’s go in.”

title: The Idiot
text: He lifted the curtain, paused—and turned to the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “Go in,” he said, motioning him to pass behind the curtain.

title: The Idiot
text: Muishkin went in.

title: The Idiot
text: “It’s so dark,” he said.

title: The Idiot
text: “You can see quite enough,” muttered Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: “I can just see there’s a bed—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Go nearer,” suggested Rogojin, softly.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince took a step forward—then another—and paused.

title: The Idiot
text: He stood and stared for a minute or two.

title: The Idiot
text: Neither of the men spoke a word while at the bedside.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince’s heart beat so loud that its knocking seemed to be distinctly audible in the deathly silence.

title: The Idiot
text: But now his eyes had become so far accustomed to the darkness that he could distinguish the whole of the bed.

title: The Idiot
text: Someone was asleep upon it—in an absolutely motionless sleep.

title: The Idiot
text: Not the slightest movement was perceptible, not the faintest breathing could be heard.

title: The Idiot
text: The sleeper was covered with a white sheet; the outline of the limbs was hardly distinguishable.

title: The Idiot
text: He could only just make out that a human being lay outstretched there.

title: The Idiot
text: All around, on the bed, on a chair beside it, on the floor, were scattered the different portions of a magnificent white silk dress, bits of lace, ribbons and flowers.

title: The Idiot
text: On a small table at the bedside glittered a mass of diamonds, torn off and thrown down anyhow.

title: The Idiot
text: From under a heap of lace at the end of the bed peeped a small white foot, which looked as though it had been chiselled out of marble; it was terribly still.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince gazed and gazed, and felt that the more he gazed the more death-like became the silence.

title: The Idiot
text: Suddenly a fly awoke somewhere, buzzed across the room, and settled on the pillow.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince shuddered.

title: The Idiot
text: “Let’s go,” said Rogojin, touching his shoulder.

title: The Idiot
text: They left the alcove and sat down in the two chairs they had occupied before, opposite to one another.

title: The Idiot
text: The prince trembled more and more violently, and never took his questioning eyes off Rogojin’s face.

title: The Idiot
text: “I see you are shuddering, Lef Nicolaievitch,” said the latter, at length, “almost as you did once in Moscow, before your fit; don’t you remember? I don’t know what I shall do with you—”

title: The Idiot
text: The prince bent forward to listen, putting all the strain he could muster upon his understanding in order to take in what Rogojin said, and continuing to gaze at the latter’s face.

title: The Idiot
text: “Was it you?” he muttered, at last, motioning with his head towards the curtain.

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, it was I,” whispered Rogojin, looking down.

title: The Idiot
text: Neither spoke for five minutes.

title: The Idiot
text: “Because, you know,” Rogojin recommenced, as though continuing a former sentence, “if you were ill now, or had a fit, or screamed, or anything, they might hear it in the yard, or even in the street, and guess that someone was passing the night in the house. They would all come and knock and want to come in, because they know I am not at home. I didn’t light a candle for the same reason. When I am not here—for two or three days at a time, now and then—no one comes in to tidy the house or anything; those are my orders. So that I want them to not know we are spending the night here—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Wait,” interrupted the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “I asked both the porter and the woman whether Nastasia Philipovna had spent last night in the house; so they knew—”

title: The Idiot
text: “I know you asked. I told them that she had called in for ten minutes, and then gone straight back to Pavlofsk. No one knows she slept here. Last night we came in just as carefully as you and I did today. I thought as I came along with her that she would not like to creep in so secretly, but I was quite wrong. She whispered, and walked on tip-toe; she carried her skirt over her arm, so that it shouldn’t rustle, and she held up her finger at me on the stairs, so that I shouldn’t make a noise—it was you she was afraid of. She was mad with terror in the train, and she begged me to bring her to this house. I thought of taking her to her rooms at the Ismailofsky barracks first; but she wouldn’t hear of it. She said, ‘No—not there; he’ll find me out at once there. Take me to your own house, where you can hide me, and tomorrow we’ll set off for Moscow. Thence she would go to Orel, she said. When she went to bed, she was still talking about going to Orel.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Wait! What do you intend to do now, Parfen?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Well, I’m afraid of you. You shudder and tremble so. We’ll pass the night here together. There are no other beds besides that one; but I’ve thought how we’ll manage. I’ll take the cushions off all the sofas, and lay them down on the floor, up against the curtain here—for you and me—so that we shall be together. For if they come in and look about now, you know, they’ll find her, and carry her away, and they’ll be asking me questions, and I shall say I did it, and then they’ll take me away, too, don’t you see? So let her lie close to us—close to you and me.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, yes,” agreed the prince, warmly.

title: The Idiot
text: “So we will not say anything about it, or let them take her away?”

title: The Idiot
text: “Not for anything!” cried the other; “no, no, no!”

title: The Idiot
text: “So I had decided, my friend; not to give her up to anyone,” continued Rogojin.

title: The Idiot
text: “We’ll be very quiet. I have only been out of the house one hour all day, all the rest of the time I have been with her. I dare say the air is very bad here. It is so hot. Do you find it bad?”

title: The Idiot
text: “I don’t know—perhaps—by morning it will be.”

title: The Idiot
text: “I’ve covered her with oilcloth—best American oilcloth, and put the sheet over that, and four jars of disinfectant, on account of the smell—as they did at Moscow—you remember? And she’s lying so still; you shall see, in the morning, when it’s light. What! can’t you get up?” asked Rogojin, seeing the other was trembling so that he could not rise from his seat.

title: The Idiot
text: “My legs won’t move,” said the prince; “it’s fear, I know. When my fear is over, I’ll get up—”

title: The Idiot
text: “Wait a bit—I’ll make the bed, and you can lie down. I’ll lie down, too, and we’ll listen and watch, for I don’t know yet what I shall do... I tell you beforehand, so that you may be ready in case I—”

title: The Idiot
text: Muttering these disconnected words, Rogojin began to make up the beds.

title: The Idiot
text: It was clear that he had devised these beds long before; last night he slept on the sofa.

title: The Idiot
text: But there was no room for two on the sofa, and he seemed anxious that he and the prince should be close to one another; therefore, he now dragged cushions of all sizes and shapes from the sofas, and made a sort of bed of them close by the curtain.

title: The Idiot
text: He then approached the prince, and gently helped him to rise, and led him towards the bed.

title: The Idiot
text: But the prince could now walk by himself, so that his fear must have passed; for all that, however, he continued to shudder.

title: The Idiot
text: “It’s hot weather, you see,” continued Rogojin, as he lay down on the cushions beside Muishkin, “and, naturally, there will be a smell. I daren’t open the window. My mother has some beautiful flowers in pots; they have a delicious scent; I thought of fetching them in, but that old servant will find out, she’s very inquisitive.”

title: The Idiot
text: “Yes, she is inquisitive,” assented the prince.

title: The Idiot
text: “I thought of buying flowers, and putting them all round her; but I was afraid it would make us sad to see her with flowers round her.”

title: The Idiot

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: "I read three pages of it. The two first and the last. And I glanced through the middle as well. But I was always meaning..."

title: The possessed :  or, The devils

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: "I wasn't joking with you then; in persuading you I was perhaps more concerned with myself than with you," Stavrogin pronounced enigmatically.

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: "You weren't joking! title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: "In the first place, I must observe that Kirillov himself told me that he is happy and that he's good. Your supposition that all this was going on at the same time is almost correct. But what of it? I repeat, I was not deceiving either of you."

text: "Are you an atheist? An atheist now?"

text: "I imagine that's a Slavophil idea."

title: The possessed :  or, The devils

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: "Not a single nation," he went on, as though reading it line by line, still gazing menacingly at Stavrogin, "not a single nation has ever been founded on principles of science or reason. There has never been an example of it, except for a brief moment, through folly. Socialism is from its very nature bound to be atheism, seeing that it has from the very first proclaimed that it is an atheistic organisation of society, and that it intends to establish itself exclusively on the elements of science and reason. Science and reason have, from the beginning of time, played a secondary and subordinate part in the life of nations; so it will be till the end of time. Nations are built up and moved by another force which sways and dominates them, the origin of which is unknown and inexplicable: that force is the force of an insatiable desire to go on to the end, though at the same time it denies that end. It is the force of the persistent assertion of one's own existence, and a denial of death. It's the spirit of life, as the Scriptures call it, 'the river of living water,' the drying up of which is threatened in the Apocalypse. It's the æsthetic principle, as the philosophers call it, the ethical principle with which they identify it, 'the seeking for God,' as I call it more simply. The object of every national movement, in every people and at every period of its existence is only the seeking for its god, who must be its own god, and the faith in Him as the only true one. God is the synthetic personality of the whole people, taken from its beginning to its end. It has never happened that all, or even many, peoples have had one common god, but each has always had its own. It's a sign of the decay of nations when they begin to have gods in common. When gods begin to be common to several nations the gods are dying and the faith in them, together with the nations themselves. The stronger a people the more individual their God. There never has been a nation without a religion, that is, without an idea of good and evil. Every people has its own conception of good and evil, and its own good and evil. When the same conceptions of good and evil become prevalent in several nations, then these nations are dying, and then the very distinction between good and evil is beginning to disappear. Reason has never had the power to define good and evil, or even to distinguish between good and evil, even approximately; on the contrary, it has always mixed them up in a disgraceful and pitiful way; science has even given the solution by the fist. This is particularly characteristic of the half-truths of science, the most terrible scourge of humanity, unknown till this century, and worse than plague, famine, or war. A half-truth is a despot... such as has never been in the world before. A despot that has its priests and its slaves, a despot to whom all do homage with love and superstition hitherto inconceivable, before which science itself trembles and cringes in a shameful way. These are your own words, Stavrogin, all except that about the half-truth; that's my own because I am myself a case of half-knowledge, and that's why I hate it particularly. I haven't altered anything of your ideas or even of your words, not a syllable."

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: "I don't agree that you've not altered anything," Stavrogin observed cautiously.

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: "You accepted them with ardour, and in your ardour have transformed them unconsciously. The very fact that you reduce God to a simple attribute of nationality..."

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: He suddenly began watching Shatov with intense and peculiar attention, not so much his words as himself.

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: "I reduce God to the attribute of nationality?" cried Shatov.

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: "On the contrary, I raise the people to God. And has it ever been otherwise? The people is the body of God. Every people is only a people so long as it has its own god and excludes all other gods on earth irreconcilably; so long as it believes that by its god it will conquer and drive out of the world all other gods. Such, from the beginning of time, has been the belief of all great nations, all, anyway, who have been specially remarkable, all who have been leaders of humanity. There is no going against facts. The Jews lived only to await the coming of the true God and left the world the true God. The Greeks deified nature and bequeathed the world their religion, that is, philosophy and art. Rome deified the people in the State, and bequeathed the idea of the State to the nations. France throughout her long history was only the incarnation and development of the Roman god, and if they have at last flung their Roman god into the abyss and plunged into atheism, which, for the time being, they call socialism, it is solely because socialism is, anyway, healthier than Roman Catholicism. If a great people does not believe that the truth is only to be found in itself alone (in itself alone and in it exclusively); if it does not believe that it alone is fit and destined to raise up and save all the rest by its truth, it would at once sink into being ethnographical material, and not a great people. A really great people can never accept a secondary part in the history of Humanity, nor even one of the first, but will have the first part. A nation which loses this belief ceases to be a nation. But there is only one truth, and therefore only a single one out of the nations can have the true God, even though other nations may have great gods of their own. Only one nation is 'god-bearing,' that's the Russian people, and... and... and can you think me such a fool, Stavrogin," he yelled frantically all at once, "that I can't distinguish whether my words at this moment are the rotten old commonplaces that have been ground out in all the Slavophil mills in Moscow, or a perfectly new saying, the last word, the sole word of renewal and resurrection, and... and what do I care for your laughter at this minute! What do I care that you utterly, utterly fail to understand me, not a word, not a sound! Oh, how I despise your haughty laughter and your look at this minute!"

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: He jumped up from his seat; there was positively foam on his lips.

The Russian peasantry is still held together somehow by the Russian God; but according to the latest accounts the Russian God is not to be relied upon, and scarcely survived the emancipation; it certainly gave Him a severe shock. And now, what with railways, what with you... I've no faith in the Russian God."

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: "And how about the European one?"

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: "I don't believe in any. I've been slandered to the youth of Russia. I've always sympathised with every movement among them. I was shown the manifestoes here. Every one looks at them with perplexity because they are frightened at the way things are put in them, but every one is convinced of their power even if they don't admit it to themselves. Everybody has been rolling downhill, and every one has known for ages that they have nothing to clutch at. I am persuaded of the success of this mysterious propaganda, if only because Russia is now pre-eminently the place in all the world where anything you like may happen without any opposition. I understand only too well why wealthy Russians all flock abroad, and more and more so every year. It's simply instinct. If the ship is sinking, the rats are the first to leave it. Holy Russia is a country of wood, of poverty... and of danger, the country of ambitious beggars in its upper classes, while the immense majority live in poky little huts. She will be glad of any way of escape; you have only to present it to her. It's only the government that still means to resist, but it brandishes its cudgel in the dark and hits its own men. Everything here is doomed and awaiting the end. Russia as she is has no future. I have become a German and I am proud of it."

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: "But you began about the manifestoes. Tell me everything; how do you look at them?"

title: The possessed :  or, The devils
text: "Every one is afraid of them, so they must be influential. They openly unmask what is false and prove that there is nothing to lay hold of among us, and nothing to lean upon. They speak aloud while all is silent. What is most effective about them (in spite of their style) is the incredible boldness with which they look the truth straight in the face. To look facts straight in the face is only possible to Russians of this generation. No, in Europe they are not yet so bold; it is a realm of stone, there there is still something to lean upon. So far as I see and am able to judge, the whole essence of the Russian revolutionary idea lies in the negation of honour. I like its being so boldly and fearlessly expressed. No, in Europe they wouldn't understand it yet, but that's just what we shall clutch at. For a Russian a sense of honour is only a superfluous burden, and it always has been a burden through all his history. The open 'right to dishonour' will attract him more than anything. I belong to the older generation and, I must confess, still cling to honour, but only from habit. It is only that I prefer the old forms, granted it's from timidity; you see one must live somehow what's left of one's life."
